translation: — The prince—he's just a formal fiancé, a done deal. My elders told me. Aglaya's agreed; they've even stopped hiding it. (After all, there had been so much secrecy up until now). Adelaide's wedding's been postponed again, so they'll have both ceremonies together, on the same day—what poetry! It's like a poem. Why don't you write a poem about the wedding? Instead of just wandering around the room aimlessly. The Belokskaya family will be here this evening; she just happened to arrive; they'll have guests. They'll introduce him to Belokskaya, though they're already acquainted; they'll probably announce it aloud. They're just afraid he might drop something and break it when he enters the room with guests, or trip over something himself; that's just him.

Every true poet is inevitably Columbus. America existed for centuries before Columbus, but only Columbus managed to find it. The multiplication table existed for centuries before R-13, but only R-13 was able to find the new Eldorado in the virgin thicket of numbers. Indeed, is there any happiness wiser, clearer than in this wondrous world? Steel rusts; the ancient God created an ancient man, i.e., a man capable of making mistakes – and therefore, He himself erred. The multiplication table is wiser, more absolute than the ancient God: it never – understand: never – makes a mistake. And there is no happiness greater than that of the numbers living by the harmonious, eternal laws of the multiplication table. No hesitation, no delusion. Truth is one, and the true path is one; and this truth is two times two, and this true path is four. And wouldn't it be absurd if these happily, ideally multiplied twos were to think about some kind of freedom, i.e., clearly – about a mistake? For me, it is an axiom that R-13 managed to grasp the most fundamental, the most…

Chichikov, in high spirits, sat in his carriage, which had been rolling along the rutted road for some time. From the previous chapter, it is already clear what his main passion and inclinations were, and therefore it is no wonder that he soon immersed himself in them entirely, both in body and soul. The thoughts, estimates, and considerations that danced across his face were clearly very pleasant, for they left traces of a satisfied smirk every minute.  Engrossed in them, he paid no attention to how his coachman, pleased with the reception he had received from Manilov's household, made quite sensible remarks to the shaggy draught horse harnessed on the right. This shaggy horse was quite cunning and only pretended to pull, while the real work was done by the sturdy bay and the brown-grey nag, called "The Session", because it had been purchased from some magistrate, who labored with all his heart, and even in their eyes one could see the pleasure they derived from it. “Cheat, cheat! I'll outwit you!”  Selifan said, lifting himself and cracking the whip at the lazy horse. “You know your job, you German pantaloon! The bay is an honorable horse; he fulfills his duty, and I’ll gladly give him an extra measure, because he is an honorable horse, and The Session is a good horse too… Well, well! What are you shaking your ears at? You fool, listen when they’re speaking! I won’t bother teaching you, you ignoramus! See where you’re crawling!” Here he cracked his whip again, adding: “Oh, barbarian! You’re a cursed Bonaparte!” Then he shouted at all of them: “Hey, my dears!”  — and whipped them all three, not as a punishment, but to show that he was pleased with them. Having delivered such pleasure, he turned back to the shaggy horse: "Do you think you can hide your behavior? No, live honestly, if you want to be shown respect. Take our landowner, for example, we were with good people there. I'd be happy to have a chat if it's a good person; with a good person, we're always our own, close friends; a cup of tea or a snack - with pleasure, if it’s a good person. A good person will be shown respect by everyone. Our master, for example, is respected by everyone because he, you hear, served the state, he's a county counselor…”

No, he didn't consider her a child! Certain looks of hers lately, certain words, terrified him. Sometimes it seemed to him that she was clinging on too tightly, restraining herself too much, and he recalled that this was what frightened him. True, all these days he tried not to think about it, he pushed away the heavy thoughts, but what was hidden in this soul? This question had been tormenting him for a long time, although he believed in this soul. And here it was all about to be resolved, to reveal itself today!  A terrible thought! And again— "this woman"! Why did it always seem to him that this woman would appear at the very last moment and tear apart his entire destiny like a rotting thread? He was now ready to swear to this, even though he was almost delirious. If he had tried to forget about her lately, it was only because he was afraid of her. What was it: did he love this woman or hate her? He hadn't asked himself this question today; his heart was pure: he knew who he loved... He wasn't so afraid of their rendezvous, not the strangeness of it, not the reason for this meeting, which was unknown to him, not its resolution in any way— he was afraid of Nastasya Filippovna herself. He remembered this later, a few days later, that in these feverish hours, almost all the time her eyes, her gaze, her words— strange words, though only a little remained in his memory after those feverish and mournful hours— were before him. He barely remembered, for instance, how Vera had brought him dinner and he had eaten, not remembering whether he had slept after dinner or not? He only knew that he had begun to discern everything clearly that evening only from the moment when Aglaya suddenly entered his study and he jumped up from the sofa and went to meet her in the middle of the room: it was a quarter to eight. Her face was pale, as it had been the day before, but her eyes sparkled with a bright, dry gleam; he had never seen such an expression in her eyes. She looked at him attentively.

He responded that he had already had the good fortune to meet them unexpectedly; he tried to add something else, but it didn't quite come out. The Governess, having said a word or two, finally moved away with her daughter to the other end of the hall to other guests, while Chichikov remained motionless in the same spot, like a person who had happily stepped out onto the street for a stroll, with his eyes ready to take in everything, and suddenly stopped, rooted to the spot, remembering that he had forgotten something, and then there is nothing stupider than such a person: the carefree expression immediately vanishes from his face; he tries to recall what he has forgotten—was it a handkerchief? But the handkerchief is in his pocket; was it money? But the money is also in his pocket, it seems like everything is with him, and yet some unknown spirit whispers in his ears that he has forgotten something. And now he looks around at the moving crowd before him, at the flying carriages, at the caps and muskets of the passing regiment, at the shop sign—and he sees nothing good. And so Chichikov suddenly became a stranger to everything that was happening around him. At this time, numerous hints and questions, imbued with subtlety and amiability, flew from the fragrant lips of the ladies toward him. "Are we, the poor inhabitants of the earth, allowed to be so bold as to ask you what you are dreaming about?"—"Where are those happy places where your thoughts flutter?"—"Can we know the name of the one who has plunged you into this sweet valley of contemplation?" But he responded to all of them with decisive inattention, and the pleasant phrases vanished, like into water. He was even so impolite that he soon left them and went in the other direction, wanting to see where the Governess had gone with her daughter. But the ladies, it seemed, did not want to leave him so soon; each inwardly resolved to use all possible means, so dangerous for our hearts, and to put into play everything that was best. It must be noted that some ladies—I am speaking of some, not all—have a small weakness: if they notice something particularly good on themselves—whether it be their forehead, mouth, or hands—they already think that the best part of their face is the first thing that will catch everyone's eye and that everyone will suddenly begin to speak in unison: "Look, look, what a beautiful Greek nose she has!" or: "What a perfect, charming forehead!" He was even so impolite that he soon left them, moving in another direction, wanting to see where the Governor's wife had gone with her daughter. But the ladies, it seems, did not want to let him go so soon; each internally resolved to use all possible means, so dangerous for our hearts, and to put into action everything that was best. It should be noted that some ladies—I am speaking of some, not all—have a little weakness: if they notice something particularly good about themselves—whether it's their forehead, mouth, or hands—they already think that the best part of their face will be the first to catch everyone's eye, and everyone will suddenly start to say in unison: “Look, look, what a beautiful Greek nose she has!” or: “What a correct, charming forehead!” And whoever has beautiful shoulders is convinced beforehand that all the young men will be completely captivated and will keep repeating, as she passes by: “Ah, what wonderful shoulders this woman has,”—and they won't even look at her face, hair, nose, or forehead, or if they do, it will be as if at something extraneous. That's how some ladies think. Each lady made an inner vow to be as charming as possible in the dances and to show in all their brilliance the superiority of what was best in them. The Postmaster's wife, waltzing, lowered her head to one side with such languor that it seemed something unearthly. One very amiable lady, who had not come at all to dance, because of a slight inconvenience, as she herself expressed it, in the form of a pea on her right foot, which made her have to even wear buckskin boots, could not resist, however, and made several circles in the buckskin boots, just so that the Postmaster's wife would not really take too much to herself.

It was already late evening; the prince still sat, listening and waiting for the general, who had begun countless anecdotes and finished none of them. Upon the prince's arrival, he asked for a new bottle and only after an hour did he finish it, then asked for another, finished that one too. It is to be supposed that in the meantime the general had managed to tell almost his whole story. Finally the prince stood up and said he could wait no longer. The general drained the last drops from the bottle, stood up, and went out of the room, walking very unsteadily. The prince was in despair. He could not understand how he could have so foolishly trusted. In truth, he had never really trusted; he had counted on the general to somehow get him into Nastasya Filippovna's presence, even if it was with some scandal, but he had not counted on such an extraordinary scandal: the general turned out to be quite drunk, in the strongest eloquence, and spoke incessantly, with feeling, with tears in his eyes. It all went on about how, because of the bad behavior of all the members of his family, everything was falling apart and that it was time to finally put an end to it. They finally stepped out onto Liteiny Street. The thaw was still going on; a dreary, warm, rotten wind whistled down the streets, carriages splashed in the mud, horses' hooves rang out on the cobblestones. Pedestrians wandered listlessly and wetly along the sidewalks. Drunken people could be seen here and there.

K. stood stock-still and looked down at the floor. For the moment he was still free, he could still go on and through one of the three small, dark wooden doors, not far in front of him, escape. It would just mean that he hadn't understood, or that he had understood but didn't want to care. If he turned around, however, he would be trapped, for then he would have admitted that he understood well, that he was indeed the one called, and that he wanted to follow. Had the priest called out again, K. would certainly have left, but as everything remained silent as long as K. waited, he turned his head slightly, because he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He stood calmly on the pulpit as before, but it was clearly visible that he had noticed K.'s head movement. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek if K. hadn't now turned completely around. He did so and was beckoned closer by the priest with a flick of his finger. Now that everything could happen openly, he ran - he did it also out of curiosity and to shorten the affair - with long, sweeping strides towards the pulpit. At the first pews he stopped, but the distance seemed too great for the priest; he stretched out his hand and pointed with his sharply lowered index finger to a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. followed suit; he had to bend his head back far to still see the priest. "You are Josef K.," said the priest and raised a hand on the railing in an indefinite movement. "Yes," said K., he thought of how openly he had always pronounced his name, it had been a burden to him for some time now, and even now people he met for the first time knew his name, how nice it was to be introduced first and then to be recognized. "You are accused," said the priest, especially softly. "Yes," said K., "I have been informed of that." "Then you are the one I'm looking for," said the priest. "I am the prison chaplain." "Oh, so," said K. "I called you here," said the priest, "to speak with you." "I didn't know that," said K. "I came here to show a visitor from Italy the cathedral." "Leave the unimportant matters aside," said the priest. "What do you have in your hand? Is it a prayer book?" "No," replied K., "it's an album of the city's sights." "Lay it down," said the priest. K. threw it away so violently that it opened and slid across the floor with crushed pages. "Do you know that your trial is going badly?" asked the priest. "It seems so to me too," said K. It was only a blind error of fortune; they should have gone to P.'s son, and not to me - a product of the whimsical fancy of a frivolous and forgetful P. If I were completely noble, delicate, just, I should have given him half of my entire inheritance; but since I am first and foremost a calculating man and understand too well that this is not a legal matter, I will not give him half of my millions. But, at the very least, it would be too low and shameless (the young man forgot that he wasn’t being calculating) on my part if I did not return now those tens of thousands that went to my idiocy from P., to his son. There was nothing to be done. Kolya, flushed, red, agitated, continued reading in a voice full of excitement: “But while our hasty millionaire was, so to speak, enjoying himself in the heavens, a completely extraneous circumstance occurred. One fine morning, a visitor appeared to him, with a calm and austere face, with polite but worthy and just speech, dressed modestly and nobly, with a visible progressive tinge in his thoughts, and in two words explained the reason for his visit: he was a well-known lawyer; he had been commissioned with a case by a young man; he was there on his behalf. This young man was none other than the son of the late P., though he bore a different name. The voluptuous P., having seduced in his youth an honest, poor girl from the servants’ quarters, but one who had been brought up in an European manner (and, of course, with the baronial rights of his past serfdom mixed in), and having noticed the inevitable, but imminent, consequence of their connection, quickly married her off to a man who was engaged in business and even served in a respectable capacity, a man with a noble character who had long loved this girl. At first, he helped the newlyweds, but soon the goodhearted husband refused his assistance. Some time passed, and P. gradually managed to forget both the girl and the son he had fathered with her, and then, as you know, he died without making a will. Meanwhile, his son, born already in a legal marriage, but raised under another surname and completely adopted by the noble-charactered husband of his mother, nevertheless, having been orphaned by death, was left entirely with his own resources and with a sick, suffering, legless mother in one of the remote provinces; while he himself earned money in the capital through daily honorable work as a teacher of commerce and thus supported himself first at a gymnasium and then as a listener to lectures that were beneficial to him, keeping in mind a future goal. But how much can one get from a Russian merchant for a lesson for a ruble, and even with a sick, legless mother who, finally, by her death in a remote province, did not really alleviate his situation? Now the question: how should this offspring have reasoned justly? You, of course, think, reader, that he said to himself: “I have used all the gifts of P. throughout my life; tens of thousands went into my upbringing, governesses, and the cure of my idiocy in Switzerland; and here I am now, with millions, while the noble-hearted son of P., innocent of his father’s folly and having forgotten him, is dying teaching commerce. Everything that went to me rightfully should have gone to him. These vast sums, spent on me, are not really mine. It was just a blind error of fortune; they were destined for P.’s son. They should have been spent on him, not on me – the product of the capricious whim of a frivolous and forgetful P. If I were truly noble, delicate, and just, I would have given his son half of my entire inheritance; but since I am, first and foremost, a practical man and understand too well that this is not a legal matter, I will not give him half of my millions. Here, there is only conscience and justice! For what would have become of me if P. had not taken me in, but had cared for his son instead?”

"Disciple, I'm kneeling here, and you won't even bow to him? Just stand by the side and smirk—what's the logic there?" The行者 said, "You don't understand. A fellow like him, so shifty and deceitful, should get a good beating. I only spared him out of respect for the Buddha. Would he even dare to accept a bow from old Sun? From a young age, I've been a man of action. I don't know how to bow to others. Even if I met the Jade Emperor or the Taishang Laojun, I'd just pay them my respects with a nod and that would be enough." The Sanzang said, "Don't be so unruly! Stop with these empty words! Get up quickly, so as not to delay our journey."  Only then did the Master get up and hurry westward.

"Apprentice, for me to bow like this, you don't even offer him a bow, just stand there and sneer, what reason is there for this?" Monkey said, "You don't understand, a sneak like him, he deserved a good beating.  I only stopped short for the sake of the Bodhisattva's face, and having not beaten him enough, does he dare accept my old Sun's bow? From a young age, I, Sun Wukong, have always been a man of action. I don't know how to kowtow, even when I see the Jade Emperor or the Supreme Laozi, I only offer a verbal salute."  Tripitaka said, "Ungrateful child! Don't speak such empty words!  Get up quickly, lest we delay our journey."  The master then got up and went westward.

The next morning, Taizong held court, assembling the court officials and military generals. He drafted a letter of authorization for the journey to the West and sealed it with the imperial seal. The Imperial Observatory reported, “Today is a day auspicious for human affairs and favorable for long journeys.” The Tang emperor was delighted.  Then the chief eunuch announced, “Your Imperial brother, the monk, is waiting for your command outside the palace gates.” He immediately summoned him to the main hall and said, “Your Imperial brother, today is a propitious day for departure. This is your official letter of authorization. Furthermore, I have a purple gold begging bowl for you to use on your journey.  Choose two capable companions to accompany you, and I will also provide a fine mare for transportation. Now, depart on your journey.” Xuanzang was overjoyed, thanked the emperor profusely, accepted the gifts, and without any delay, set out. The emperor personally led the procession, accompanied by numerous officials, all the way to the pass. There, they saw the monks from Hongfu Temple and Xuanzang’s disciples, who had placed his winter and summer garments outside the pass. The emperor, seeing this, first ordered them to gather Xuanzang’s luggage and prepare his mount. Then, he instructed an attendant to pour wine.  Taizong raised his cup and asked, “What is your esteemed monastic sobriquet?” Xuanzang replied, “As a lay disciple, I do not dare to have a title.” Taizong said, “According to the Buddha, there are three sutras in the Western Paradise. Your Imperial brother, why not take a sutra as your title?  How does ‘Three-Basket’ sound?”  Xuanzang thanked the emperor once more, accepted the cup of wine, and said, “Your Majesty, alcohol is the foremost prohibition for monks. Since I have not yet become a monk, I cannot drink.” Taizong said, “Today’s departure is an extraordinary occasion. This is pure rice wine, please have just this one cup to show my respect and good wishes.” Xuanzang could not refuse. He took the cup, about to drink, when he saw the emperor lower his head and flick a pinch of dust into the wine.

The Bodhisattva led the crowd inside, paid respects to the Jade Emperor, and then greeted Lao Jun and the Queen Mother, each taking their seats. He then inquired, “How was the Peach Banquet?” The Jade Emperor replied, “Every year it’s a joyous occasion, but this year it was disrupted by the Monkey King, making it a very empty affair.” The Bodhisattva asked, “Where does this Monkey King come from?” The Jade Emperor said, “The Monkey King was born from a stone egg on Flower Fruit Mountain in the country of Ao Lai in the Eastern Bliss Continent. Upon his birth, his eyes emitted golden light, shooting towards the Doufu. Initially, this was overlooked, but he continued to grow, subduing dragons and tigers, eliminating himself from the death register. The Dragon King and the King Yama reported this to me. I wished to capture him, but Chang Geng Xing informed me, ‘Among the three realms, any being with nine orifices can become a celestial.’ So I bestowed upon him the role of Assistant Horse Keeper in the Imperial Stables, as a way of guiding him to the heavens, and enfeoffed him there. However, the Monkey King was dissatisfied with his low position and rebelled against heaven. I then dispatched the Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, and subsequently issued an edict to appease him, summoning him back to the heavens and enfeoffed him as ‘Great Sage Equal of Heaven,’ although without any salary. Bored with idleness, he wandered around east and west. Fearing further trouble, I had him manage the Peach Garden. But he disregarded the laws, eating the large peaches from the old trees. Since he was a low-ranking official without an invitation, he devised a scheme to trick the barefoot immortals, disguised himself, and sneaked into the banquet, stealing all the immortal food and wine. He even stole Lao Jun’s immortal pills and a large quantity of imperial wine to share with the monkeys back at his mountain. This deeply troubled me, so I dispatched one hundred thousand heavenly soldiers with celestial nets to capture him. However, there’s been no news of their success or failure today.”

The Bodhisattva led the crowd inside and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, greeted Laojun and the Queen Mother, and they all sat down.  He then asked, "How was the Peach Feast?"

I sent Li Tianwang and Nezha, the Prince of the Sea, to subdue him, and then issued an edict to calm the situation and invited him to the upper realm, where he was given the title 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven,' but with no salary. Having nothing to do, he wandered east and west. I feared further trouble, so I appointed him to oversee the Peach Garden. But he disregarded the rules and ate all the old trees and peaches. He then concocted a plan to trick the barefooted immortals, disguised himself, entered the feast, and stole all the celestial delicacies and liquor, as well as stealing Laojun's elixir of immortality and a quantity of imperial wine, which he took back to share with his mountain tribe. The Bodhisattva led the crowd inside and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, met with Lao Jun and the Queen Mother, taking their seats. When he first appeared, his eyes emitted golden light, piercing the celestial court. Therefore, I dispatched 100,000 celestial troops and set a heavenly net to capture him. But I haven’t received any news yet and don’t know the outcome of the battle.”

While the servants busied themselves, the gentleman went into the common room. Anyone passing through knows full well what these common rooms are like: the same walls, painted with oil paint, darkened at the top from pipe smoke and stained at the bottom by the backs of various travelers, and even more so by local merchants, for the merchants came in on trading days, six or seven at a time, to drink their well-known couple of cups of tea; the same smoke-stained ceiling; the same smoked chandelier with its multitude of dangling glass pieces, which would jump and tinkle whenever the waiter, hurrying along the worn oilcloths, swung his tray bearing an abyss of teacups, like birds on the seashore; the same wall-size paintings, done in oil paints—in short, all the same as everywhere else; the only difference was that one of the pictures showed a nymph with such enormous breasts, which, surely, the reader has never seen. Such a play of nature, however, happens in various historical paintings, brought to us in Russia at an unknown time from an unknown place and by unknown people, sometimes even by our own nobles, lovers of art, who had bought them in Italy on the advice of their couriers. The gentleman took off his tricorne and unrolled the woolen, multicolored scarf from his neck, the kind that married men have prepared by their wives, who provide appropriate instructions on how to wrap it, while for bachelors—I can’t say for sure who makes them, God knows, I’ve never worn such scarves. Having unrolled the scarf, the gentleman ordered his dinner. While various ordinary tavern dishes were being served to him, such as cabbage soup with a layered pastry, deliberately kept for travelers for several weeks, brains with peas, sausages with cabbage, fried puff pastry, a pickled cucumber, and a perpetually available layered sweet pastry, always ready to serve; while all this was being served, both hot and cold, he instructed the servant, or waiter, to tell him all sorts of nonsense—about who had owned the tavern before and who now, and how much profit it yielded, and how much of a scoundrel their owner was; to which the waiter, as was customary, replied: “Oh, a big one, sir, a real swindler.” Just as in enlightened Europe, so too in enlightened Russia there are now many respectable people who cannot eat in a tavern without talking to the servant, and sometimes even making fun of him. However, the traveler did not ask only pointless questions; he inquired with extraordinary precision about who the governor of the city was, who the chairman of the Chamber of Commerce was, who the prosecutor was—in short, he did not miss a single important official; but even more meticulously, and perhaps even with sympathy, he inquired about all the important landowners: how many serfs each had, how far they lived from the city, what kind of character they had, and how often they visited the city; he asked in detail about the state of the region: whether there had been any diseases in their province—epidemics, deadly fevers, smallpox, and so on—and all with such thoroughness and precision that it showed more than just simple curiosity. In his manner, the gentleman had something solid, and he snuffled very loudly. It is unknown how he did it, but his nose sounded like a trumpet. This, in my opinion, completely harmless quality, however, earned him a great deal of respect from the tavern servant, so that whenever he heard this sound, the latter would shake his hair, straighten up more respectfully, and, bowing his head from above, would ask: “Is there anything you need?” After dinner, the gentleman finished a cup of coffee and sat down on the divan, putting a pillow behind his back, which in Russian taverns, instead of elastic wool, is stuffed with something very similar to brick and cobblestones. There he began to yawn and ordered himself to be taken to his room, where, having lain down, he slept for two hours. Having rested, he wrote on a scrap of paper, at the request of the tavern servant, his rank, name, and surname for reporting to the authorities. When the waiter, going down the stairs, read the note syllable by syllable, it said: “Collegiate Assessor Pavel Ivanovich Chikchov, a landowner, for his own needs.” When the waiter was still deciphering the note, Pavel Ivanovich Chikchov himself went out to see the city, which he seemed to be satisfied with, for he found that the city was in no way inferior to other provincial towns: the yellow paint on the stone houses struck the eye strongly, and the gray paint on the wooden houses modestly darkened. The houses were one, two, and one and a half stories high, with a permanent mezzanine, very beautiful, in the opinion of provincial architects. Sometimes these houses seemed to be lost among the wide, like a field, streets and endless wooden fences; sometimes they were crowded together, and here there was more movement of people and life. One could see almost washed-out signs with bagels and shoes, in some places with blue pants painted and the signature of some Arshavsky tailor; a shop with tricorns, forage caps, and the inscription: “Foreigner Vasily Fedorov”; somewhere a billiards table was painted with two players in frock coats, the kind worn by our theatergoers in the last act when they enter the stage. The players were depicted with cues aimed at the balls, their hands slightly turned back, and legs set diagonally, just having made a bow in the air. Under all this was written: “And here's the establishment.” In some places, tables with nuts, soap, and gingerbread, similar to soap, stood directly on the street; somewhere there was an inn with a painted thick fish and a fork stuck into it. Most often, however, one could see darkened double-headed eagles, which are now replaced by the laconic inscription: “Drinks House.” The pavement was everywhere in poor condition. He also stopped by the city garden, which consisted of thin trees, poorly taken root, with supports at the bottom in the shape of triangles, very beautifully painted green with oil paint. However, although these trees were no higher than reeds, they were described in the newspapers, when describing the illumination, as “a garden, which enriched our city thanks to the care of the civil governor, consisting of shady, wide-branched trees, giving coolness on a sweltering day,” and that “it was very touching to watch how the hearts of citizens trembled with gratitude and shed streams of tears in gratitude to the city manager.” Having inquired in detail from the builder where he could walk closer, if needed, to the cathedral, to the government buildings, to the governor, he set off to look at the river, which flowed in the middle of the city. On the way, he tore off a poster nailed to a post, intending to read it carefully at home, glanced intently at a lady of no small beauty passing along the wooden sidewalk, followed by a boy in a military uniform, with a knot in his hand, and, once again glancing around, as if to memorize the location well, went home straight to his room, supported slightly by the tavern servant on the stairs. After having eaten his tea, he sat down at the table, ordered a candle, took out the poster from his pocket, held it up to the candle, and began to read, squinting his right eye slightly. There was not much remarkable about the poster: a drama by Mr. Koteb was being staged, in which Rola was played by Mr. Pop Levin, Cora—by Miss Zyablova, and the other characters were even less remarkable; however, he read them all, even got to the price of the orchestra seats, and learned that the poster was printed in the printing house of the provincial administration. Then he turned it over: to see if there was anything else on the other side, but, not finding anything, he wiped his eyes, folded it neatly, and put it in his box, where he had a habit of putting everything that came his way. The day, it seems, ended with a portion of cold beef, a bottle of sour cabbage soup, and a strong sleep, as they say in other parts of the vast Russian state, "all the way to the pump."

After his meal, the gentleman sipped a cup of coffee and sat on the couch, putting a pillow behind his back, the kind that in Russian inns, instead of elastic wool, is filled with something very much resembling brick and cobblestone. Here he began to yawn and ordered to be taken to his room, where, having lain down, he slept for two hours. After resting, he wrote on a scrap of paper, at the request of the innkeeper's servant, his rank, name, and surname for transmission to the police. As the servant descended the stairs, he read aloud the following: "Collegiate Assessor Pavel Ivanovich Chizhikov, landowner, for his needs." When the servant was still deciphering the note, Pavel Ivanovich Chizhikov himself went out to see the town, which he seemed satisfied with, because he found that the town was in no way inferior to other provincial towns: the yellow paint on the stone houses struck him strongly, and the gray paint on the wooden ones looked modestly subdued. The houses were one, two, and one and a half stories high, with an eternally present mezzanine, very beautiful, in the opinion of provincial architects. Sometimes these houses seemed lost among the wide, field-like streets and endless wooden fences; sometimes they huddled together, and here there was more movement of people and life. There were almost rain-washed signs with bagels and boots, somewhere with blue trousers drawn and signed by some Arshavsky tailor; there was a shop with hats and caps and the inscription: "Foreigner Vasily Fedorov"; somewhere a billiards table was depicted with two players in frock coats, the kind worn by our theatergoers in the final act as they enter the stage. The players were depicted with cues aimed, slightly turned backwards arms, and crossed legs, just having done an air-turn. Under all this it was written: "And here is the establishment." Sometimes, simply on the street, there were tables with nuts, soap, and gingerbread, looking very much like soap; there was a tavern with a fat fish drawn on it and a fork stuck into it. Most often, however, one could see the darkened double-headed state eagles, which have now been replaced by a laconic inscription: "Drinking House." The pavement was everywhere in poor condition. He looked into the town park as well, which consisted of thin trees, poorly planted, with supports at the bottom, in the shape of triangles, very beautifully painted green with oil paint. However, although these trees were not higher than reeds, it was said in the newspapers when describing the illumination, that "our town has been adorned, thanks to the care of the civil governor, with a garden consisting of shady, broad-leaved trees, which give coolness on a hot day," and that "it was very touching to watch how the hearts of citizens trembled with gratitude and shed streams of tears in gratitude to the town head." Having asked the carpenter in detail how to get closer, if necessary, to the cathedral, to the administrative buildings, to the governor, he went to look at the river flowing through the middle of the town. On the way, he tore down an advertisement pinned to a post, so that, having returned home, he could read it properly, looked closely at a lady of not unattractive appearance passing along the wooden pavement, followed by a boy in a military livery, with a bundle in his hand, and, once again, scanning everything with his eyes, as if to remember the location well, went straight home to his room, supported slightly on the stairs by the innkeeper's servant. After having a snack of tea, he sat down at the table, ordered a candle, took the advertisement out of his pocket, brought it closer to the candle and began to read, squinting his right eye a little. However, there was not much remarkable about the advertisement: the drama by Mr. Kocebu was being staged, in which Rolla was played by Mr. Poplyvin, Cora by the young woman Zyablova, the other roles were even less notable; however, he read them all, even reached the price of the orchestra seats and found out that the advertisement was printed in the provincial government printing house. Then he turned it over: to see if there was anything else on the other side, but not finding anything, wiped his eyes, neatly folded it and put it in his small chest, where he had a habit of putting everything that came his way. The day, it seems, was closed with a portion of cold veal, a bottle of sour cabbage soup and a deep sleep, deep and long, as they say in some parts of the vast Russian state.

But his silent standing must have been noticeable, and indeed the girl and the court officer looked at him as if some great transformation were about to happen to him in the next minute, which they couldn't miss observing. And in the doorway stood the man whom K. had earlier noticed in the distance; he held himself on the rail of the low door and swayed a little on his toes, like an impatient spectator. The girl, however, first recognized that K.'s demeanor was due to a slight discomfort; she brought a chair and asked, "Would you like to sit down?" K. sat down immediately and, to get even better support, rested his elbows on the arms. "You have a little dizziness, don't you?" she asked him. His face was now close before her, it had the stern expression that some women have even in their most beautiful youth. "Don't worry about it," she said, "it's nothing unusual here, almost everyone gets such an attack when they come here for the first time. You're here for the first time? Well, that's nothing unusual then. The sun beats down on the roof frame here, and the hot wood makes the air so dull and heavy. That's why this place is not very suitable for office spaces, although it offers other great advantages. But as for the air, on days of great party traffic, and that's almost every day, it's hardly breathable. And if you also consider that laundry is often hung out to dry here – you can't entirely forbid the tenants – then you won't be surprised that you feel a little sick. But one gets used to the air very well. When you come here for the second or third time, you'll hardly feel the heaviness here anymore. Do you feel better already?" K. didn't answer, it was embarrassing for him to be so exposed to the people here because of this sudden weakness, moreover, now that he knew the cause of his nausea, he didn't feel any better, but rather a little worse.

The Great Sage had arrived at the mouth of the Guàn River. With a flicker, he transformed into the likeness of Erlang Shen, descending through the clouds and entering the temple. The Ghost Judges did not recognize him, each bowing their heads to greet him. He took his seat in the center, checking the incense and offerings: he saw Li Hu's sacrifice of three offerings, Zhang Long's vow for blessings, Zhao Jia's petition for a child, and Qian Bing's prayer for healing. Just as he was examining them, someone reported, "Another elder has arrived!" The Ghost Judges hurriedly looked up, their hearts filled with alarm. The True Monarch asked, "Is there a Great Sage named Qitian here?" The Ghost Judges replied, "We haven't seen any Great Sage, only an elder checking the offerings." The True Monarch burst through the door. The Great Sage revealed his true form and said, "Sir, there's no need to shout; this temple belongs to the Sun family now." The True Monarch raised his three-pointed, double-edged divine blade and swung it at the Great Sage's face. The Monkey King moved with incredible agility, dodging the blade, and drew out his embroidered flower needle, its needle glowing, striking at the True Monarch.  The two clashed, their fight spilling out of the temple, amidst a swirl of mist and clouds. They continued their battle, finally reaching Huaguoshan, where the Four Heavenly Kings and the others were alarmed, their vigilance heightened. Kang and Zhang Taifu, along with the others, rushed to meet the True Monarch, working together to surround the Monkey King.

The Four Heavenly Kings and the others were frightened and braced themselves. The generals Kang and Zhang greeted the True Monarch and, with combined effort, encircled the Monkey King.

After this manner, he had removed the woman's objections, the quiet conversation at the window became too long for him; he tapped with his knuckles on the podium and then with his fist. The student glanced briefly over the woman's shoulder at K., but he let himself not be disturbed, indeed he even pressed closer to the woman and embraced her. She lowered her head deeply, as if listening to him attentively, he kissed her, as she bent down, loudly on the neck, without interrupting his speech much. K. saw in this the tyranny that the student exercised over him, as the woman had complained, stood up, and paced the room. He considered, with sidelong glances at the student, how he could get him out of there as quickly as possible, and it was not unwelcome to him when the student, apparently disturbed by K.'s pacing, which had by now become a trampling, remarked: "If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, no one would have missed you. Yes, you should even have left, and that right from my entrance, and quickly." This remark may have expressed all possible anger, but it also contained the arrogance of the future magistrate speaking to a disliked defendant. K. stood very close to him and said with a smile: "I am impatient, that's true, but this impatience will be most easily eliminated by your leaving us. But if you have perhaps come to study – I heard that you are a student – then I will gladly make room for you and leave with the woman. You will have to study a lot more, however, before you become a judge. I don't know your legal system very well yet, but I assume that it's not enough to simply deliver those coarse speeches, which you already know how to do quite shamelessly." "One shouldn't have let him run around so freely," said the student, as if to give the woman an explanation for K.'s insulting speech, "it was a mistake. I told the examining magistrate. One should have kept him in his room at least between the interrogations. The examining magistrate is sometimes incomprehensible." "Useless talk," said K. and reached for the woman, "come." "Oh no," said the student, "no, no, you won't get her," and with a strength one wouldn't have attributed to him, he lifted her onto one arm and ran towards the door, bending his back and gazing at her tenderly. There was a certain fear of K. in this, nonetheless, he dared to provoke him further by stroking and pressing the woman's arm with his free hand. K. ran a few steps alongside him, ready to grab him and, if necessary, strangle him, when the woman said: "It's no use, the examining magistrate is going to fetch me, I'm not allowed to leave with you, this little monster," she slapped the student's face, "this little monster won't let me." "And you don't want to be freed!" K. shouted and put his hand on the student's shoulder, who snapped his teeth at her. "No!" cried the woman and pushed K. away with both hands, "no, no, not that, what are you thinking! That would be my ruin. Let him go, please, let him go. He's only carrying out the examining magistrate's order and taking me to him." "Then let him run and I will never see you again," said K., furious with disappointment, and gave the student a shove in the back, so that he stumbled briefly, only to jump even higher with his burden, pleased that he hadn't been knocked down. K. walked slowly after them, he realized that this was the first undeniable defeat he had suffered from these people. It was, of course, no reason to worry, he only received this defeat because he sought out the fight. If he stayed at home and lived his usual life, he was a thousand times superior to each of these people and could sweep each of them out of his way with a single kick. And he imagined the most ridiculous scene, which would, for example, take place if this pitiful student, this pompous child, this crooked-bearded man, would kneel before Elsa's bed and beg for mercy with folded hands. K. liked this idea so much that he decided, if only an opportunity arose, to take the student to Elsa once.

Immediately, he called out, "My children, I've come!"

In these times, he snatched our fire and captured many of our offspring, forcing us to remain awake day and night, guarding our home. We are fortunate that the Great King has arrived! The monkeys bowed their heads and said, "We humbly inform our Great King, he calls himself the Demon King of the Mixed World and resides in the northwest."

He almost fell as he entered, for there was a step behind the door. "No consideration is given to the audience," he said. "No consideration at all," said the court officer, "just look at this waiting room." It was a long corridor from which roughly hewn doors led to the individual compartments of the attic. Although there was no direct light entering, it was not completely dark, because some compartments had, instead of solid board walls facing the corridor, merely wooden grilles reaching to the ceiling, through which some light streamed and one could see individual officials writing at tables or standing right by the grille, observing the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were, probably because it was Sunday, only a few people in the corridor. They made a very modest impression. At nearly regular intervals, they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches lining the corridor. They were all dressed shabbily, although most, judging by their expressions, bearing, beards, and many barely ascertainable small details, belonged to the higher classes. As there were no coat racks, they had placed their hats, probably one following the example of the other, under the benches. When those sitting nearest the door, K. and the court officer, were seen, they rose to greet them, and as the following ones saw this, they thought they too had to greet, so that everyone rose as the two passed by. They never stood completely upright; their backs were bent, their knees bent, they stood like beggars. K. waited for the court officer, who was walking a little behind him, and said, "How humiliated they must be." "Yes," said the court officer, "they are all accused, everyone you see here is an accused." "Really!" said K. "Then they are my colleagues." And he turned to the next man, a tall, slender, almost gray-haired man. "What are you waiting for here?" K. asked politely. But the unexpected address made the man confused, which was all the more embarrassing as it was apparently an experienced man who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not easily relinquish the superiority he had acquired over many. Here, however, he couldn't answer such a simple question and looked at the others as if they were obliged to help him, and as if no one could demand an answer from him if they failed to do so. The court officer then approached and said, to reassure and cheer up the man, "The gentleman here is just asking what you are waiting for. Answer him." The man's probably familiar voice seemed to work: "I am waiting –" he began, and then faltered. Apparently, he had chosen this beginning to answer the question exactly, but now he couldn't find the continuation. Some of the waiting people had come closer and surrounded the group, the court officer said to them: "Go away, go away, clear the way." They moved back a little, but not to their former seats. Meanwhile, the person questioned had recovered and even answered with a little smile: "I made some motions for evidence in my case a month ago and am waiting for their processing." "You seem to be making a lot of effort," said K. "Yes," said the man, "it is my case, after all." "Not everyone thinks like you," said K., "I, for example, am also accused, but as I hope to be saved, I haven't filed any motions for evidence, or done anything of the sort. "I don't know exactly," said the man again, completely uncertain; he apparently thought K. was making a joke with him, so he probably would have liked to repeat his previous answer, out of fear of making a new mistake, but in the face of K.'s impatient look, he only said, "As for me, I have filed motions for evidence." "You don't believe I'm accused?" asked K. "Oh, of course," said the man, and stepped aside a little, but there was no belief in his answer, only fear. Though there was no direct light coming in, it was not completely dark, for some compartments had, instead of uniform wooden walls facing the corridor, merely wooden grilles reaching up to the ceiling, through which some light penetrated and one could see individual officials writing at tables or standing right by the grille, observing the people in the corridor through the gaps. There were, probably because it was Sunday, few people in the corridor. They made a very modest impression. At almost regular intervals they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches that ran along either side of the corridor. All were dressed plainly, though most, judging by their facial expressions, posture, beards, and many barely ascertainable small details, belonged to the higher classes. As there were no coat racks, they had placed their hats, probably one following the example of the other, under the benches. When those seated closest to the door, K. and the bailiff, were seen, they rose to greet them, so that when the others saw this, they too thought they had to greet them, so that all rose as the two passed by. They never stood completely upright, their backs were bent, their knees were bent, they stood like beggars on the street. K. waited for the bailiff, who was walking slightly behind him, and said, "How humiliated they must be." "Yes," said the bailiff, "they are all accused, everyone you see here is an accused person." "Really!" said K. "Then they are my colleagues." And he turned to the next man, a tall, slender, almost gray-haired man. "What are you waiting for here?" K. asked politely. 

But the unexpected address confused the man, which was all the more embarrassing since it was clearly a man of experience who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not readily give up the superiority he had acquired over many. Here, however, he could not answer such a simple question and looked at the others as if they were obliged to help him and as if no one could demand an answer from him if this help did not come. Then the bailiff stepped forward and said, to reassure and encourage the man: "The gentleman here is just asking what you are waiting for. Answer him." The man's probably familiar voice seemed to work better: "I'm waiting - " he began and then stopped. Apparently, he had chosen this beginning to answer the question exactly, but now he couldn't find the continuation. Some of those waiting had approached and surrounded the group; the bailiff said to them, "Move aside, make way for the corridor." They moved back a little, but not to their former seats. Meanwhile, the man addressed had regained his composure and even answered with a small smile: "I made some motions for evidence in my case a month ago and am waiting for their resolution." "You seem to be making a lot of effort," said K. "Yes," said the man, "it is my case after all." "Not everyone thinks like you," said K., "I, for example, am also accused, but as I hope to be saved, I have not made any motions for evidence, nor have I taken any other such action. Do you think that's necessary?" "I don't know exactly," said the man again, completely uncertain; he apparently believed K. was making a joke with him, so he probably would have liked to repeat his previous answer out of fear of making some new mistake, but under K.'s impatient gaze, he only said, "As far as I'm concerned, I have filed motions for evidence." "You don't think I'm accused?" asked K. "Oh, certainly," said the man, and stepped back a little, but there was no belief in the answer, only fear. "You don't believe me?" asked K. and, unconsciously prompted by the man's humble nature, grasped his arm as if to force him to believe. But he didn't want to cause him pain, he had only touched him very lightly, yet the man screamed as if K. had grasped him not with two fingers, but with a burning tongs. This ridiculous scream made K. utterly fed up; if they didn't believe he was accused, then all the better; maybe he even thought him a judge. And now, as a farewell, he gripped him more firmly, pushed him back onto the bench, and walked on. "Most of the accused are so sensitive," said the bailiff. Now almost all the waiting people gathered around the man, who had stopped screaming, and seemed to question him closely about the incident. 

Now a guard came towards K., who was mainly recognizable by his saber, the scabbard of which, at least in color, seemed to be aluminum. K. was amazed and even reached out with his hand. The guard, who had come because of the screaming, inquired about what had happened. The bailiff tried to reassure him with a few words, but the guard declared that he still had to see for himself, saluted, and continued on, with very hurried, but very short, probably gout-measured steps.

— Un-Christian faith, first of all! — the prince said again, his voice trembling with extraordinary agitation, — that's the first thing, and secondly, Roman Catholicism is even worse than atheism itself, that's my opinion! Yes! That's my opinion! Atheism preaches only zero, but Catholicism goes further: it preaches a distorted Christ, a Christ defiled and reviled, a Christ opposite to the true one! It preaches antichrist, I swear to you, I assure you! This is my long-held personal conviction, and it has tormented me... Roman Catholicism believes that without universal state power the church cannot stand on earth, and it cries: “Non possumus!” [31] In my view, Roman Catholicism is not even a religion, but a definite continuation of the Western Roman Empire, and everything in it is subordinate to this idea, starting with faith. The Pope seized the land, the earthly throne, and took up the sword; ever since, things have gone this way, only the sword has been joined by falsehood, cunning, deceit, fanaticism, superstition, villainy, they have played on the most sacred, truthful, simple, ardent feelings of the people, they have traded everything, everything for money, for low earthly power. And is this not the teaching of antichrist?! How could atheism not have arisen from them? Atheism arose from them, from Roman Catholicism itself! Atheism began first with them; could they believe in themselves? It strengthened out of aversion to them; it is the offspring of their lies and spiritual impotence! Atheism! Here, only exceptional strata do not yet believe, as Eugene Pavlovich aptly expressed it the other day, those who have lost their roots; but there, in Europe, already terrifying masses of the people themselves are beginning to disbelieve, — first from darkness and from lies, but now already from fanaticism, from hatred of the church and of Christianity!

Reporting to the Tripitaka Master, the Sandy announced: "Master, our horse must have been eaten by that dragon. We can't find it anywhere." The Tripitaka Master said, "Disciple, how could that creature, with its big mouth, have eaten the entire horse, saddle and bridle? I think it must have been startled, breaking its reins and run off into a valley. You take a closer look." The Monkey said, "You don't know my abilities! My eyes can see a thousand li in daylight, for fortune and misfortune.  Within a thousand li, even if a dragonfly spreads its wings, I can see it. How could I not have seen that horse?" "My dear Uncle," said K., "this excitement is useless; it's on your side, and would be on mine too. One doesn't win cases with excitement; let my practical experience count for something, as I value yours, even if it surprises me, always and especially now. Since you say that the family would also be affected by the trial—which I, for my part, cannot understand at all, but that is secondary—I'm willing to follow your lead in everything. Only, I don't think a country stay would be beneficial, even in your sense, because that would mean flight and a guilty conscience. Besides, I'm being more pursued here, but I can also better handle the case myself."

"Right," said the Uncle in a tone as if they were finally coming closer to each other, "I only suggested it because I thought, if you stayed here, I would be jeopardizing the case with your indifference, and it would be better if I worked for you instead of you. But if you want to tackle it with all your strength, it's naturally far better."

"We're agreed then," said K. "And do you have a proposal now for what I should do first?"

"I naturally have to think about it," said the Uncle, "you must bear in mind that I've been on the country almost continuously for twenty years now, and my sense of these things has dulled. Various important connections with people who might be better informed in this area have simply loosened up on their own. I'm a bit stranded in the country, as you know. One only really notices it at such times. Partly, your case also came as a surprise to me, even though I strangely enough suspected something of the sort after Erna's letter and today, at your arrival, almost knew it for sure. But that's immaterial, the most important thing is not to waste time."

Even as he spoke, he had stood on tiptoe, beckoned to a passing car, and now, while simultaneously giving the chauffeur an address, pulled K. behind him into the vehicle.

"We're going to Advocate Huld now," he said, "he was my schoolmate. You surely know the name? Not? That's strange. He has a considerable reputation as a defender and a lawyer for the poor. I, however, have particular trust in him as a person."

"I'm happy with whatever you do," said K., although the uncle's hasty and insistent approach to the matter gave him a feeling of unease. It wasn't very pleasant, as the accused, to go to a lawyer for the poor. "I didn't know," he said, "that you could even hire a lawyer in such a case."

"But of course," said the Uncle, "that goes without saying. Why not? And now tell me, so that I can be fully informed, everything that has happened so far."

K. began to tell him immediately, without omitting anything. His complete openness was the only protest he allowed himself against his uncle's view that the trial was a great shame. He only mentioned Fräulein Bürstner's name once and briefly, but that didn't detract from his openness, as Fräulein Bürstner had no connection to the trial. As he spoke, he looked out the window and observed how they were approaching the very suburbs where the court offices were located. "You damned," he started, his voice gurgling, and incomprehensible at first. K. was startled, although he had expected something like this, and ran towards the uncle, with the intention of closing his mouth with both hands. Fortunately, however, the patient rose from his bed behind the girl. The uncle made a grimace, as if swallowing something disgusting, and then said calmer: "We haven't lost our minds, of course. If what I was asking for wasn't possible, I wouldn't ask it. Please, leave now!"

The nurse stood upright by the bed, facing the uncle, and with one hand, as K. thought, stroked the hand of the lawyer. "You can tell me anything in front of Leni," said the lawyer, undoubtedly in a tone of urgent plea. "It doesn't concern me," said the uncle, "it's not my secret."

And he turned around, as if he didn't intend to engage in any further negotiations, but was granting a small moment of contemplation. "Who does it concern then?" asked the lawyer in a voice that was fading away, and lay back again. "My nephew," said the uncle, and introduced him: "Procurer Josef K." "Oh," said the lawyer, much more lively, and held out his hand to K., "excuse me, I didn't notice you. Go, Leni," he then said to the nurse, who didn't resist, and she gave him her hand as if it were a farewell for a long time. "So you're not," he finally said to the uncle, who had approached him in a conciliatory manner, "come to pay me a sick visit, but you've come on business."

"Dear Uncle," said K., "this excitement is pointless, it's on your side, and it would be on mine too. You don't win cases with excitement, allow my practical experience to count for something, as much as yours, even if it surprises me, which it always does, and even now very much. Since you say the family would also be affected by the case - which, by the way, I cannot at all understand - I'm happy to follow your lead in everything. Only I don't consider a country stay to be beneficial in your view, because it would mean fleeing and feeling guilty. Besides, while I'm being pursued here, I can also handle the case more actively."

"Right," said the uncle in a tone as if they had finally understood each other, "I only suggested it because, if you stayed here, I thought you were in danger of neglecting the case because of your indifference, and I thought it better if I worked for you instead. But if you want to tackle it with all your might, then of course that is much better." "We agree on that, then," said K. "And do you have a suggestion for what I should do first?" "I naturally have to think about the case first," said the uncle, "you have to bear in mind that I've been in the country for almost twenty years without a break, and my contacts in those circles have dwindled. I'm a bit isolated here in the country, as you know. You only really realize it at moments like these. Your case also came to me rather unexpectedly, though oddly enough, I had already suspected something like this after Erna's letter, and today, upon seeing you, I was almost certain. But that's unimportant, the most important thing now is not to waste time."

Already while speaking, he, standing on tiptoe, had beckoned to a passing car and now, as he gave the driver an address, pulled K. into the car. "We're going to Attorney Huld now," he said, "he was my schoolmate. You must know the name, surely? That's strange. He has a renowned reputation as a lawyer and public defender. But I have particular trust in him as a person." "I trust whatever you do," said K., although the uncle's hasty and urgent approach to the matter bothered him. It wasn't very reassuring to be going to a public defender as a defendant. "I didn't know," he said, "that you could even hire a lawyer for a case like this." "Of course," said the uncle, "that goes without saying. Why not? Now tell me, so that I am fully informed, everything that has happened so far." K. immediately began to tell his story, omitting nothing. His complete openness was the only protest he allowed himself against his uncle's view that the trial was a disgrace. He only mentioned Fräulein Bürstner's name once and fleetingly, but this didn't affect the openness, because Fräulein Bürstner had no connection to the case. As he spoke, he looked out the window and observed how they were approaching the very suburb where the court offices were located. He pointed this out to his uncle, who didn't find the coincidence particularly noteworthy.

The car stopped in front of a dark house. The uncle rang the doorbell on the ground floor immediately. While they waited, he smiled and flashed his large teeth, whispering, "Eight o'clock. An unusual time for a social call. But Huld won't mind." Two large, dark eyes appeared in the peephole, looked at the two guests for a moment, and then disappeared. The door didn't open. The uncle and K. confirmed to each other that they had seen the two eyes. "A new maid, afraid of strangers," said the uncle and knocked again. The eyes appeared again, they could almost be described as sad now, perhaps that was just a trick of the flickering gas flame, which burned strongly overhead but gave little light. "Open up!" called the uncle and slammed his fist against the door, "We are friends of the attorney!" "The attorney is ill," a voice whispered from behind them. A man in a dressing gown stood in a door at the other end of the small hallway and made this announcement in an extremely quiet voice. The uncle, already irritated by the long wait, turned around abruptly, shouted, "Ill? You say he is ill?" and approached him almost threateningly, as if the man himself were the illness.

"The door is open," said the man, pointed at the attorney's door, pulled his dressing gown together, and disappeared. The door had indeed been opened; a young girl - K. recognized the dark, somewhat sunken eyes again - stood in the hallway in a long, white apron, holding a candle in her hand. "Next time, open sooner!" said the uncle instead of a greeting, as the girl made a small curtsy. "Come, Josef," he then said to K., who slowly pushed past the girl. "The attorney is ill," the girl said, as the uncle, without stopping, walked toward a door. K. was still watching the girl as she turned to close the apartment door again. She had a doll-like round face; not only were her cheeks and chin round, but also her temples and forehead. "Josef!" the uncle called out again, and he asked the girl, "Is it heart trouble?" "I believe so," said the girl, she had found time to walk forward with the candle and open the room door. In a corner of the room, where the candlelight didn't reach, a face with a long beard rose in the bed. "Leni, who is it?" asked the attorney, who, blinded by the candlelight, couldn't recognize the guests. "Albert, your old friend is here," said the uncle. "Ah, Albert," said the attorney and slumped back on the pillows as if he didn't need to pretend anything. "Is it really that bad?" asked the uncle and sat down on the edge of the bed. "I don't think so. It's an attack of your heart trouble and will pass like the others." "Perhaps," said the attorney quietly, "but it's worse than it's ever been. I breathe heavily, can't sleep at all, and I'm losing strength every day." "Well," said the uncle and pressed his Panama hat firmly onto his knee. "That's bad news. Are you getting the right care? It's so sad here, so dark. It's been a long time since I was here last, it seemed friendlier then. And your little maid doesn't seem very cheerful either, or maybe she's just putting on a show."

The girl was still standing by the bed, fully facing the uncle, she stroked, as K. thought he could notice, the hand of the attorney. "You can tell me anything in front of Leni," said the attorney, undoubtedly in the tone of an urgent plea. "It doesn't concern me," said the uncle, "it's not my secret." And he turned around, as if he didn't intend to enter into any further negotiations, but was still allowing for a moment's contemplation. "Who does it concern then?" asked the attorney with a fading voice and lay back again. "My nephew," said the uncle, "I brought him with me." And he introduced: "Procurator Josef K." "Oh," said the attorney much more lively and held out his hand to K., "excuse me, I didn't notice you at all. Go, Leni," he said to the maid, who didn't even resist, and offered her her hand as if it were a farewell for a long time. "So you," he finally said to the uncle, who had stepped closer, reconciled, "haven't come to make a sick call, but you're here on business."

The monster heard this, mumbled repeatedly, put away his precious staff, and let Muzha drag him to see Guanyin. He bowed his head in reverence and said, "Bodhisattva, forgive my sins, let me explain. See that Monkey King, parting the watercourse, he went straight back to the Iron Plate Bridge. He climbed up, and there were four old monkeys, leading a multitude of monkeys, all waiting by the bridge. Suddenly, seeing Sun Wukong leap out of the water, his body completely dry, gleaming golden, walking up the bridge, the monkeys all knelt down together and cried, "Great King, so splendid! So splendid!" Sun Wukong, with a spring in his step, ascended his throne and planted his iron staff in the center. Those monkeys, not knowing any better, all came to take the treasure, but they were like dragonflies striking at iron trees, unable to budge it even a hair's breadth. Each bit their finger, stuck out their tongues, and said, "Grandfather! It's so heavy, how did you even manage to lift it?" Sun Wukong stepped forward, opened his hand, and grasped it, saying to them with a smile, "Every thing has its owner. This treasure lies in the depths of the sea, who knows for how many centuries. Only this year has it emitted light. The Dragon King only saw it as a piece of black iron, calling it the Heaven River's Bottom Divine Treasure. He couldn't even lift it, so he asked me to get it. Back then, this treasure was over two zhang long and as thick as a tub. I whacked it once, and it was too big, so I whacked it again, it got smaller, and whacked it again, it got smaller and smaller. When I looked up at the sky, there was a line of writing: 'Ruyi Golden Cudgel, 13,500 jin.' You all stand back, let me call it to change size again." He tossed the treasure in his hand and said, "Small! Small!" Immediately, it shrunk to the size of an embroidery needle, small enough to be tucked into the ear. The monkeys were amazed and cried, "Great King! Please show us another transformation!"  The Monkey King took it out from his ear, held it in his palm, and said, "Big! Big! Big!"  And it grew back to the size of a tub, two zhang long. He enjoyed it for a while, jumped off the bridge, out of the cave, clutching the treasure. He used a magical display of heaven and earth, bent over, shouted "Long!" and instantly grew to a height of ten thousand zhang. His head was like Mount Tai, his waist like a mountain range, his eyes like lightning, his mouth like a blood basin, his teeth like swords and halberds. The tiger, leopard, wolf, monster, goblins, seventy-two cave demon kings, all were terrified, bowing and paying respects, trembling in fear. In an instant, he retracted his magical display, turned the treasure back into an embroidery needle, tucked it in his ear, and returned to the cave.  The demon kings, alarmed, all came to pay their respects.

You see this Monkey King, parting the waters, going directly back to the Iron Plate Bridge. He charged towards it, and saw four old monkeys, leading a multitude, all waiting by the bridge. Suddenly, seeing Sun Wukong jump out of the water, not a drop of it on him, gleaming golden, he walked onto the bridge. Frightened, the monkeys all knelt down and cried, “Great King, what splendor! What splendor!” 

Sun Wukong, beaming, ascended his throne, placing his iron staff upright in the center. Those monkeys, not knowing any better, all came to touch the treasure, but it was like a dragonfly trying to shake a steel tree, not even able to budge it. One by one they bit their fingers, stuck out their tongues, and said, “Grandfather! This is so heavy, how can you even carry it?” Sun Wukong stepped closer, spread his hands, and with a sweep, said to them, “Everything has an owner. This treasure resides in the Sea’s depths, for perhaps thousands upon thousands of years, and this year just happened to glow. The Dragon King only took it to be a piece of black iron, also called the Heavenly River’s Bottom Divine Treasure. That fellow couldn’t bear its weight, so he asked me to retrieve it. At the time, this treasure was over two zhang long and as thick as a dou. I struck it once, thinking it was too big, and it reduced in size. And then I struck it again, it became even smaller, and then smaller still. In a hurry, I looked towards the heavens, and on it there was a line of characters, ‘Ruyi Golden-Hooped Staff, weighing one thousand three hundred and fifty jin.’ You all stand aside, let me call out to him and see if he changes size again.” He twirled the treasure in his hand and said, “Smaller!
