This ordered presentation startled K. at first, then he said as quietly as the painter, “I believe you contradict yourself.”

“How so?” the painter asked patiently, leaning back with a smile. 

This smile gave K. the feeling that he was now about to discover contradictions not in the painter’s words, but in the court proceedings themselves. Nonetheless, he didn’t back down and said, “You earlier remarked that the court is inaccessible for reasons of evidence, later you restricted this to the public court, and now you even say that the innocent don’t need help from the court. That’s a contradiction. Furthermore, you earlier said that judges can be personally influenced, but now you deny that a real acquittal, as you call it, can ever be achieved through personal influence. That’s the second contradiction.”

“These contradictions are easy to clear up,” the painter said. “Here two different things are being discussed: what the law states and what I have personally experienced; you mustn’t confuse the two. The law, which I haven’t actually read, naturally states on the one hand that the innocent are acquitted, but on the other hand it doesn’t state that judges can be influenced. Now, however, I have experienced the opposite. I know of no real acquittals, but many influences. It’s of course possible that in all the cases I know of there was no innocence. But isn’t that unlikely?  Even as a child, I listened closely to my father when he talked about trials at home, even the judges who came to his atelier talked about the court; in our circles we talk about nothing else; as soon as I had the opportunity to go to court myself, I always took it; I’ve attended countless trials in important stages, and as far as they are visible, I have followed them, and – I must admit – not experienced a single real acquittal.”

“Not a single acquittal then,” K. said, as if speaking to himself and his hopes. “That confirms the opinion I already had of the court. So it’s useless from this side as well. A single executioner could replace the whole court.”

“You mustn’t generalize,” the painter said, dissatisfied, “I’ve only spoken from my experiences.”

“That’s enough,” said K., “or have you heard of acquittals from earlier times?”

“Such acquittals,” the painter replied, “may have existed. But it’s very difficult to ascertain that. The final decisions of the court are not published, they aren’t even accessible to the judges; as a result, only legends have survived about old court cases. These even contain, in the majority, real acquittals; you can believe them, they are verifiable, but not completely. Nonetheless, we mustn’t completely disregard them; they certainly contain a certain truth, and they are very beautiful; I myself have painted some pictures based on these legends.”

“Bare legends don’t change my mind,” K. said, “can you not appeal to these legends in court either?” 

The painter laughed. “No, you can’t,” he said.

“Then it’s pointless to talk about it,” K. said; he was willing to accept the painter’s opinions for now, even if he found them unlikely and contrary to other reports. He didn’t have the time to check or even refute everything the painter said; it was the utmost he could achieve to convince the painter to help him in some way, even if it wasn’t decisive. Therefore, he said, “Let’s set aside the question of a real acquittal, you mentioned two other possibilities.”

“The apparent acquittal and the postponement. That’s all that remains,” the painter said. “But before we discuss them, don’t you want to take off your coat? It’s getting quite warm in here.”

“Yes,” said K., who had been paying attention only to the painter’s explanations, but now, reminded of the heat, broke out in a sweat. “It’s almost unbearable.”

The painter nodded, as if he understood K.’s discomfort very well. “Couldn’t we open the window?” K. asked.

“No,” the painter said. “It’s just a fixed glass pane, you can’t open it.” Now K. realized that he had been hoping all along that the painter or he himself would suddenly go to the window and fling it open. He had been prepared to breathe in the mist with his mouth agape. The feeling of being completely shut off from the air caused him dizziness. He lightly struck the feather bed beside him and said in a weak voice, “This is uncomfortable and unhealthy.”

“Oh no,” the painter said, defending his window, “because it can’t be opened, even though it’s just a simple pane, it holds the heat better than a double-glazed window. If I want to air out the room, which isn’t really necessary, since air seeps in through the joists, I can open one of my doors, or even both.” 

K., comforted slightly by this explanation, looked around for the second door. The painter noticed this and said, “It’s behind you, I had to push it in with the bed.” 

K. now saw the small door in the wall. “It’s just all too small for an atelier,” the painter said, as if anticipating K.’s criticism. “I had to make do as best I could. The bed in front of the door is naturally in a very bad place. The judge, for example, whom I’m painting now, always comes through the door by the bed, and I’ve also given him a key to this door so that he can wait for me here in the atelier, even if I’m not at home. Now he usually comes early in the morning, while I’m still asleep. It naturally rips me out of my deepest sleep when the door opens next to the bed. You would lose all respect for the judges if you heard the curses I give him when he steps over my bed in the morning. I could take the key away from him, but it would only make things worse. You can break down all the doors here with the slightest effort.”

During this entire speech, K. pondered whether to take off his coat; however, he realized that if he didn’t, he wouldn’t be able to stay any longer. So he took off his coat, but laid it over his knees, so that he could put it back on if the conversation ended.

No sooner had he taken off his coat than one of the girls cried out, “He’s taken off his coat!” and K. heard them all crowding around the slits to see the spectacle. “The girls think,” the painter said, “that I’m going to paint you and that’s why you’re taking off your coat.”

“Well,” said K., only slightly amused, because he didn’t feel much better than before, even though he was now sitting in his shirt sleeves. Almost grumpily, he asked, “What were the two other possibilities called again?” 

He had already forgotten the terms. 

“The apparent acquittal and the postponement,” the painter said. “It’s up to you which one you choose. Both are achievable with my help, of course not without effort; the difference lies in this, that the apparent acquittal demands a collected, temporary effort, while the postponement demands a smaller but lasting one. First, then, the apparent acquittal. If you desire this, I will write a confirmation of your innocence on a sheet of paper. The text for such a confirmation has been passed down to me from my father and is completely irrefutable. With this confirmation, I will make my rounds among the judges I know. I will start, for example, by presenting the confirmation to the judge I am painting now, this evening, when he comes to the session. I will present it to him, explain that you are innocent, and vouch for your innocence. This is not just an outward, but a real, binding guarantee.” 

There was a reproachful look in the painter’s eyes as if blaming K. for imposing such a burden on him.


“That would be very kind,” K. said. 

“And the judge would believe me and still not actually acquit you?”

“As I already said,” the painter replied. “Besides, it’s not at all certain that everyone would believe me. Some judges, for example, will demand that I bring you to them myself. “So I’m free then,” K. said hesitantly.

“Yes,” said the painter, “but only seemingly free, or, better expressed, temporarily free. On these we must, even if I certainly won't fail to try several times, give up, but we may also do that, because individual judges cannot decide the outcome here. If I now have a sufficient number of signatures from the judges on this confirmation, I will go to the judge who is currently conducting your trial with it. It's possible that I even have his signature, then everything will develop a little faster than usual. In general, there are then hardly any more obstacles, it is then the time of highest hope for the accused. It is remarkable, but true, that people are more hopeful during this time than after the acquittal. There is no need for any special effort anymore. The judge possesses the guarantee of a number of judges in the confirmation, can acquit you without any worries, and will, after going through various formalities, undoubtedly do so for me and other acquaintances. You then leave the court and are free." "So I am then free," said K. hesitantly. "Yes," said the painter, "but only seemingly free, or, better expressed, temporarily free. The lower judges, to whom my acquaintances belong, do not have the right to acquit definitively, this right belongs only to the highest court, which is completely unreachable for you, for me, and for all of us. What it looks like there, we do not know and do not want to know. The great right to be acquitted of the accusation does not belong to our judges, but they do have the right to release from the accusation. This means that if you are acquitted in this way, you are temporarily released from the accusation for the moment, but it still hangs over you and can come into effect immediately as soon as the higher command comes. Since I am so well connected with the court, I can even tell you how the difference between the real and the apparent acquittal is shown purely externally in the regulations of the court offices. In the case of a real acquittal, the case files are completely filed away, they disappear completely from the proceedings, not only the accusation, but also the trial and even the acquittal are destroyed, everything is destroyed. It is different with the apparent acquittal. With the act, nothing further has happened than that it has been enriched with the confirmation of innocence, the acquittal and the justification for the acquittal. In all other respects, however, it remains in the proceedings, it is passed on to the higher courts, comes back to the lower ones and oscillates up and down with larger and smaller swings, with larger and smaller interruptions. These paths are unpredictable. From the outside, it may sometimes appear that everything has long been forgotten, the act lost and the acquittal complete. An insider will not believe that. No act is lost, there is no forgetting at court. One day - no one expects it - some judge picks up the act more carefully, realizes that the accusation is still alive in this case, and orders immediate arrest. I have assumed here that a long time passes between the apparent acquittal and the new arrest, which is possible, and I know of such cases, but it is just as possible that the acquitted person comes home from court and there are already people waiting to re-arrest him. Then the free life is naturally over." "And the trial begins again?" asked K., almost unbelievingly. "Certainly," said the painter, "the trial begins again, but there is again the possibility of achieving an apparent acquittal, as before. One must gather all one's strength again and not give up." The painter said this last part perhaps under the impression that K., who had slumped a little, was making on him. "But," asked K., as if wanting to anticipate any further revelations from the painter, "would not the achievement of a second acquittal be more difficult than the first?" "We can't say anything definite about that," replied the painter. "You probably mean that the judges, through the second arrest, are less inclined in their judgment?"

— Gentlemen, I'm speaking about those frequent famines that existed back then. I heard about it, though I don't know much history. But it seems that it had to be this way. When I arrived in the Swiss mountains, I was terribly astonished by the ruins of old castles, built on the mountain slopes, on steep cliffs, and at least a half-mile vertically (that's several miles along the paths). A castle, as you know, is a whole mountain of stone. The work is terrible, impossible! And these, of course, were all built by those poor people, the vassals. Besides, they had to pay all sorts of taxes and support the clergy. Where could they find the means to feed themselves and cultivate the land? There must have been few of them, they must have died terribly from hunger, and there was literally probably nothing to eat. I sometimes even thought: how did this nation not perish completely back then, and what did not happen to them, how could they withstand and endure? If there were cannibals, and perhaps there were many, then Lebedev, undoubtedly, is right; but I don't know why he brought up monks here and what he wants to say with that?

About the evening gathering at the Ypanchins' dacha, for which they were expecting Belockonskaya, Varvara Ardalionovna had told her brother quite accurately; the guests were indeed expected that very evening; but, as before, she had expressed this rather more sharply than was necessary. In truth, the matter had been arranged too hastily and even with a certain, quite unnecessary, agitation, and this was precisely because in this family "everything was done in a way that no one else did it." Everything was explained by the impatience of Elizaveta Prokofievna, "who no longer wished to have any doubts," and the fervent tremors of both parental hearts about the happiness of their beloved daughter. Moreover, Belockonskaya was indeed leaving soon; and since her patronage did indeed mean a great deal in society, and since they hoped she would be favorable to the prince, the parents counted on "society" accepting Aglaya's fiancé straight from the hands of the all-powerful "old woman," and therefore, if there was anything strange about it, under such patronage it would appear much less strange. The whole matter was that the parents were simply unable to decide for themselves: "Was there, and to what extent, anything strange about all this? Or was there nothing strange at all?".  A friendly and frank opinion of authoritative and competent people would have been just what was needed at this moment, when, thanks to Aglaya, nothing had been finally decided. In any case, sooner or later, the prince had to be introduced into society, about which he had no slightest notion. In short, he was going to be "shown." The evening, however, was planned simply: only "house friends" were expected, and in very small numbers. Besides Belockonskaya, they were expecting one lady, the wife of a very important nobleman and official. From the young men, they were counting on scarcely even Evgeny Pavlovich; he was to appear, accompanying Belockonskaya.

Someone must have slandered Josef K., for one morning he was arrested without having done anything wrong. The cook for Mrs. Grubach, his landlady, who brought him breakfast every day around eight o'clock, didn't come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited a while longer, saw the old woman who lived opposite him observing him with an unusual curiosity, and then, both bewildered and hungry, he rang the bell. Immediately, someone knocked, and a man, whom he had never seen in this apartment before, entered. He was slender yet sturdy, wearing a close-fitting black suit that, like a traveler's outfit, was adorned with various pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, making it appear particularly practical, although it wasn't clear what it was intended for. "Who are you?" asked K., sitting up halfway in bed. The man, however, ignored the question, as if his appearance should be taken for granted, and simply said, "You rang the bell?" "Anna should bring me breakfast," said K. and tried, first silently, to determine, through observation and thought, who this man actually was. But the man didn't subject himself to his gaze for long, but turned towards the door, which he opened slightly, to say to someone who was apparently just behind the door, "He wants Anna to bring him breakfast." A small laugh came from the next room; it wasn't clear from the sound whether it wasn't several people involved. Although the stranger couldn't have learned anything from this that he didn't already know, he said to K. in a tone of announcement, "It's impossible." "That would be news," said K., jumped out of bed, and quickly pulled on his trousers. "I want to see who's in the next room and how Mrs. Grubach will justify this disturbance to me." It occurred to him immediately that he shouldn't have said that out loud and that he was thereby acknowledging a kind of supervisory authority over the stranger, but it didn't seem important to him now. Nevertheless, the stranger seemed to grasp this, for he said, "Wouldn't you rather stay here?" "I don't want to stay here, nor do I want to be addressed by you until you introduce yourself." "It was meant well," said the stranger, and now voluntarily opened the door wider. In the next room, into which K. entered slower than he wanted to, it looked almost exactly the same as the previous evening. It was Mrs. Grubach's living room; perhaps there was a little more space in this room crammed with furniture, blankets, porcelain, and photographs than usual, one couldn't tell immediately, all the less so because the main change consisted in the presence of a man sitting by the open window with a book, from which he now looked up. "You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you?" "Yes, what do you want?" said K., looking from the new acquaintance to the man named Franz, who had remained in the doorway, and then back again. Through the open window, one could see the old woman again, who had stepped to the window opposite with truly senile curiosity to continue seeing everything. "I want to see Mrs. Grubach –," said K., made a movement as if to tear himself away from the two men, who were standing far away from him, and wanted to move on. "No," said the man by the window, threw the book onto a small table, and stood up. "You can't leave, you're under arrest." "It seems so," said K. "And why?" he then asked. "We're not obliged to tell you that. Go back to your room and wait. The proceedings have now been initiated, and you'll learn everything in due time. I'm exceeding my mandate by being so friendly with you. But I hope it's not heard by anyone else but Franz, and he himself is friendly to you despite all regulations. If you continue to have as much luck as you had with the selection of your guards, you can be confident." K. wanted to sit down, but now he saw that there was no seating available in the entire room, except for the armchair by the window. "You'll see how true this all is," said Franz and at the same time approached K. together with the other man. Especially the latter considerably outweighed K. and patted him on the shoulder several times. Both examined K.'s nightshirt and said that he would now have to put on a much worse one, but that they would keep this one, as well as his other clothes, and, if things turned out favorably for him, return them. "It's better if you give us the things rather than the depot," they said, "because there are often thefts at the depot, and moreover, after a certain time, they sell everything there, regardless of whether the proceedings are over or not. And how long do such procedures last, especially lately! You would eventually receive the proceeds from the depot, but first, the amount itself is already small, because the selling price isn't determined by the bid, but by the amount of the bribe, and further, such proceeds tend to decrease as they are passed from hand to hand and year after year." K. paid little attention to these words; he didn't highly value the right of disposal over his possessions that he might still have possessed. Much more important to him was to gain clarity about his situation; however, in the presence of these people, he couldn't even think. Again and again, the stomach of the second guard – they had to be guards – bumped friendly against him; when he looked up, he saw a dry, bony face with a strong, sidelong nose, which did not fit the thick body at all, and which exchanged glances with the other guard. What kind of people were these? What were they talking about? To which authority did they belong? K. lived in a state of law, everywhere there was peace, all laws were upheld; who dared to attack him in his apartment? He always tended to take everything as easily as possible, believing the worst only when the worst happened, not taking any precautions for the future, even when everything threatened. This time, however, it seemed different to him; since the first sight of the guard Franz, he had been determined not to give up the slightest advantage he might have over these people. K. saw a small risk in the fact that later people might say he hadn't understood the joke; however, he remembered – without it being his usual habit to learn from experience – some insignificant cases in which he had acted carelessly, to the detriment of himself, unlike his friends, without the slightest feeling for the possible consequences. It shouldn't happen again, at least not this time; if it was a comedy, he wanted to play along.

In the next room, into which K. entered slower than he wanted to, it looked almost exactly the same as the night before. It was Frau Grubach's living room, perhaps there was a little more space in this room overflowing with furniture, covers, porcelain, and photographs than usual, one couldn't tell right away, all the less so because the main change consisted in the presence of a man who was sitting by the open window with a book, from which he now looked up. "Yes, what do you want?" said K., looking from the new acquaintance to the one named Franz, who had remained in the doorway, and then back again. Through the open window, one could see the old woman who, with truly senile curiosity, had moved to the opposite window to continue watching everything. "I want to see Frau Grubach –," said K., making a movement as if he wanted to break free from the two men, who were standing far away from him, and move forward. I'm exceeding my mandate if I'm so friendly to you. But I hope it's not heard by anyone else besides Franz, and he himself is exceptionally friendly to you, despite all regulations. If you continue to have as much luck as you have had in the appointment of your guards, then you can be confident." K. wanted to sit down, but now he saw that there was no place to sit in the whole room except for the armchair by the window. And how long do such proceedings usually take, especially lately! You would eventually receive the proceeds from the depot, of course, but this amount is firstly already low, because in the sale, the amount of the bid, not the amount of the bribe, decides, and furthermore, such proceeds tend to decrease, the more they are passed from hand to hand and year to year." K. paid little attention to their words; the right of disposal over his belongings, which he may still have possessed, he didn't value highly; much more important was it for him to gain clarity about his situation; but in the presence of these people, he couldn't even think; again and again the belly of the second guard – they must be guards – literally friendlily bumped into him; but when he looked up, he saw a dry, bony face with a strongly side-tilted nose, which was quite incongruous with that thick body, and which communicated with the other guard. What kind of people were they? What were they talking about? To which authority did they belong? K. lived in a state of law, there was peace everywhere, all laws were upheld, who dared to raid him in his apartment? He always tended to take everything as lightly as possible, believing the worst only at the point of its occurrence, not taking any precautions for the future, even when everything threatened. This time, however, it didn't seem right to him; one could, of course, view the whole thing as a joke, as a rude joke that, for unknown reasons, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday, his colleagues at the bank had played on him; it was certainly possible, perhaps all he needed was to laugh at the guards' faces in some way, and they would laugh along; maybe they were men from the street corner, they didn't look unlike them – nevertheless, this time, since the first sight of the guard Franz, he had been determined not to give up the slightest advantage he might have over these people. Someone must have denounced Josef K., for without having done anything wrong, he was arrested one morning. The cook of Frau Grubach, his landlady, who brought him breakfast every day at about eight o'clock, didn't come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited a while longer, saw from his pillow the old woman who lived opposite him, who was observing him with an unusual curiosity, then, both bewildered and hungry, he rang the bell. Immediately, there was a knock and a man, whom he had never seen in the apartment before, entered. He was slender yet solidly built, wearing a close-fitting black suit, which, like travel suits, was equipped with various pleats, pockets, buckles, buttons, and a belt, and as a result, without it being clear what it was supposed to be used for, appeared particularly practical.  "Who are you?" asked K., sitting up half-straight in bed. The man ignored the question, as if his appearance was something to be accepted, and simply said, "You rang?" "Anna is supposed to bring me breakfast," said K., trying first to ascertain silently, through attention and consideration, who this man actually was. But he didn't let himself be scrutinized for too long, but turned towards the door, which he opened slightly, to say to someone who was apparently just behind the door, "He wants Anna to bring him breakfast." A small chuckle came from the next room, it wasn't certain from the sound whether or not several people were involved. Although the stranger couldn't have learned anything from this that he didn't already know, he now said to K. in the tone of a report, "It's impossible." "That would be new," said K., jumped out of bed and quickly pulled on his trousers. "I want to see who these people are in the next room, and how Frau Grubach will answer for this disturbance." It did occur to him that he shouldn't have said it aloud and that he was thereby implicitly acknowledging a supervisory right of the stranger, but it didn't seem important to him now.  After all, the stranger took it that way, for he said, "Wouldn't you rather stay here?" "I don't want to stay here, nor be spoken to by you, as long as you don't introduce yourself." "It was meant well," said the stranger and now voluntarily opened the door.  In the next room, into which K. entered slower than he wanted to, it looked almost exactly the same as the evening before. "You should have stayed in your room! Didn't Franz tell you so?" Through the open window, one could see the old woman again, who had come to the opposite window with truly senile curiosity to see everything. "I want to see Frau Grubach –," said K., made a movement as if to pull himself away from the two men, who were standing far away from him, and wanted to go on. "No," said the man by the window, threw the book onto a table and stood up. "You can't leave, you are under arrest." "That seems to be the case," said K. "And why?" he then asked. "We are not authorized to tell you that. Go back to your room and wait. The proceedings have now been initiated, and you will learn everything in due time. I'm going beyond my mandate if I speak to you so amicably. But I hope it isn't heard by anyone else but Franz, and he himself is friendly to you despite all regulations. If you continue to be as lucky with your wardens as you have been so far, you can be confident." K. wanted to sit down, but then he saw that there was no seating anywhere in the room except for the armchair by the window. "You will see how true all this is," said Franz, and walked towards K. at the same time as the other man. Particularly the latter was considerably taller than K. and patted him repeatedly on the shoulder. Both examined K.'s nightgown and said that he would now have to put on a much better one, but that they would keep this one, as well as his other laundry, and, if things went well for him, return it to him. "It's better if you give the things to us rather than to the depot," they said, "because things often get mislaid at the depot, and moreover, they sell everything after a certain time, regardless of whether the proceedings have ended or not. And how long do such processes take, especially lately! You would eventually get the proceeds from the depot, of course, but these proceeds are firstly already small, because in the sale, it's not the amount offered that counts, but the amount of the bribe, and furthermore, such proceeds tend to decrease if they are passed from hand to hand and year after year." K. paid little attention to these remarks; the right of disposal over his belongings, which he may have still possessed, he did not highly value. It shouldn't happen again, at least not this time; if it was a comedy, he wanted to play along.

—  Ah, morality! As if I were still a boy, I know that myself, — Gan’ya interrupted heatedly, — and at least for having had this conversation with you. I am not going into this darkness for money, Your Highness, — he continued, speaking as if wounded in his youthful pride, —  I would probably make a mistake calculating it, both in my mind and in character. I am going because of passion, because of my calling, because I have a major goal. You think that I will receive seventy-five thousand and immediately buy a carriage. No, I will be wearing my third-year old frock coat for years to come and abandon all my club acquaintances. We have few people who can endure, even though everyone here is a moneylender, and I want to endure. The main thing is to see it through to the end — that's the whole point!  Ptitsyn, at seventeen, slept on the street, peddled pocket knives, and started from a single kopek; now he has sixty thousand, but only after such a workout! I'll leap over that entire workout and start right from capital; in fifteen years they'll say, "Here is Ivlogin, the king of the Jews." You say I'm not an original person.  Understand this, dear prince, there is nothing more offensive to a man of our time and kind than to say that he is not original, weak-willed, without special talents, an ordinary person. You haven't even considered me a decent scoundrel, and you know, I wanted to eat you for it the other day! You offended me more than Epantin, who considers me — without conversation, without temptation, in the pureness of his soul, mark this — capable of selling his wife to me! This, father, has been bothering me for a long time, and I want money. You know, once I have money, I will be a man of the highest degree of originality. Money is the most insidious and hateful thing, precisely because they even give talents. And they will continue to do so until the end of the world. You'll say it's all childish or perhaps poetry — well, all the better for me, and the deed will still be done. I'll see it through and endure. Rira bien qui rira le dernier!  [7]  Why does Epantin offend me so much? Out of malice, you say? Never. Simply because I am too insignificant. Well, and then…  But enough of this.  It's time. Kolya has stuck his nose out twice already: he's inviting you to dinner.  And I'm from the courtyard. I'll drop by your place sometimes. You'll have it good with us; now they'll accept you into the family right away. Just watch out, don't reveal it. It seems to me that we will either be friends or enemies. And what do you think, prince, if I had kissed your hand yesterday — as sincerely as I offered — would I have become your enemy for that later?

The Great Heavenly Sovereign summoned all the civil and military officials, as well as the immortal ministers, and asked, "How many years has this demon monkey lived? Which generation was he born into, to be so learned?" Before he could finish, Thousand-Eyed and Wind-Eared amongst them stepped forward and said, "This monkey is a stone monkey born three hundred years ago. At the time, it was thought nothing of, unaware that over these years he has cultivated himself into an immortal, subduing dragons and tigers, and even defying death. " The Jade Emperor said, "Should the God of Roads be sent down to subdue him?" Before he could finish, Great White, Chang Geng Star, bowed his head and presented his opinion: "In the Three Realms, all beings with nine orifices can cultivate into immortals. But this monkey was born of heaven and earth, nurtured by the sun and moon. He walks on the heavens and earth, eats dew and drinks the morning mist; now that he has achieved the immortal way, with the power to subdue dragons and tigers, why is he so different from mortals? Your Majesty, I beseech you, in the spirit of compassion for all living beings, issue a decree to invite him up to heaven, grant him a position of power, and enroll him in the celestial registers, confining him to this realm. If he obeys destiny, then he can be promoted again. If he defies destiny, he will be apprehended. Three years had passed. The Master ascended the throne once more and spoke to the gathered crowd. He discussed koans and parables, expounding on outward appearances and inner substance. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Sun Wukong?" Sun Wukong stepped forward and knelt. "Disciple is here." The Master said, "What path have you been cultivating?" The Master said, "Since you've grasped Dharma nature and found your root, you've already entered the realm of the divine body, yet you are merely guarding against the 'three calamities and great dangers.'" Sun Wukong, upon hearing this, pondered for a long time before saying, "Master's words are amiss. I have often heard that those of high virtue live long lives, equal to heaven's, able to pass through fire and water unharmed, free from all ailments. How can there be such a thing as the 'three calamities and great dangers'?" The Master said, "This is an extraordinary path: one that takes away the Heaven's creative force, violating the celestial mysteries. After achieving the elixir, spirits and ghosts find it difficult to approach. Although your appearance may remain youthful, after five hundred years, a heavenly thunderbolt will strike you down. You must attain enlightenment and open your mind beforehand to avoid it. If you manage to evade it, you will live as long as heaven; if not, you will perish. Another five hundred years later, a fire calamity will descend. This fire is not heavenly fire nor mortal fire; it is called 'yin fire.' It will rise from the wellspring below your womb, piercing through the palace walls, turning your five viscera into ash and your limbs into decay, rendering your millennia of ascetic practices illusory. Another five hundred years later, a wind calamity will strike. This wind is not a wind from the east, west, south, or north, nor is it the wind that dries gold, blows back the moon, or rustles through flowers, willows, pines, and bamboos. It is called 'pi feng.' It will blow into your six internal organs from the fontanelle, pass through your dantian, and pierce your nine orifices, causing your flesh and bones to dissipate, leading to your self-dissolution. He bowed his head in reverence and said, "Great Master, you have shown mercy by revealing the method to avoid the three calamities. I will never forget your kindness." The Master said, "It is not difficult. It is simply that you are different from others, hence I cannot pass on the method directly." Sun Wukong said, "I too have a round head that reaches the heavens, feet that spread wide on the ground, nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six organs. How am I different from others?" It was a very rainy, stormy morning when K., full of annoyance at the day ahead, arrived at the office at seven o’clock, in order to get some work done before the visitor took everything away from him. He was very tired, because he had spent half the night studying an Italian grammar in preparation; the window, which he had spent far too much time sitting by recently, was more tempting than the desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately, the servant just then entered and reported that the Director had sent him to see if the Commercial Manager was already there; if he was, he should kindly come to the reception room, as the gentleman from Italy was already there. “I’m coming,” said K., stuffed a small dictionary into his pocket, grabbed an album of city sights he had prepared for the foreigner, and walked through the deputy director’s office into the director’s room. He was happy to have come to the office so early and to be immediately available, something no one had probably seriously expected. The deputy director’s office was, of course, still empty as if in the deepest night; probably the servant had also been asked to summon him to the reception room, but without success. When K. entered the reception room, the two gentlemen rose from the deep armchairs. The Director smiled friendly, obviously very pleased with K.’s arrival, he immediately arranged for the introduction, the Italian shook K.’s hand firmly and, with a smile, called someone a “morning person.” K. did not quite understand who he meant; besides, it was a peculiar word, the meaning of which K. did not grasp until after a while. He responded with a few smooth sentences, which the Italian received with laughter, while he repeatedly ran his nervously over his gray-blue, bushy mustache. This mustache was obviously perfumed, one was almost tempted to approach and smell it. 

As everyone sat down and a small introductory conversation began, K. noticed with great discomfort that he only understood the Italian in fragments. When he spoke quite calmly, he understood him almost completely; but these were only rare exceptions; mostly, the words gushed from his mouth, he shook his head as if in pleasure over it.  At such times, however, he would regularly get involved in some dialect that sounded nothing Italian to K., but which the Director not only understood but also spoke, which K. could have predicted, after all, the Italian came from Southern Italy, where the Director had lived for some years.  In any case, K. realized that the opportunity to understand the Italian was largely taken from him, because even his French was difficult to understand, and besides, the mustache obscured the lip movements, whose sight might have helped with understanding. K. began to foresee a lot of inconvenience; for the moment, he gave up trying to understand the Italian—in the presence of the Director, who understood him so easily, it would have been unnecessary effort—and he limited himself to observing him with displeasure, as he sank deeply and yet lightly into the armchair, how he often tugged at his short, sharply cut frock, and how once he raised his arms and moved his hands loosely in the joints, trying to depict something that K. couldn’t understand, although he kept his eyes on the hands without looking away.  Finally, the earlier fatigue took hold of K., who was otherwise watching the back and forth of the conversation with an unengaged gaze, and he caught himself, fortunately just in time, on the verge of getting up, turning around, and leaving. 

Finally, the Italian looked at his watch and jumped up. After bidding farewell to the Director, he pressed himself against K., so close that K. had to push his armchair back to move. The Director, who certainly recognized K.’s plight in the face of this Italian, intervened in the conversation, and so cleverly and delicately that it seemed as if he were only offering small pieces of advice, while in reality he made everything the Italian, tirelessly throwing at him, understandable to K. in short.  K. learned from him that the Italian had some business to take care of for the time being, that he unfortunately wouldn’t have much time at all, that he certainly did not intend to rush through all the sights, that he had, however,—although only if K. agreed, the decision rested with him—decided to visit only the Cathedral, but to thoroughly examine it. He was extremely happy to be able to take this tour in the company of such a learned and amiable man—K. was meant, who was busy with nothing other than eavesdropping on the Italian and quickly catching the Director’s words—and he asked him, if he was free, to meet him in the Cathedral in two hours, around ten o’clock. He himself hoped to be there for sure by then. K. replied something appropriate, the Italian first shook the Director’s hand, then K.’s, then again the Director’s hand and, followed by both, half turned away from them, still not stopping talking, went to the door. K. then stayed with the Director for a while longer, who looked particularly ill today. He felt he had to apologize to K. in some way and said—they stood close together confidentially—that he had initially intended to go with the Italian himself, but then—he didn’t give a closer reason—he had decided to send K. instead. If K. didn’t understand the Italian at first, he shouldn’t be surprised, the understanding came very quickly, and even if he didn’t understand much at all, it wasn’t so bad, because it wasn’t so important for the Italian to be understood.  By the way, K.’s Italian was surprisingly good, and he would certainly get along excellently with it. With that, K. was dismissed. 

The time he still had free, he spent writing down rare vocabulary that he needed for guidance in the Cathedral from the dictionary. It was extremely tedious work; servants brought the mail, officials came with various requests and stayed by the door, since they saw K. busy, without moving away, until they had been heard by him; the deputy director didn’t let the opportunity pass to interrupt K., often came in, took the dictionary from his hand and leafed through it seemingly aimlessly; even parties appeared, when the door opened, in the dim light of the anteroom and bowed hesitantly—they wanted to attract attention, but were not sure if they had been seen—all of this moved around K. as if around his center, while he himself compiled the words he needed, then searched for them in the dictionary, then wrote them down, then practiced their pronunciation and finally tried to memorize them. But his earlier good memory seemed to have deserted him entirely; sometimes he became so angry with the Italian, who caused him this effort, that he buried the dictionary under papers, with the firm intention of not preparing any more, but then he realized that he could not just walk around with the Italian mutely in and out of the art works in the Cathedral, and he pulled the dictionary out again with even greater anger.

Anyway, K. realised that the possibility of understanding the Italian was largely taken away from him, because even his French was only hard to understand, and his moustache also obscured the lip movements, whose sight might have helped with understanding. Finally, the earlier tiredness overtook K., who was otherwise idly following the back and forth of the conversation with his eyes, and he caught himself, fortunately still in time, about to stand up, turn around and walk away in his distraction. Finally, the Italian looked at the clock and jumped up. After he had said goodbye to the Director, he pushed himself against K., so close that K. had to push back his armchair to be able to move. The Director, who certainly recognized K.'s plight in the face of this Italian, joined the conversation, and so cleverly and subtly that it seemed as if he was only adding small pieces of advice, while in reality he was explaining everything that the Italian, tirelessly falling into his speech, had said, in the shortest possible way to K. K. learned from him that the Italian still had some business to attend to, that unfortunately he would only have a little time, that he certainly did not intend to rush through all the sights, but rather - although this was only if K. agreed, the decision lay solely with him - he had decided to only visit the Cathedral, but thoroughly. He was immensely delighted to be able to make this visit in the company of such an erudite and amiable man - which meant K., who was occupied with nothing else but listening to the Italian and quickly grasping the Director's words - and asked him, if the hour was convenient for him, to meet him at the Cathedral in two hours, around ten o'clock. K. replied something appropriate, the Italian first shook hands with the Director, then with K., and then again with the Director, and went out, still half turned towards them, but still not stopping talking, followed by both. He believed that he had to apologize to K. in some way and said - they stood confidentially close together - that he had first intended to go with the Italian himself, but then - he gave no further reason - he had decided to send K. instead. By the way, K.'s Italian was surprisingly good, and he would certainly get along excellently with the task. With that, K. was dismissed. In recent years, all three of the general's daughters – Alexandra, Adelaide, and Aglaya – had grown up and reached maturity. True, all three were only daughters of the Epanchins, but they were of princely lineage on their mother's side, with considerable dowries, and their father, who might well aspire to a very high position in the future, and, which was also quite important, all three were remarkably beautiful, not excluding the eldest, Alexandra, who was already twenty-five years old. The middle daughter was twenty-three, and the youngest, Aglaya, had just turned twenty. This youngest was even a veritable beauty and was beginning to attract a great deal of attention in society. But that was not all: all three distinguished themselves by their education, intellect, and talents. It was known that they loved each other dearly and supported one another. Even whispers circulated about some supposed sacrifices made by the two elder sisters for the benefit of their younger sister, the darling of the family. In society, they not only avoided drawing attention to themselves but were even excessively modest. No one could reproach them for arrogance or conceit, yet everyone knew that they were proud and understood their own worth. The eldest was a musician, the middle sister a remarkable painter; but this was known to almost no one for many years, and it only came to light very recently, and quite accidentally. In short, they were spoken of in the most flattering terms. But there were also detractors.

It turned out that one had to calm down, look cool, and wait. But alas, the calm did not last even ten minutes. The first blow to coolness was dealt by news of what had happened on Kamenny Island during Mama's absence. (Lizaveta Prokofievna's trip took place the very next morning after the prince had come at one o'clock instead of ten the previous night.) The sisters, in response to their mother's impatient questions, answered in great detail, first of all, that "apparently nothing, really, had happened without her," that the prince had come, that Aglaya had not come out to him for half an hour, then had gone out and, as soon as she did, had immediately proposed to the prince that they play chess; that the prince did not know how to play chess at all, and Aglaya had immediately defeated him; she had become very merry and terribly ridiculed the prince for his inability, laughing at him so much that it was a pity to look at him. Then she proposed to play cards, "Duraki." But then things turned out completely differently: the prince turned out to be such a formidable "Duraki" player, as... as a professor; he played masterfully; Aglaya both cheated and switched cards, and even stole in his very eyes, and still, he beat her every time; five times in a row. Aglaya became terribly agitated, even completely lost herself; she said such sharp and bold things to the prince that he stopped laughing and completely paled when she finally said to him that "her foot would not be in this room as long as he was sitting there, and that it was even shameless on his part to come to them, and even at night, at one o'clock, after all that had happened." Then she slammed the door and left. The prince left like from a funeral, despite all their consolations. Suddenly, a quarter of an hour after the prince had left, Aglaya rushed upstairs to the terrace, and with such haste that she didn't even wipe her eyes, although they were red from crying; she ran away because Kolya had come and brought a hedgehog. They all began to look at the hedgehog; in response to their questions, Kolya explained that the hedgehog was not his, but that he was now going with a friend, another student, Kostya Lebedev, who had remained outside and was ashamed to enter because he was carrying an ax; that he and the hedgehog had bought it from a passing peasant. The peasant had sold the hedgehog for fifty kopecks, and they had already persuaded him to sell the ax because it was handy and a very good one. Suddenly, Aglaya began to insist terribly on Kolya selling her the hedgehog, getting worked up, even calling Kolya "dear." Kolya resisted for a long time, but finally couldn't stand it and called Kostya Lebedev, who really came in with an ax and was very embarrassed. K. stared at the guard. Could he possibly be getting lessons in obedience from a younger man? Was his openness being punished with a rebuke? And nothing about the reason for his arrest, or who had ordered it, had been revealed to him? He grew agitated, pacing back and forth, unhindered by anyone, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair, passed the three men, and said, "It's pointless," whereupon they turned to him, looking at him with a mixture of openness and seriousness, and finally came to a halt in front of the guard's table again. "The state attorney Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "can I call him?" "Certainly," said the guard, "but I don't see what purpose that would serve, unless you have some private matter to discuss with him." "What purpose?" cried K., more distressed than angry. "Who are you? You're talking about purpose, and conducting the most pointless act imaginable! Isn't it infuriating? The men first attacked me, and now they sit or stand here, letting me perform a lesson in absurdity for them. What purpose would there be in calling a state attorney when I'm supposedly under arrest? Well, I won't call." "But do," said the guard, and stretched out his hand towards the next room, where the telephone was, "please, make the call." "No, I won't," said K., and went to the window. Across the street, the group was still at the window and seemed only now, as K. approached, to be slightly disturbed by his presence. The older men wanted to rise, but the man behind them calmed them. "There are also spectators over there!" shouted K. to the guard, pointing with his finger. "Away from there!" he then called over to them. The three of them immediately stepped back a few steps, the two older ones even behind the man who shielded them with his broad body, and according to his movements, was saying something unintelligible to a distance. But they didn't disappear completely, they seemed to be waiting for the moment when they could approach the window unnoticed. "Intrusive, disrespectful people!" said K. as he turned back into the room. The guard possibly agreed, as K. believed he saw with a side glance, but it was equally possible that he hadn't been listening, because he had a hand firmly pressed on the table, seemingly comparing the length of his fingers. The two guards were sitting on a trunk covered with a decorative cloth, rubbing their knees. The three young men had their hands on their hips and looked around aimlessly. It was as quiet as in some forgotten office. "Well, gentlemen," said K., it seemed to him for a moment as if he were carrying the weight of everything on his shoulders, "judging by your appearance, my matter must be finished. I believe it is best not to dwell on the legitimacy or illegitimacy of your actions and to bring this matter to a conciliatory close with a handshake. If you agree with me, then please—" and he stepped towards the guard's table and extended his hand. The guard raised his eyes, nibbled his lips, and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed the guard would strike him. However, the guard stood up, picked up a hard, round hat that was lying on Fräulein Bürstner's bed, and carefully placed it on his head with both hands, as one does when trying on a new hat. "How simple everything seems to you!" he said to K. "We should bring this matter to a conciliatory close, did you say? No, no, that really won't do. Not that I want you to despair, of course. No, why should you? You are simply arrested, that's all. I told you that, I did, and I saw how you received it. That's enough for today, and we can say goodbye, though only provisionally. You'll probably want to go to the bank now?" "To the bank?" asked K., "I thought I was under arrest." K. asked with a certain defiance, because although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt, especially since the guard had stood up, increasingly independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He intended, if they were to leave, to run after them to the front door and offer them his arrest. Therefore, he repeated: "How can I go to the bank when I'm under arrest?" "Ah, so," said the guard, who was already at the door, "you misunderstood me. You are arrested, certainly, but that shouldn't prevent you from fulfilling your duties. Your usual way of life should not be hindered either." "Then being arrested isn't very serious," said K., and approached the guard. "I never meant it otherwise," said the guard. "It seems, then, that the announcement of the arrest wasn't even very necessary," said K., and moved even closer. All of them had now gathered in a cramped space by the door. "It was my duty," said the guard. "A stupid duty," said K. stubbornly. "Perhaps," answered the guard, "but we don't want to waste our time with such talk. I assumed you wanted to go to the bank. Since you are paying attention to every word, I add: I am not forcing you to go to the bank, I just assumed you wanted to. And to make this easier for you and to make your arrival at the bank as discreet as possible, I have had these three gentlemen, your colleagues, at your disposal." "What?" cried K., staring at the three of them. These so uncharacteristic, bloodless, young men, whom he still only remembered as a group in photographs, were actually officials from his bank, not colleagues, that was too much to say and proved a gap in the guard's all-knowingness, but they were indeed subordinate bank officials. How had K. overlooked this? How had he had to endure the guard and the guards just to not recognize these three? The stiff Rabensteiner, Kullich with his deep-set eyes and Kaminer with the unbearable smile caused by a chronic muscle spasm. "Good morning!" said K. after a while, and extended his hand to the three men who bowed politely. "I didn't recognize you at all. Well, then we'll get to work, shall we?" The men nodded eagerly and laughingly, as if they had been waiting for this all along. Just as K. missed his hat, which had been left in his room, they all ran after him to fetch it, which at least suggested a certain awkwardness. K. stood still and watched them go through the two open doors, the last one being the nonchalant Rabensteiner, who simply struck an elegant stride. Kaminer handed him the hat, and K. had to say expressly, as was often necessary at the bank, that Kaminer's smile wasn't intentional, that he couldn't smile intentionally at all. In the foyer, Frau Grubach, who didn't look very guilty, opened the apartment door for the whole company, and K. saw, as he often did, on her apron tie, which was unnecesarily cut low into her mighty body. Downstairs, K. decided, with the watch in his hand, to take a car to avoid further unnecessary delay. Kaminer ran to the corner to get the car, the other two obviously tried to distract K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the opposite gate, where the large man with the blonde pointed beard appeared, and, slightly embarrassed at first by the fact that he was now showing his full height, retreated to the wall and leaned against it. "Don't look!" he blurted out, without noticing how unusual such a statement was towards independent men. It was, however, unnecessary, because just then the car arrived, they got in, and drove off. At that moment, K. remembered that he hadn't noticed the guard and the guards leaving at all. The guard had concealed the three officials, and now the officials concealed the guard. It didn't show much wit, and K. made a note to observe himself more closely in this regard. Yet, he involuntarily turned his head back and leaned over the back of the car to possibly catch a glimpse of the guard and the guards. Although he didn't appear to need encouragement at the moment, the men seemed tired, Rabensteiner looked out the right side of the car, Kullich out the left, and only Kaminer stood with his grin available, which unfortunately humanity forbade one from mocking.

The more he thought about it, the angrier he became, unable to bear the humiliation.  Gnashed his teeth and leaped out, snarling, "Where did you come from, you wicked demon?  You dare to offend me!" 

The pilgrim said, "Don't bother with where I come from. Just return the horse, and I'll spare your life!" 

The dragon replied, "I swallowed your horse. How can I spit it back out? What can I do if I don't return it?" 

The pilgrim said, "If you don't return the horse, you'll face my wrath! I'll beat you to death and avenge my horse!"

The two clashed fiercely under the cliff. After countless blows, the young dragon, truly unable to withstand the onslaught, flickered, transformed into a water snake, and slithered into the grass.

The Monkey King strode forward, leapt to the edge of the chasm, and unleashed his power to churn the river, clearing the once crystal-clear water of the Eagle's Sorrow Ravine, turning it into a churning expanse like the Yellow River in flood.  The evil dragon, deep in the ravine, sat and lay in calm contemplation, thinking to himself: “This is a double blessing and a single calamity.  Having just escaped death under Heaven's decree, after less than a year of leisurely living, I stumble upon this kind of vicious demon. He has come to harm me!”  The more he thought, the angrier he became, unable to bear the humiliation. Gnawing his teeth, he leaped out and snarled, “Where do you come from, you demonic fiend? How dare you humiliate me!” 
The pilgrim said, “Don’t concern yourself with where I come from.  Just return the horse, and I will spare your life!” The dragon replied, “I have swallowed your horse, how can I spit it out? If I don’t return it, what can you do?” 
The pilgrim said, “If you don’t return the horse, prepare to face my staff! I will beat you to death and avenge my horse.”
They clashed again and again beneath the cliff face. After many rounds, the young dragon, unable to hold out, suddenly flickered, transformed into a water snake, and slithered into the grass.

Tri-Pillar praised him endlessly, saying, "You're truly a mountain god, Taibao!"

He held a fork in one hand and dragged the tiger with the other, leading the way. Tri-Pillar followed, leading his horse, as they strolled over the hillside. Suddenly, they saw a mountain lodge. The entrance was truly remarkable: towering ancient trees, winding wild vines. The wind rustled through the valleys, dust filled the air, and the cliffs possessed a strange, unique grandeur. A path through wild flowers released their fragrance, while several bamboo stalks stood green and lush. A thatched roofed gatehouse, a walled courtyard, both worthy of being depicted in art; stone slab bridge, white mud walls, truly delightful and rare. The autumn scene was desolate yet refreshing, the atmosphere solitary and majestic. Fallen yellow leaves lined the road, white clouds drifted across the peaks. Birds called within the sparse woods, while a dog barked at the lodge entrance. Berchinn arrived at the gate, threw the dead tiger down, and shouted, "Where are you lads?" Three or four servants with strange and sinister appearances came out, dragging and pulling the tiger inside. Berchinn ordered, "Hurry and skin it, prepare it for our guests." He then turned back to welcome Tri-Pillar inside.

— As for life in prison, one can perhaps disagree, — the prince said. — I once heard a story about a man who spent twelve years in prison; he was one of my professor's patients. He had fits, was sometimes agitated, cried, and even tried to kill himself. His life in prison was very sad, I assure you, but certainly not cheap. And his only companions were a spider and a sapling that grew under his window... But I'd rather tell you about another encounter I had last year with a man. There was one very strange circumstance about it—strange because such a thing rarely happens. This man was once led, along with others, to the scaffold and sentenced to death by firing squad for a political crime. Twenty minutes later, a pardon was read and a different punishment was assigned. But, however, during that twenty-minute interval, between two sentences, he lived under the unshakeable conviction that he would die in a few minutes. I was terribly eager to listen when he sometimes recalled those impressions, and I several times started questioning him again. He remembered everything with extraordinary clarity and said that he would never forget a single moment of those minutes. Twenty paces from the scaffold, where the crowd and soldiers were gathered, there were three stakes driven in the ground, as there were several convicts. The first three were led to the stakes, tied up, dressed in their executioner's robes (long white smocks), and white hoods were pulled over their eyes so they couldn't see the rifles; then, against each stake, a squad of several soldiers stood in line. My acquaintance was eighth in line, so he had to go to the stakes in the third group. The priest went around all of them with a cross. It seemed that there were five minutes left, no more. He said that those five minutes seemed to him an endless amount of time, an enormous fortune; it seemed to him that in those five minutes he would live so many lives that there was no need to think about the last moment now, so he made various arrangements: he allotted two minutes to say goodbye to his companions, then another two minutes to think about himself for the last time, and then, for one last look around. He remembered very well what he had done precisely those three things and how he had calculated the time. He was twenty-seven years old, healthy and strong; when saying goodbye to his companions, he remembered that he had asked one of them a rather extraneous question and was even very interested in the answer. Then, after he had said goodbye to his companions, the two minutes came that he had allotted to think about himself; he knew in advance what he would be thinking about: he wanted to imagine as quickly and vividly as possible what it would be like: that now he exists and lives, but in three minutes he will be something else, someone or something—but who? Where? All this he tried to decide in those two minutes! There was a church not far away, and the spire of the cathedral with its gilded roof sparkled in the bright sun. He remembered that he stared stubbornly at that roof and the rays emanating from it; he couldn't tear his gaze away; it seemed to him that those rays were his new nature, that in three minutes he would somehow merge with them... The uncertainty and aversion to this new thing, which was about to come upon him, were terrible; but he says that nothing was heavier for him at that time than the constant thought: 'What if I didn't have to die! What if I could turn back time—what an eternity! And it would all be mine! I would turn each minute into a whole century, I would lose nothing, I would count each minute, and I would not waste anything for nothing!' He said that this thought finally turned into such a rage within him that he even wished for them to shoot him sooner.

My acquaintance stood eighth in line, so he had to go to the poles in the third group. The priest walked around all of them with a cross. It seemed that he had five minutes left, no more. He said that those five minutes seemed to him like an endless span, a huge treasure; he felt that in those five minutes he would live so many lives that there was no need to even think about the last moment yet, so he made several arrangements: he allocated two minutes to say goodbye to his companions, then another two minutes to think for the last time about himself, and then, to look around one last time. He very clearly remembered making exactly these three arrangements and calculating them that way. He was twenty-seven years old, healthy and strong; when saying goodbye to his companions, he remembered asking one of them a rather irrelevant question and even becoming quite interested in the answer. Then, when he had said goodbye to his comrades, the two minutes came that he had set aside to think about himself; he knew in advance what he would think about: he wanted to imagine as quickly and vividly as possible what it would be like: he is now existing and living, and in three minutes he will be something else, someone or something—but who? Where? He tried to resolve all this in those two minutes! A church was not far away, and the gilded spire of the cathedral glinted in the bright sun. He remembered that he stared intensely at that spire and the rays emanating from it; he couldn't tear himself away from the rays; it seemed to him that these rays were his new nature, that in three minutes he would somehow merge with them... The uncertainty and disgust at this new thing that would come upon him immediately were terrible; but he says that nothing was heavier for him at that time than the incessant thought: 'What if I didn't die! What if I could turn back life—what an infinity! And all this would be mine! I would then turn each minute into a whole century, I would lose nothing, I would count every minute, I would not waste anything for nothing!' He said that this thought finally grew into such a frenzy that he wanted to be shot sooner."

As for life in prison, one might disagree, the prince said, I once heard a story from a man who had been incarcerated for about twelve years. He was one of my professor's patients; a sick man. He had seizures, was sometimes agitated, wept, and even tried to take his own life. His life in prison was undeniably gloomy, I assure you, but certainly not cheap. His only companions were a spider and a sapling that grew beneath his window. But I would rather tell you about another encounter I had last year with a man. There was one very strange circumstance about it, strange precisely because such a case is rarely encountered. This man was once led to the scaffold, along with others, and the death sentence by firing squad was read to him for a political crime. Twenty minutes later, a pardon was read and a different punishment was decreed. However, during that interval between two verdicts, twenty minutes, or at least a quarter of an hour, he lived under the unshakeable conviction that he would die within minutes. I was terribly eager to hear him recount his experiences from that time, and I several times started questioning him anew. He remembered everything with extraordinary clarity and said that he would never forget those minutes.

Right after the greeting – settling into the armchair, which K. invited him to do, he had no time – he asked K. for a short private conversation. "It's necessary," he said, swallowing with effort, "for my peace of mind, it's necessary." K. immediately sent the servants out of the room, with the instruction not to let anyone in. "What have I heard, Josef?" the uncle exclaimed when they were alone, sat down on the table, and stuffed various papers under himself, without looking, to sit better. K. was silent, he knew what was coming, but, suddenly relaxed from the strenuous work he had been doing, he initially gave himself over to a pleasant lethargy and looked out the window at the opposite side of the street, of which only a small, triangular section was visible from his seat, a piece of bare wall between two shop windows. "You're looking out the window!" the uncle called out with raised arms, "for heaven's sake, Josef, answer me! Is it true, can it really be true?" "Dear Uncle," said K., tearing himself from his distraction, "I don't even know what you want from me." "Josef," said the uncle warningly, "you've always told the truth, as far as I know. Should I take your last words as a bad omen?" "I guess I know what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "That's right," replied the uncle, nodding slowly, "I've heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she doesn't have any contact with you, you don't care much for her, unfortunately, but she found out. Today I received the letter and naturally drove over immediately. For no other reason, but it seems like a sufficient reason. I can read you the passage of the letter that concerns you." He pulled the letter out of his wallet. "Here it is." She writes: 'Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time, last week I was once at the bank, but Josef was so busy that I wasn't allowed in; I waited for almost an hour, but then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak to him, perhaps an opportunity will arise soon. For my name day, he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very kind and thoughtful. I had forgotten to write to you about it back then, only now, since you are asking, do I remember. Chocolates, you must know, disappear from the boarding house immediately, as soon as one becomes aware that one has been gifted with chocolates, they are already gone. But as for Josef, I wanted to tell you something else. As mentioned, I wasn't allowed in to him at the bank because he was negotiating with a gentleman. After I had waited quietly for a while, I asked a servant if the negotiation would last long. He said that it probably would, because it was probably about the trial against the head clerk. I asked what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, but he said he wasn't mistaken, it was a trial, and a serious one, he didn't know more. He himself would like to help the head clerk, because he is a good and just man, but he doesn't know how to start, and he just wishes that influential gentlemen would take over. This will certainly happen, and it will eventually have a good ending, but for now, as he could gather from the mood of the head clerk, it is not going well at all. I didn't pay much attention to this speech, of course, I also tried to reassure the simple servant, forbade him to talk about it to anyone else, and consider the whole thing as nonsense. Nevertheless, it might be good if you, dearest father, looked into the matter during your next visit, it will be easy for you to find out more and, if it really becomes necessary, to intervene with your great, influential acquaintances. Should it not be necessary, which is probably the most likely, then it will at least give your daughter the opportunity to hug you soon, which would make her happy.' – 'A good child,' said the uncle when he finished reading, and wiped away some tears. K. nodded, he had completely forgotten Erna due to the various disturbances of recent times, even her birthday had slipped his mind, and the story about the chocolate was apparently only invented for the purpose of protecting him in front of his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theater tickets, which he wanted to send her regularly from now on, certainly not adequately rewarded, but visits to the boarding house and conversations with an eighteen-year-old schoolgirl did not feel appropriate to him now. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all the haste and excitement through the letter and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" exclaimed the uncle.

— Yes, that's definitely Vakhramey's, by Derebin. Imagine Derebin's good fortune: his aunt quarreled with her son over his marriage to a serf, and now she's bequeathed him the whole estate. I'm thinking, if only I had such an aunt for the future! But what is it, brother, you've become so withdrawn, you never go anywhere? Of course, I know that you're sometimes occupied with scholarly pursuits, you like to read (why Nozdryov concluded that our hero is engaged in scholarly pursuits and enjoys reading, this, we must confess, we can't say for certain, and Chichikov even less so). Guests continued to stare in amazement, whispering and glancing at each other, but it became absolutely clear that everything was planned and orchestrated in advance, and that Nastasya Filippovna, though she had, of course, gone mad, was now beyond any influence. Everyone was tormented by an awful curiosity. Moreover, there was no one to be truly afraid of. There were only two ladies: Daria Aleksandrovna, a lively woman who had seen all sorts of things and was difficult to fluster, and a beautiful but silent foreigner. But the silent foreigner could hardly understand anything: she was a recent arrival from Germany and knew no Russian. Besides, it seemed she was as dumb as she was beautiful. She was new in town and had already been invited to several prominent gatherings, adorned in the most elaborate attire, coiffed like a showpiece, and seated like a pretty picture to brighten up the evening – much like others procured a painting, vase, statue, or screen from acquaintances for a single evening. As for the men, Ptitsyn, for example, was acquainted with Rogozhin; Ferdyushchenko was in his element; Ganka could not yet recover his composure, but even dimly felt an uncontrollable, feverish need to endure to the bitter end by his shameful pillar; the old teacher, who barely understood what was happening, was on the verge of tears and literally trembling with fear, sensing the extraordinary turmoil around him and in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he adored like his granddaughter; but he would rather have died than leave her at such a moment. As for Afanasya Ivanovich, of course, he could not compromise himself in such adventures; but he was too deeply involved in the case, even if it had taken such a crazy turn; and besides, Nastasya Filippovna had let slip a couple of words about him that made it impossible to leave without finally clarifying the situation. He resolved to sit it out to the end and remain completely silent, becoming only an observer, which, of course, was required by his dignity. Only General Ypanchin, who had just been insulted by such an unceremonious and comical return of his gift, could now be even more offended by all these extraordinary eccentricities or, for example, the appearance of Rogozhin. And a man like him, who had already condescended to sit beside Ptitsyn and Ferdyushchenko, could certainly, at last, be overcome by a sense of duty, a sense of obligation, rank, and importance, and in general by respect for himself, so that Rogozhin and his company, in his presence at least, were simply impossible.
