As K. passed the corridor separating his office from the main staircase that evening – he was going home almost last, only two servants were still working in the small pool of light from a bare bulb – he heard sighs coming from behind a door, a door behind which he had always assumed was just a storeroom, though he had never actually seen inside. He stopped, surprised, and listened again to make sure he wasn’t mistaken – for a while there was silence, then the sighs came again. At first he wanted to call for one of the servants, one might need a witness, but then an overwhelming curiosity seized him, and he practically flung the door open. It was, as he had rightly suspected, a storeroom. Useless, old printing plates and discarded empty ink bottles lay scattered just beyond the threshold. But inside the chamber, three men were crouched in the low-ceilinged space. A single candle fastened to a shelf gave them light. “What are you doing here?” asked K., rushing forward in excitement, though not loudly. The one man, who seemed to be in charge of the others and was the first to look at him, was dressed in a kind of dark leather, which left his neck exposed down to his chest and his entire arms bare. He didn’t reply. But the two others cried out, “Sir, we’re being punished because you complained about us to the investigator.” And now K. realized that it was truly the guards Franz and Willem, and that the third man held a rod in his hand, ready to strike them. “Well,” said K., staring at them, “I didn’t complain; I merely stated what happened in my apartment. And you certainly didn’t behave impeccably.” “Sir,” said Willem, while Franz seemed to seek safety behind him, “if you knew how poorly paid we are, you would judge us differently. I have a family to feed, and Franz here wanted to get married, one has to make ends meet somehow, simple work doesn’t do it, not even the hardest work. Your fine laundry enticed me; it’s naturally forbidden for guards to act this way, it was wrong, but it’s tradition that the laundry belongs to the guards, it’s always been that way, believe me; it’s understandable, after all, what it means for someone unfortunate enough to be arrested, to have to endure this. If they then bring it to public attention, then punishment must follow.” “I didn’t know about this,” said K., “and I certainly didn’t demand your punishment; it was a matter of principle for me.” “Franz,” Willem turned to the other guard, “didn’t I tell you the gentleman didn’t demand our punishment? Now you hear that he didn’t even know we were to be punished.” “Don’t be swayed by their words,” said the third man to K., “the punishment is as just as it is inevitable.” “Don’t listen to him,” Willem interrupted, only to quickly cover his hand, which had received a lash, with his mouth, “we are only being punished because you reported us. Otherwise nothing would have happened to us, not even if they had found out what we did. Can you call that justice? We two, especially I, had proven ourselves as guards for a long time – you must admit, from the point of view of the authorities, we did a good job – we had prospects, we would have certainly become examiners soon, just like this one who was fortunate enough not to be reported, because such reports are really very rare. And now, sir, everything is lost, our careers are over, we will have to do even more menial work than guard duty, and besides, we are going to get these terribly painful beatings.” “Can a rod actually cause that much pain?” asked K., and he examined the rod that the examiner was brandishing. “We will have to strip completely naked,” said Willem. “Ah, so,” said K., and he looked the examiner directly in the eye, who was tanned like a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. “Is there no way to spare the two of them?” he asked him. “No,” said the examiner and shook his head with a smile. “Strip!” he ordered the guards. And to K. he said, “You mustn’t believe everything they say, they’ve become a bit feeble-minded from the fear of the beatings. What this one, for example” – he pointed at Willem – “says about his future career is laughable. Look at him, how fat he is – the first blows will disappear entirely into the fat. Do you know why he’s so fat? He has the habit of eating the breakfast of every arrested person. Didn’t he also eat your breakfast?” “Well, I said so,” said the examiner. “But a man with such a belly can never become an examiner, that’s absolutely impossible.” “There are examiners like that too,” Willem claimed. “No,” said the examiner, and he stroked Willem’s neck with the rod so violently that he flinched, “you should not listen, but strip.” Franz, who had probably been rather reserved throughout the whole thing, expecting a favorable outcome from K.’s intervention, now stepped forward, dressed only in his trousers, and clung to K.’s arm, whispering: “If you can’t get us both off, at least try to free me. Willem is older than me, in every way less sensitive, and he has already been given a light beating a few years ago, but I am still unblemished, and I was only brought to this by Willem, who has been my teacher for better and worse. My poor bride is waiting for me outside the bank, she's so ashamed.” He wiped his tear-streaked face with K.’s coat. “I'm not waiting any longer,” said the examiner, grabbed the rod in both hands, and struck Franz, while Willem crouched in a corner, secretly watching without turning his head. Then Franz let out a scream, a scream that seemed not to come from a human being, but from a tortured instrument, a scream that echoed through the whole corridor, a scream that must have been heard by the whole house. “Don’t scream,” cried K., he couldn’t help himself, and while he looked tensely in the direction where the servants must be coming, he pushed Franz, not hard, but hard enough that the helpless man fell down and searched the floor in a spasm; but he didn't escape the blows, the rod found him even on the ground; as he writhed beneath it, its tip swung rhythmically up and down. And in the distance, a servant appeared, and a second a few steps behind him. K. had slammed the door shut, stepped to one of the windows, and opened it. The screaming had completely stopped. To prevent the servants from approaching, he called out: “It’s me!” “Good evening, Mr. Clerk!” they replied. “Is anything the matter?” “No, no,” answered K., “it’s just a dog barking in the yard.” When the servants still didn’t move, he added: “You can stay with your work.” He leaned out the window so as not to have to engage in conversation with the servants. When he looked back into the corridor after a while, they were gone. But K. remained by the window; he didn’t dare to go back into the storeroom, and he didn’t want to go home either. It was a small, square courtyard that he looked down at, surrounded by offices, all the windows were dark now, only the upper ones caught a glimmer of moonlight. K. strained his eyes, trying to peer into the darkness of a corner of the courtyard, where some handcarts were piled up. It tormented him that he had not been able to prevent the beating, but it wasn’t his fault that it hadn’t succeeded; if Franz hadn’t screamed – yes, it must have hurt a lot, but at a crucial moment one has to keep a cool head – if he hadn’t screamed, then K. would have, at least very likely, found another way to persuade the examiner. If the entire lower ranks of the bureaucracy were scoundrels, why should the examiner, who had the most inhumane job, have been an exception? K. had also observed well how his eyes had gleamed at the sight of the banknote, he had only pretended to be serious with the beating, apparently only to inflate the bribe. And K. wouldn’t have spared it; it was really important to him to free the guards; if he had already started to fight against the corruption of this judicial system, it was naturally necessary for him to intervene on this side too. But the moment Franz started screaming, of course, everything was over. K. couldn’t allow the servants and perhaps even all sorts of other people to come and surprise him in a conversation with the Society in the storeroom. This sacrifice really couldn’t be expected of K. If he had intended to do so, it would have been simpler; K. could have stripped himself and offered to take the guards’ place. After all, the examiner certainly wouldn’t have accepted this substitute, because he would have violated his duty, and probably doubly so, because K. must have been inviolable for all employees of the court, as long as he was involved in the case. Of course, special regulations might apply here. At any rate, K. hadn’t had any other choice but to shut the door, even though this didn’t completely eliminate the danger for him. That he had given Franz a push in the end was regrettable and only excusable by his excitement.

For example, this one,” he pointed to Willem, “what he said about his possible career is ridiculous. Look at him, how fat he is – the first blows will be lost in the fat. In his youth, the sound of the drums and bells did indeed stir the three Sea Dragon Kings. In a moment, they arrived and gathered outside. Ao Chin said, "Elder Brother, what urgent matter is there to strike the drums and ring the bells?" The elder Dragon replied, "Younger Brother, it's hard to say! There's a person born a saint on Flower Fruit Mountain, who came this morning to claim me as a neighbor. Later, he requested a weapon. He found the steel fork too small and the painted spear too light. He took a piece of the celestial iron from the bottom of the Heavenly River, wielded it in his own hand, and threw out some calculations. Now, sitting in the palace, he demands something else to wear. I have nothing here, so I rang the bells and beat the drums, inviting Younger Brother to come. Do you have anything he could wear? Send him a set and just chase him out the door." Ao Chin, upon hearing this, became enraged and said, "Brothers, assemble the troops, let's subdue him!" The elder Dragon said, "Don't even think about fighting! That iron, if touched, will bring death, if struck, will cause harm. A little touch will break the skin, a slight rub will injure the tendons!" Ao Run, the West Sea Dragon King, said, "Second Brother, don't engage with him; just give him a set of armor to wear, dismiss him, and send a report to Heaven. Heaven will take care of him." But I still snuck out for an hour and saw Nastasia Filippovna again; I didn't sleep the whole night. The next morning, my father gave me two five-percent bonds, each worth five thousand, "Go," he said, "and sell them, and bring seven thousand five hundred to the Andrev's office, pay it, and bring the rest of the ten thousand back to me, without going anywhere else." I sold the bonds, got the money, but I didn't go to the Andrev's office, but went, not looking anywhere, to the English shop and bought two pendants, each with a diamond, almost like walnuts, costing four hundred rubles. I gave them my name, they believed me. I went to Zalyzhev with the pendants: "Here we go, brother, let's go see Nastasia Filippovna." We set off. I don't remember what was under my feet, what was before me, or what was on the sides; I just walked straight to her box, she came out to meet us. I didn't say then that it was me; "From Parfen, says Zalyzhev, Rogozhin, to you in memory of yesterday's meeting; please accept it." She opened it, looked, smiled: "Thank you," she said, "your friend, Mr. Rogozhin, for his kind attention," and curtsied and left. Well, why didn't I die right then! And if I didn't die, it was because I thought, "It's all the same, I won't be coming back alive anyway." But what hurt me most was that this beast Zalyzhev took all the credit for himself. I was short, dressed like a lackey, standing there, silent, staring at her, feeling ashamed, and he was all fashionable, in rouge and curls, with a checkered scarf, he was just overflowing with charm, and probably she took him for me instead! "Well," I said when we came out, "you don't even think about doing that again, understand?" He laughed: "But how will you explain yourself to Semyon Parfenovich then?" I wanted to jump into the river, not going home, but I thought, "Well, it doesn't matter anyway," and like a damned man, I went home.

— Well, my dear, — said Sobakevich, — if I were the one doing this, but I'll tell you straight to your face that I won't eat any of that muck. I wouldn't take a frog even if it was covered in sugar, and I wouldn't touch an oyster either: I know what an oyster is like. Take the lamb, — he continued, addressing Chichikov, — that's a lamb leg with porridge! It's not those fricassees that are made in manor kitchens out of lamb that has been lying in the market for four days! They all came up with this diet, treating illness with fasting! Those Germans and Frenchmen, with their liquid German natures, they imagine they can sweeten up a Russian stomach! No, it's all nonsense, it's all... — Here Sobakevich even shook his head angrily. — They talk about enlightenment, enlightenment, but this enlightenment is... — He would have said another word, but it would have been improper at the table. Not with me. When I have pork, bring the whole pig to the table, when it's lamb, bring the whole lamb, when it's goose, bring the whole goose! I'd rather eat two servings, but eat in moderation, as my soul demands. — Sobakevich confirmed this with his actions: he overturned half the lamb leg onto his plate, ate everything, gnawed, licked every last bone.

"Well, my dear fellow," said Sobakevich, "if I were the one making the arrangements, I'd say straight to your face that I won't eat any of that nonsense.  I wouldn't take a frog even if it were covered in sugar, and I wouldn't touch an oyster either: I know what an oyster is like. Take a lamb," he went on, addressing Chichikov, "that's a lamb's chop with porridge! It's not those fancy fricassée dishes they make in grand houses with lamb that's been lying on the market for four days! It's all made up by those German and French doctors, I'd hang them for it! They invented a diet, curing people with starvation!  They think that just because they're German and have a watery disposition, that they know what's good for a Russian stomach! No, no, it's all made up, it's all..." Here Sobakevich shook his head irritably.  "They talk about enlightenment, enlightenment, but this enlightenment is poppycock! I could say something else, but it wouldn't be proper at the table.  I don't do things that way. When there's pork, I want the whole pig on the table, lamb—the whole lamb, goose—the whole goose! I'd rather eat two courses, and eat to my heart's content." Sobakevich proved his point: he overturned half the lamb chop onto his plate and ate it all, gnawing, licking, until not a single bone was left.

The prince removed his tin cross, Parfen his golden one, and they exchanged them. Parfen remained silent. With a heavy feeling of surprise, the prince noticed that the former distrust, the former bitter and almost mocking smile, still lingered on his godbrother's face, at least in moments it was very apparent. Finally, without a word, Rozhgin took the prince's hand and stood there for a while, as if unable to decide on something; then suddenly he pulled him along, speaking in a barely audible voice: "Come." They crossed the first floor landing and knocked on the door opposite the one from which they had come. It was opened quickly. An old woman, hunched over and dressed in black, her head covered with a headscarf, silently and respectfully bowed to Rozhgin; he asked her something quickly and, without waiting for an answer, led the prince further through the rooms. Once again they entered dark rooms, of an extraordinary, cold purity, furnished coldly and austerely with antique furniture in white, clean covers. Without announcing their arrival, Rozhgin directly led the prince into a small room, resembling a living room, separated by a gleaming red-wood partition, with two doors on the sides, behind which was probably a bedroom. In the corner of the living room, by the stove, in armchairs, sat a little old woman, not yet very old in appearance, even with a rather healthy, pleasant and round face, but completely gray-haired and (at first glance it was possible to conclude) fallen into a state of complete childhood. She was wearing a black woolen dress, with a large black headscarf on her neck, a white clean cap with black ribbons. Her feet rested on a stool. Beside her sat another, cleaner old woman, older than her, also in mourning and also in a white cap, probably some kind of housekeeper, and she silently knitted stockings. Both of them, apparently, were constantly silent. The first old woman, seeing Rozhgin and the prince, smiled at them and several times gently inclined her head in a sign of pleasure.

— Parfen, I am not your enemy and have no intention of interfering with you. I am repeating this just as I stated before, once, at almost the same moment. When your wedding was taking place in Moscow, I did not interfere with you, you know. The first time, she herself ran to me, almost from under the wedding canopy, begging to be "saved" from you. I am repeating her own words to you. Then she ran away from me, you again found her and led her to the altar, and now, they say, she has run away from you here again. Is this true? Lebedev told me this, that's why I came. And about the fact that things have worked out again between you here, I only learned yesterday in the train for the first time from one of your former acquaintances, from Zalejev, if you want to know. I came here with the intention: I wanted to finally persuade her to go abroad to improve her health; she is very distressed both in body and soul, especially in her mind, and, in my opinion, needs a lot of care. I myself did not want to accompany her abroad, but I had in mind to arrange all this without myself. I am telling you the absolute truth. If it is absolutely true that things have worked out again between you, then I will not even show my face to her, and I will never come to you again. You yourself know that I am not deceiving you, because I have always been open with you. I have never hidden my thoughts about this from you and have always said that inevitable doom awaits her behind you. Doom also awaits you... perhaps even more so than her. If you had parted ways again, I would have been very happy; but I have no intention of upsetting and breaking you up myself. Be calm and do not suspect me. And you yourself know: was I ever your true rival, even when she ran to me? Here you are laughing now; I know what you are smiling about. Yes, we lived separately and in different cities, and you probably know all this. I have already explained to you before that I love her "not with love, but with pity." I think that I am defining this precisely. You said then that you understood my words; is that true? Did you understand? Look at you, how spitefully you are looking! I came to reassure you, because you are dear to me. I love you very much, Parfen. And now I'll go and never come back. Goodbye.

Their faces were pale as autumn leaves, their bodies trembling like young willow branches. The crown prince's legs went weak, unable to bear the weight of the mourning staff; the court officials' spirits fled, how could they wear the mourning hat and observe proper filial piety? Concubines tumbled over each other, their splendor shattered like wilted peonies. The maidservants toppled, like water lilies scattered by a sudden storm. All the officials were struck with terror, their bones softened, their muscles numb. They trembled and staggered, like fools in a trance. The White Tiger Hall, usually so majestic, resembled a collapsed bridge, and the funeral platform appeared like a ruined temple. One day, the Master was playing with his disciples at the front of the Sanxing Cave as the evening light faded. The Master said, "Sun Wukong, is it done?" Sun Wukong said, "Many thanks to Master for your kindness, disciple has fulfilled his task and is ready to ascend to heaven by riding the clouds." The Master said, "Show me how you do it." Sun Wukong used his skill, gave a sudden jolt, did a head-over-heels somersault, leaped off the ground five or six zhang, stepped on the clouds, and flew off for a moment, returning within three li. Landing in front of the Master, he clasped his hands and said, "Master, this is what it means to fly and ride the clouds." The Master laughed, "This isn't riding the clouds, it's merely climbing them. It's said in ancient times, 'Immortals journey to the North Sea in the morning and to Cangwu in the evening.' If you're only going a half-day journey, not even reaching three li, then climbing clouds is not enough!" Sun Wukong asked, "What do you mean by 'journey to the North Sea in the morning and Cangwu in the evening'?" The Master said, "Those who ride the clouds, start from the North Sea in the morning, travel over the East Sea, the West Sea, the South Sea, and return to Cangwu. Cangwu is just another name for the North Sea. Only if you can travel across all four seas within a day can you be said to ride the clouds." Sun Wukong said, "This is too difficult! It's too difficult!" The Master said, "There is nothing difficult in the world, only those who lack the heart to do it." Upon hearing this, Sun Wukong bowed in respect and said, "Master, 'a man must be thorough,' out of compassion, please bestow upon me this skill of riding the clouds and I will never forget your kindness." The Master said, "All immortals who ride the clouds leap with their feet off the ground, but you did not. I saw you simply leap onto them with a head-over-heels somersault. So, I will teach you 'Cloud-Hopping' based on that." Sun Wukong bowed again in supplication, and the Master passed down a secret incantation, saying, "With this cloud, grasp the incantation, chant the true words, clench your fists, shake your body, and jump. With one leap, you can cover one hundred and eighty thousand li!" Upon hearing this, the crowd burst into laughter. "Good fortune for Sun Wukong! If he masters this skill, he could be a messenger, delivering packages and letters, finding a meal anywhere he goes!"  

As dusk fell, the Master and his disciples each returned to their cave. That night, Sun Wukong concentrated his mind and practiced the skill, mastering the Cloud-Hopping technique. From then on, he was free to travel wherever he pleased, living a carefree life of immortality.

K. didn't pay much attention to him and the company on the corridor, especially since he saw the possibility about halfway down the hallway to turn right through a doorway without a door. He asked the court officer whether that was the right way, the court officer nodded, and K. actually turned there. It was bothersome to him that he always had to walk one or two steps ahead of the court officer; at least at this place it could look as if he were being led away in custody. So he often waited for the court officer, but he immediately fell behind again. Finally, K. said, in order to put an end to his discomfort, "Now I've seen what it looks like here, I want to leave now." "You haven't seen everything yet," said the court officer, completely unconcerned. "I don't want to see everything," said K., who was actually feeling tired, "I want to go, how do I get to the exit?" "Haven't you already gotten lost?" asked the court officer, surprised, "You go to the corner and then down the corridor to the right, straight ahead to the door." "Come with me," said K., "show me the way, I'll miss it, there are so many ways here." "It's the only way," said the court officer now with an accusatory tone, "I can't go back with you, I have to make my report and have already lost a lot of time because of you." "Come with me!" repeated K. now sharper, as if he had finally caught the court officer in a lie. "Don't shout so," whispered the court officer, "there are offices everywhere here. If you don't want to go back alone, then come a little way with me, or wait here until I've finished my report, then I'd be happy to go back with you." "No, no," said K., "I won't wait and you have to come with me now." K. hadn't even looked around in the room where he was, only when one of the many wooden doors standing around opened, did he look. The decision to take his own defense into his hands presented itself as more daunting than he had initially imagined. As long as he had left the defense to the lawyer, he had still been largely unaffected by the trial; he had observed it from a distance and had barely been touched by it directly. He could look in on his case whenever he wanted, but also withdraw his head whenever he pleased. Now, however, if he took his own defense, he would have to subject himself – at least for the time being – entirely to the court; the success of which should be his complete and final release later on, but to achieve this, he would have to expose himself to far greater danger than he had been in before. If he had any doubts, his meeting today with the deputy director and the factory owner would have convinced him otherwise. How benumbed he had been by the mere decision to defend himself! But how would it be later? What days lay ahead for him? Would he find the path that led through it all to a good end? Didn’t a careful defense – and everything else was pointless – simultaneously mean the necessity of adhering to everything else as much as possible? Would he manage to survive that? And how could he carry it out at the bank? It wasn’t just the submission, for which a vacation might have been enough, though even applying for a vacation right now would have been a major risk; it was an entire trial, the duration of which was unpredictable. What a sudden obstacle had been thrown in K.'s path!

How well the Deputy Director managed to appropriate everything that K. was now forced to give up! But did K. not give up more than absolutely necessary? While he made his way to an unknown painter with uncertain and, as he had to admit, very faint hopes, his reputation here suffered an irreparable injury. It would have probably been much better to take off the winter coat again and at least win back the two gentlemen who were still waiting next door. K. might have tried that, if he hadn't seen the Deputy Director in his room just then, searching through the bookcase as if it were his own. As K. approached the door excitedly, he called out: "Ah, you haven't left yet!" He turned to him, his many tight wrinkles seeming to evidence not age but strength, and immediately began searching again. "I'm looking for a contract," he said, "which, as the company representative claims, is in your possession. Won't you help me look for it?" K. took a step, but the Deputy Director said: "Thank you, I've found it already," and returned to his room with a large bundle of papers, which not only contained the contract but certainly much else besides.

The first knock at the lawyer's door was, as usual, pointless. "Leni could be quicker," thought K. But it was an advantage that the other party didn't interfere, as they usually did, whether it was the man in his dressing gown or someone else starting to bother him. While K. pressed the button a second time, he glanced back at the other door, but this time it remained closed. Finally, two eyes appeared at the peephole of the lawyer's door, but they weren't Leni's. Someone opened the door, but propped it open, called back into the apartment, "He's here!" and then opened it fully. K. had been pushing against the door, because he already heard the key being hastily turned in the lock behind him in the other apartment. So when the door finally opened in front of him, he practically rushed into the hallway and saw Leni, alerted by the door opener's call, running away in her shirt. He watched her for a moment and then looked around for the door opener. It was a small, thin man with a full beard, holding a candle in his hand. "Are you employed here?" asked K. "No," answered the man, "I'm a stranger here, the lawyer is just my representative, I'm here about a legal matter." "Without a coat?" asked K. and gestured with his hand at the man's inadequate clothing. "Oh, excuse me!" said the man and illuminated himself with the candle as if he were seeing his condition for the first time. "Is Leni your lover?" asked K. briefly. He had spread his legs slightly, crossed his hands, in which he held his hat, behind his back. Already by possessing a strong overcoat, he felt very superior to the thin little man. "Oh God," said the man and raised one hand in startled defense in front of his face, "no, no, what do you think?" "You look convincing," said K. with a smile, "nevertheless - come along." He waved him on with his hat and let him walk in front. "What's your name?" asked K. on the way. "Block, merchant Block," said the little man and turned around towards K. as if presenting himself, but K. did not let him stop. "Is that your real name?" asked K. "Of course," was the answer, "why would you doubt that?" "I thought you might have reason to conceal your name," said K. He felt as free as one usually is only when speaking to lower people abroad, keeping everything that concerns oneself to oneself, merely talking indifferently about the interests of others, thereby elevating them in front of oneself, but also being able to let them fall away at will. At the door to the lawyer's study, K. stopped, opened it and called to the merchant, who had been walking along obediently, "Don't be so quick! Shine a light here!" K. thought Leni might be hiding here, he made the merchant search every corner, but the room was empty. In front of the portrait of the Judge, K. held the merchant back by the trouser strap. "Do you know him?" he asked and pointed with his finger upwards. The merchant lifted the candle, blinked upwards and said, "It's a judge." "A high judge?" asked K. and stepped sideways in front of the merchant to observe the impression the picture made on him. The merchant looked upwards in admiration. "It's a high judge," he said. "You don't have much insight," said K. "Among the lower examining magistrates, he is the lowest." "Ah, now I remember," said the merchant and lowered the candle, "I've heard that too." "Of course," exclaimed K., "I forgot, of course you must have heard it." "But why, why?" asked the merchant, while he was driven towards the door by K.'s hands. Out in the hallway, K. said: "You know where Leni is hiding, don't you?" "Hiding?" said the merchant, "no, but she's probably in the kitchen, making soup for the lawyer." "Why didn't you say that right away?" asked K. "I wanted to show you the way, but you called me back," answered the merchant, bewildered by the contradictory orders. "You think you're very clever," said K., "so lead the way!" The kitchen was a place K. had never been in before, it was surprisingly large and well-equipped. Only the stove was three times the size of ordinary stoves, but you couldn't see any details of the rest, because the kitchen was only illuminated now by a small lamp hanging at the entrance. At the stove stood Leni in a white apron, as always, emptying eggs into a pot that was simmering on a spirit stove. "Good evening, Josef," she said with a side glance. "Good evening," said K. and pointed with his hand to a chair standing off to the side, which the merchant should sit on, which he also did. K. went right up behind Leni, bent over her shoulder and asked, "Who is the man?" Leni took K.'s hand with one hand, the other stirred the soup, pulled him forward to her and said, "He's a poor man, a poor merchant, a certain Block. Just look at him." They both looked back. The merchant was sitting on the chair that K. had indicated, he had extinguished the candle, whose light was now unnecessary, and was pressing down on the wick with his fingers to prevent the smoke. "You were in your shirt," said K. and turned her head back towards the stove with his hand. She remained silent. "Is he your lover?" asked K. She reached for the soup pot, but K. took both her hands and said, "Now answer!" She said, "Come to the study, I'll explain everything to you." "No," said K., "I want you to explain it here." She leaned against him and wanted to kiss him, but K. pushed her away and said, "I don't want you to kiss me now." "Josef," said Leni and looked at K. pleadingly and yet openly in the eyes, "you won't be jealous of Mr. Block, will you? – Rudi," she said then, turning to the merchant, "so help me, you see, I'm being suspected, let's have the candle." One might have thought he wasn't paying attention, but he was fully initiated. "I wouldn't know why you should be jealous," said he rather awkwardly. "I don't really know either," said K. and looked at the merchant with a smile. Leni laughed out loud, used the merchant's distraction to throw her arms around K. and whispered, "Leave him alone, you see what kind of person he is. I've taken a bit of notice of him because he's a big client of the lawyer, for no other reason. And you? Do you still want to speak to the lawyer today? He's very sick today, but if you want, I'll sign you up. But you stay with me overnight, for sure. You haven't been here for so long, even the lawyer has asked after you. Don't neglect the case! I also have some things to tell you that I've learned. But first, take off your coat!" She helped him out of it, took his hat off, ran with the things into the hallway to hang them up, ran back and looked at the soup. "Shall I register you first or bring the soup to him first?" "Register me first," said K. He was angry, he had originally intended to discuss his matter with Leni, especially the problematic termination, in detail, but the presence of the merchant had taken away his desire to do so. Now, however, he considered his matter too important for this little merchant to possibly intervene decisively, and so he called Leni back, who was already on the way, "Bring him the soup first," he said, "he needs to be strengthened for the conversation with me, he'll need it." "You're also a client of the lawyer," said the merchant quietly, as if stating a fact. This was not well received. "What does that concern you?" said K., and Leni said, "Will you be quiet? – Then I'll bring him the soup first," said Leni to K. and poured the soup onto a plate. "It's to be feared that he'll fall asleep soon after eating, he falls asleep soon after eating." "What I'll tell him will keep him awake," said K., he wanted to keep letting it be known that he intended to discuss something important with the lawyer, he wanted Leni to ask him what it was, and then to ask her for advice. But she fulfilled only the explicitly expressed commands. As she passed him with the cup, she accidentally bumped him lightly and whispered, "As soon as he's eaten the soup, I'll register you immediately so that I can get you back as soon as possible." "Go on," said K., "go on." "Be nicer," she said and turned around in the doorway with the cup again.

He felt as free as one is only when speaking to low people in a foreign country, keeping everything to himself that concerned him, talking about the interests of others indifferently, thereby elevating them but also being able to let them fall just as easily. At the lawyer's study door, K. stopped, opened it, and called to the merchant, who had been walking along obediently: "Don't rush! Light here!" K. thought Leni might be hiding here, he made the merchant search all the corners, but the room was empty. In front of the portrait of the judge, K. held the merchant back by the trousers. “Do you know him?” he asked and pointed with his index finger upwards. The merchant raised the candle, blinked upwards and said: "It's a judge." "A high judge?" asked K. and positioned himself sideways in front of the merchant to observe the impression the portrait made on him. The merchant looked up in admiration. "It's a high judge," he said. "You don't have much insight," said K. "Among the lower court judges, he's the lowest." "Now I remember," said the merchant and lowered the candle, "I've heard it said before." "Of course," said K., "I forgot, of course you must have heard it." "I wanted to lead you there, but you called me back," said the merchant, confused by the contradictory orders. "You think you're very clever," said K., "so lead the way!" The kitchen was a place K. had never been in before, surprisingly large and well-equipped. Only the stove was three times as large as ordinary stoves, nothing else could be seen clearly, since the kitchen was only lit by a small lamp hanging at the entrance. At the stove, Leni stood in her white apron, as always, pouring eggs into a pot that was on a spiritus burner. "Good evening, Josef," she said with a sideways glance. "Good evening," said K. and gestured with a hand to an armchair standing off to the side, which the merchant sat down on. K. himself went very close behind Leni, leaned over her shoulder and asked: "Who is the man?" Leni clasped K. with one hand, the other stirred the soup, pulled him forward to her and said: "It's a pitiful man, a poor merchant, a certain Block. Just look at him." They both looked back. The merchant was sitting in the armchair K. had indicated, he had extinguished the candle, whose light was now unnecessary, and pressed the wick with his fingers to prevent the smoke. "You were in your shirt," said K. and turned her head with his hand back to the stove. She was silent. “He’s your lover?” asked K. She wanted to reach for the soup pot, but K. took both her hands and said: “Now answer!” She said: “Come into the study, I’ll explain everything to you.” “No,” said K., “I want you to explain it here.” She leaned against him and wanted to kiss him. K. pushed her away and said: “I don’t want you to kiss me now.” “Josef,” said Leni and looked at K. pleadingly but openly in the eyes, “you won't be jealous of Mr. Block. – Rudi,” she said then, turning to the merchant, “help me, you see, I’m being suspected, put the candle out.” One might have thought he hadn't been paying attention, but he was fully in the know. “I wouldn't know why you should be jealous,” he said, not very cleverly. “I don’t really know either,” said K. and looked at the merchant with a smile. I won't lie: reality hooked me too during these six months, even before, pulling me in so deeply that I forgot about my sentence, or rather, didn't want to think about it and even did things. Speaking of my situation back then. When I fell terribly ill, eight months ago, I ended all my connections and left all my former comrades. As I've always been a rather gloomy person, my comrades easily forgot about me; of course, they would have forgotten me anyway. My surroundings at home, that is, "within the family," were also isolating. Five months ago, I locked myself inside my room and separated myself from the rest of the family completely. I was constantly obeyed, and no one dared enter except at a designated hour to tidy up and bring me my meal. Mother trembled at my commands and didn't even dare to utter a word in my presence when I occasionally allowed her in. She constantly punished the children for making noise and disturbing me; I often complained about their screams; well, they must love me now! "True Kolya," as I called him, I also, I think, tormented him considerably. Lately, he tormented me too; it was all natural, people are created to torment each other. But I noticed he endures my irritability as if he had beforehand promised himself to spare the sick man. Naturally, this irritated me; but it seems he decided to imitate the prince in "Christian humility," which was rather comical. He is a young and hot-headed boy and, of course, imitates everything; but it seemed to me sometimes that he was about time to start living with his own mind. I love him very much. I tormented Surikov as well, who lived above us and ran about all day on errands for someone; I constantly proved to him that he was to blame for his poverty, so that he finally became afraid to come to me. This is a very humble man, the humblest creature (NB. They say humility is a terrible force; one should find out about this from the prince, it's his own expression); but when, in March, I went up to him to see how they had "frozen," as he said, the child, and unintentionally smiled at the sight of his infant's corpse because I again started explaining to Surikov that he "was to blame," this wretch's lips suddenly quivered, and he, with one hand, grabbed me by the shoulder, with the other, showed me the door, and quietly, almost in a whisper, said to me: "Go away." I left, and I really liked it, liked it even then, at the very moment he was escorting me out; but his words made a heavy impression on me later, upon remembering them, a strange, contemptuous pity, which I certainly didn't want to feel. Even in the moment of such an insult (I do feel that I offended him, even though I didn't intend to), even in that moment this man couldn't get angry! His lips trembled then not from anger, I swear to you: he grabbed my hand and uttered his magnificent "go away" decisively, without being angry at all. There was dignity, even a lot of it, even too much for him (so, to be honest, there was a lot of comedy here), but there was no anger. Perhaps he simply began to despise me. From that day on, a couple of times, when I met him on the stairs, he suddenly began taking off his hat in front of me, something he had never done before, but he no longer stopped as he used to, but ran past, embarrassed. If he despised me, then it was in his own way: he "humbly despised." Or maybe he was taking off his hat simply out of fear, like a son of his creditor's wife, because he constantly owes my mother money and can't get out of debt. And this is even more likely... I wanted to explain myself to him, and I know for sure that in ten minutes he would have started asking for forgiveness; but I decided it was better not to bother him.

There was dignity there, even a lot, even too much, really, it wasn’t quite befitting him (so, honestly, there was a lot of comedy in it), but there was no anger. Maybe he simply started to despise me then. From that day on, two or three times when I met him on the stairs, he suddenly started taking off his hat before me, which he had never done before, but didn’t stop, as he used to, but would run past, blushing. If he despised me, it was still in his own way: he “humbly despised.” Or perhaps he took off his hat simply out of fear, like a son to his creditor's wife, because he constantly owes my mother money and can’t seem to get out of debt. And this is even more likely... I wanted to explain things to him, and I know for sure that in ten minutes he would have started begging my forgiveness; but I decided that it was better not to bother him.

Varvara Ardalionovna was a girl of twenty-three, of medium height, rather slender, with a face not particularly beautiful, but one that held a certain secret allure, a power to charm without beauty and to attract with a kind of passionate intensity. She resembled her mother very closely, even dressing in much the same way, out of a complete unwillingness to adorn herself. Her gray eyes could be very cheerful and affectionate at times, if not more often serious and thoughtful, sometimes even too much so, especially lately.  Determination and resolve were evident in her face, but one sensed that this firmness could be even more energetic and enterprising than her mother's. Varvara Ardalionovna was rather quick-tempered, and her brother sometimes even feared her temper. Ivan Petrovich Ptcyin, their guest now, also feared her. He was a rather young man, about thirty, dressed modestly but elegantly, with pleasant, but somehow overly dignified manners. His dark-brown beard marked him as someone not engaged in menial work. He was able to converse intelligently and interestingly, but more often remained silent. Overall, he made a rather pleasant impression. He was clearly not indifferent to Varvara Ardalionovna and did not hide his feelings. Varvara Ardalionovna treated him amicably, but hesitated to answer some of his questions, even disliked them; Ptcyin, however, was far from discouraged. Nina Alexandrovna was kind to him and, in recent times, had even begun to confide in him a great deal. It was known, however, that he was specifically engaged in making money by lending it out at high interest with more or less reliable collateral. He was on very friendly terms with Ganya.

"Don't cry, Mrs. Grubach," K. said, looking out the window. He could only think of Miss Bürstner and how she had taken in a stranger to her room. "Don't cry," he said again, turning back to the room and seeing Mrs. Grubach was still weeping. "It wasn't really meant so badly back then either. We simply misunderstood each other. That can happen even to old friends." Mrs. Grubach pulled her apron up under her eyes to see if K. was truly reconciled. "Well, that's it," K. said, and now, judging from Mrs. Grubach's demeanor, ventured to add, since the Hauptmann hadn't revealed anything: "Do you truly believe that I would quarrel with you over a stranger?" "That's just it, Mr. K.," Mrs. Grubach said. It was her misfortune that as soon as she felt even a little freer, she would always say something clumsy. "I always wondered: Why does Mr. K. take such an interest in Miss Bürstner? Why does he argue with me about her, even though he knows that every unkind word from him takes my sleep away? I haven't said anything bad about the girl, just what I saw with my own eyes." K. said nothing to this; he should have sent her out of the room with the first word, but he didn't want to. He was content to drink his coffee and let Mrs. Grubach feel her uselessness. Outside, they heard the dragging steps of Miss Montag again, crossing the whole antechamber. "Do you hear that?" K. asked, pointing with his hand towards the door. "Yes," Mrs. Grubach said and sighed, "I wanted to help her and even get the maid to help, but she's stubborn, she wants to move everything herself. I wonder about Miss Bürstner. It often bothers me that I have Miss Montag as a tenant, but Miss Bürstner even takes her into her room." "That's none of your concern," K. said, crushing the sugar residue in his cup. "Do you suffer any harm from it?" "No," Mrs. Grubach said, "in itself, I'm quite happy about it. I get a room free that way and can accommodate my nephew, the Hauptmann. I was already worried that he might have disturbed you these last few days while I had to let him stay in the living room next door. He doesn't take much notice." "What kind of thoughts!" K. said, standing up, "there's no talk of that at all. You seem to think me oversensitive because I can't stand these wanderings of Miss Montag – now she's going back again." Mrs. Grubach felt quite powerless. "Should I, Mr. K., tell her to postpone the rest of the move? I'll do it right away if you want me to." "But she should move to Miss Bürstner's!" K. said. "Yes," Mrs. Grubach said, she didn't quite understand what K. meant. "Well then," K. said, "she must move her things over there." Mrs. Grubach just nodded. This silent helplessness, which outwardly looked no different than defiance, irritated K. even more. He began to pace back and forth in the room from the window to the door, thereby preventing Mrs. Grubach from leaving, which she probably would have done otherwise.

As they were enjoying wine and revelry, someone came to report, "Your Majesty, two single-horned demon kings are outside and wish to see you." The Monkey King said, "Tell them to come in." The demon kings straightened their clothes and ran into the cave, bowing down. The Monkey King asked, "What brings you to see me?"  The demon king replied, "I have long heard of your Majesty's recruitment of talent and yearned for an audience. Now that I see you have received the Heavenly Mandate and returned in triumph, I specially offer this ochre-yellow robe to celebrate with you. Please do not disregard my humble status and accept me as a follower, allowing me to contribute like a loyal dog or horse."

The Monkey King was overjoyed. He put on the ochre-yellow robe, and everyone present stood in order and bowed. He immediately appointed the demon king as the General Commanding the Vanguard of the Front Line. After the demon king had paid his respects, he continued, "Your Majesty, how is it that you have been bestowed a position by the Jade Emperor?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor considers me worthy and has made me a 'Stable Master.'" Hearing this, the demon king further proposed, "Your Majesty possesses such great abilities, why would you tend to horses? Simply become a 'Great Sage, Equal of Heaven.' Why is that not possible?"

Upon hearing this, the Monkey King was overjoyed, repeatedly exclaiming, "Good! Good! Good!" He then ordered his four most valiant generals, "Quickly make a banner for me, with the words 'Great Sage, Equal of Heaven' inscribed upon it.  Erect it immediately and display it prominently." From this point forward, refer to me only as 'Great Sage, Equal of Heaven,' and do not use 'Your Majesty' anymore.  Also, please inform all the demon kings in the various caves, so they are all aware." This was readily carried out.

A shout from the next room startled him so badly that he bit down on the glass. “The guard is calling you!” it said. It was only the shouting that had frightened him, that short, clipped, military shout, which he wouldn’t have dared to attribute to Guard Franz. The order itself was very welcome to him. “Finally!” he called back, barred the cupboard and hurried into the next room. There the two guards stood and hustled him back into his room as if it were perfectly natural. “What do you think you’re doing?” they called. “Going before the guard in your shirt? He’ll have you beaten and us with you!” “Let me be, damn it!” cried K., already pushed back to his wardrobe, “If they attack me in bed, you can’t expect me to be found in my evening clothes.” “It won’t do any good,” said the guards, who always, whenever K. shouted, became quite calm, almost sad, and thus bewildered or somehow brought him to his senses. “Ridiculous ceremonies!” he grumbled, but he already picked up a coat from the chair and held it for a moment with both hands, as if submitting it to the judgment of the guards. They shook their heads. “It must be a black coat,” they said. K. threw the coat to the floor and said – he didn’t know himself in what sense –: “It’s not the main hearing yet.” The guards smiled, but stuck to their: “It must be a black coat.” “If it speeds things up, let it be so,” said K., opened the wardrobe himself, searched for a long time among the many clothes, chose his best black suit, a jacket suit, which had almost caused a stir among his acquaintances for its cut, then pulled out another shirt and began to dress carefully. In secret, he believed he had accelerated the whole thing by the guards forgetting to force him to bathe. He watched them, to see if they might remember, but of course they didn’t, whereas Willem didn’t forget to send Franz the message that K. was getting dressed.

Having crossed himself according to Russian custom, he proceeded with the task. Under the guise of choosing a place to live and under other pretexts, he undertook to visit the different corners of our state, and particularly those that had suffered most from misfortunes, crop failures, deaths, and so on, and so on—in a word, where it would be most convenient and cheapest to buy what the people needed. He did not approach every landowner indiscriminately, but selected people more to his taste or those with whom he could make similar deals with less difficulty, striving first to get acquainted, to win them over, so that, if possible, to acquire the serfs through friendship rather than purchase. So, dear readers, do not blame the author if the characters who have appeared so far are not to your liking; it is the fault of Chichikov; here he is the absolute master, and wherever he wants to go, that is where we must follow. As for us, if, indeed, the accusation falls on us for the paleness and mediocrity of the faces and characters, we will only say that one never sees the full scope and breadth of a work at the beginning. Entering any city, even the capital, is always somehow pale; at first everything is gray and monotonous: endless factories and workshops stretch out, shrouded in smoke, and then the corners of six-story buildings, shops, shop signs, vast avenues, all adorned with church towers, columns, statues, towers, with the city's glitter, noise, and thunder, and all that the human hand and mind have produced in wonder. As for the initial purchases, the reader has already seen how they were made; how things will proceed further, what successes and failures will befall the hero, how he will have to resolve and overcome more difficult obstacles, how colossal images will appear, how hidden levers of a vast narrative will be set in motion, how its horizon will expand, and how it will take on a majestic, lyrical flow—that will be seen later. There is still a long journey ahead for the entire traveling party, consisting of a gentleman of middle age, a buggy in which bachelors travel, a valet named Petrushka, a coachman named Selifan, and a team of three horses, already known by name from the “Saboteur” to the “curly-headed scoundrel.” So, here is our hero, such as he is! But perhaps they will demand a final definition in a single line: who is he in terms of moral qualities? It is clear that he is not a hero, full of perfections and virtues. So, is he a villain? Why a villain? Why be so harsh on others? We don't have villains anymore; there are only well-intentioned, pleasant people, and those who would expose their physiognomy to public shame are perhaps only two or three people, and even those now speak of virtue. It is most fair to call him: a master, an acquirer. Acquisition is the root of all evil; because of it, deeds have occurred that the world does not give a very clean name to. It is true, there is something repellent in such a character, and the same reader who on his life's journey will be friends with such a person, will share bread-and-salt with him and spend pleasant time, will look at him askance if he finds himself the hero of a drama or poem. But wise is he who does not disdain any character, but, peering into it with an examining glance, probes it to its first causes. Everything transforms quickly in a human being; you don't have time to blink, and already a terrible worm has grown inside, having selfishly turned all the vital juices to itself. Then Miss Montag, as always with her head held unusually erect, said: “I don’t know if you know me. K. looked at her with narrowed eyes.” “Certainly,” he said, “You’ve been living at Mrs. Grubach’s for some time now.” “But I believe you don’t concern yourself much with the boarding house,” Miss Montag said. “No,” said K. “Won’t you sit down?” said Miss Montag. They both silently pulled two armchairs to the far end of the table and sat facing each other. But Miss Montag immediately stood up again, for she had left her handbag on the window ledge and went to fetch it; she shuffled around the whole room. As she returned, handbag swinging lightly in her hand, she said: “I only want to speak a few words with you on behalf of my friend. She wanted to come herself, but she’s not feeling quite well today. You’ll excuse her and listen to me instead. She couldn’t have said anything different to you than I will say. In fact, I believe I can even tell you more, since I am relatively uninvolved. Don’t you think so?”

Although he had already foreseen this the day before, based on a certain anecdote (as he was accustomed to saying), and had even worried about it before going to sleep, he still felt a shiver of apprehension. The daughters came up to kiss him; although they were not angry with him, there was still something peculiar about this, too. Truth be told, due to certain circumstances, the general had become overly suspicious; but as he was an experienced and clever father and husband, he immediately took measures.

The Prince, however, did not die before his wedding, neither in reality nor "in a dream," as Eugene Pavlovich had predicted. Perhaps he truly slept poorly and had bad dreams; but during the day, among people, he appeared kind and even content, sometimes only very pensive, but that was when he was alone. The wedding was rushed; it took place about a week after Eugene Pavlovich's visit. With such haste, even the Prince's best friends, if he had any, would have been disappointed in their efforts "to save" the unfortunate madman. Rumors circulated that General Ivan Fedorovich and his wife, Elizaveta Prokofievna, were partly to blame for Eugene Pavlovich's visit. But if they both, with their boundless goodness of heart, had wished to save the poor wretch from the abyss, they certainly should have limited themselves to only this feeble attempt; neither their position nor, perhaps, even, naturally, their heartfelt disposition could correspond to more serious efforts. We mentioned that even those around the Prince partly revolted against him. Vera Lebedeva, however, limited herself to tears alone and also spent more time at home and visited the Prince less frequently than before. Kolya was burying his father at that time; the old man died from a second stroke, eight days after the first. The Prince took a great interest in the family's grief and for the first few days spent several hours with Nina Alexandrovna; he was at the funeral and in church. Many noticed that the congregation in the church involuntarily greeted and saw off the Prince with hushed whispers; the same happened on the streets and in the garden: when he walked or drove by, there was talk, they called him, pointed at him, his name Nastasya Filippovna was heard. They were looking for her at the funeral, but she was not there. The captainess, whom Lebedev had managed to stop and shorten in time, was also not at the funeral. The funeral service made a strong and painful impression on the Prince; he whispered to Lebedev even in the church, in response to some question, that this was the first time he was present at an Orthodox funeral and that he only remembered another one from his childhood in some village church.

She arrived at the dharma hall, took incense and bowed, then instructed Elder Fahming to distribute it among the monks. When Xuanzang saw that the monks had dispersed and the hall was empty, he knelt down in front of her.  As the young lady told him to remove his shoes and socks, she saw that his left foot was indeed missing a little finger.  At that moment, the two of them embraced and wept, thanking the elder for his upbringing. "You know what?" the prince exclaimed, his voice fervent. "You've noticed this, and others notice it just as keenly as you, and that's precisely what the machine, the guillotine, is designed for.  And at that moment, a thought struck me: what if it's even worse? You might find it amusing, even absurd, but even with a little imagination, the thought could creep into your head. Think about it: if, for instance, there's torture; suffering and wounds, bodily pain, and thus, it all distracts from the mental anguish, so that you only suffer through the wounds, until you die. But the main, the most powerful pain, might not be in the wounds, but rather, what you surely know—that in an hour, then in ten minutes, then in half a minute, then now, this very moment—your soul will depart from your body, and you'll cease to be a man, and that this is certain; the certainty of it is the worst. Like when you lay your head beneath the very blade and hear it glide over your head—those quarter of a second are the most terrifying. You know, this isn't my fancy, but something many have said. I believe it so strongly that I'll tell you my opinion outright. To kill for a murder is a punishment disproportionately greater than the crime itself. Murder by sentence is infinitely more dreadful than murder by bandits. He who is killed by bandits is cut down in the night, in the forest, or some other way, and he always hopes for salvation until the very last moment. There have been cases where his throat has been slit, and he still hopes, or runs, or begs. But here, all that final hope, with which it is ten times easier to die, is taken away; here, there's the sentence, and in the certainty of inescapable death, all the terrible anguish resides, and there's no greater suffering in the world.  Stand a soldier before a cannon on the battlefield and shoot him, he'll still hope, but if you read him the sentence, he'll either go mad or weep. Who said that human nature can withstand this without madness? What a terrible, hideous, senseless, needless outrage! Perhaps there is a man to whom a sentence has been read, who has been tortured, and then they said: 'Go, you are pardoned.' Perhaps that man could tell us. About this anguish and this horror, Christ spoke. No, we cannot treat people this way!

Execution is disproportionately more terrible than a murder committed in robbery. Perhaps there is such a person who was sentenced, tortured, and then told: "Go, you are forgiven." Maybe that person could tell us about this anguish and this horror. Christ himself spoke about this torment and this horror. No, one shouldn't treat people this way!

He entered, closed the door, silently looked at me, and quietly walked to the corner to the table that stood nearly under the lamp. I was very surprised and watched expectantly; Rogozhin leaned on the table and began to silently look at me. Two or three minutes passed, and I remember that his silence very much offended and annoyed me. Why didn't he want to speak? The fact that he had come so late seemed strange to me, of course, but I remember I was not terribly surprised by this. On the contrary: although I hadn't explicitly expressed my thought to him in the morning, I know that he understood it; and this thought was such that, of course, it was possible to come talk about it again, even very late. I thought that's why he had come. We had parted rather hostilely in the morning, and I even remember, he looked at me twice with a mocking expression. It was this mockery that I now read in his gaze, and that's what offended me. I had no doubts at all from the beginning that this was really Rogozhin, and not a vision, not a hallucination. There wasn't even a thought of it.

You have to buy gunpowder first, pistol powder, not wet and not the kind they use in cannons; then you put the gunpowder in, get some felt from somewhere, like from a door, and then you put the bullet in, but not the bullet first, because it won't fire.  You hear, Keller: because it won't fire. Ha-ha! Isn't that a splendid argument, my friend Keller? Oh, Keller, did you know that I'm going to hug you and kiss you right now? Ha-ha-ha! It is already known that Chichikov was deeply concerned for his descendants. Such a sensitive matter! Another, perhaps, would not have plunged so deeply into it if not for the question that, for some unknown reason, comes to mind of its own accord: what will the children say? And so, the future progenitor, like a cautious cat, glancing only sideways with one eye, sees if the master is watching, and quickly snatches everything that is near: whether it's soap, candles, bacon, or a canary that happened to come under his paw—in a word, he misses nothing. So complained and wept our hero, but meanwhile the activity did not die in his head; there everything wanted to be built up and was waiting only for a plan. Once again he shrank, once again he took up a difficult life, once again he restricted himself in everything, once again, from purity and decency, he sank into the mud and a base life. And in anticipation of better times, he was even forced to take on the position of a procurator, a title that had not yet acquired citizenship among us, pushed from all sides, poorly respected, a petty, clerical creature, and even by the clients themselves, condemned to fawning in front of them, rudeness, and so on, but necessity compelled him to agree to everything. Among the assignments, one was given to him, in particular: to fuss about the founding of several hundred serfs in the guardianship council. The estate was ruined in the extreme degree. It was ruined by cattle losses, by rogue stewards, by bad harvests, by epidemic diseases that had wiped out the best workers, and, finally, by the landowner’s own greed, who had built himself a house in Moscow in the latest fashion and had spent his entire fortune on this furnishing, so that there was nothing left to live on. For this reason, it was finally necessary to mortgage the last remaining estate. Mortgage to the treasury was then still a new thing, and people did not dare to resort to it without fear. Chichikov, as a procurator, having first arranged everyone (it is known that without preliminary arrangement, even a simple document cannot be obtained, after all, even a bottle of Madeira has to be poured into every throat), and so having arranged everyone who needs to be arranged, he explained the following circumstance: half the peasants had perished, so that there were no further ties...

That’s how our hero complained and wept, and yet the activity in his head did not die down; there, everything wanted to be built, and it was only waiting for a plan. Once again he hunched over, resumed his difficult life, once again limited himself in everything, once again, from purity and propriety, descended into the mud and a base existence. And in anticipation of better times, he was even forced to take up the position of a procurator, a position that had not yet acquired citizenship among us, pushed from all sides, poorly respected as a petty official and even by the very clients, condemned to servility, rudeness, and the like, but necessity forced him to agree to everything. His crown was yet to be closed, his hair not yet covering his shoulders. He was extraordinary, quick-witted and enlightened, his bones graceful and beautiful. Wukong laughed, "Little prince, your milk teeth haven't even fallen out, your baby hair hasn't dried, yet you dare speak such grandiose words? I shall spare your life and not strike you. Just look at the characters on my banners and offer them to the Jade Emperor: if it's that sort of official rank, I shall willingly surrender. The great sage roared "Transform!" and also became a three-headed, six-armed being, transforming his golden cudgel into three rods, each held by his six hands. This battle was truly earth-shattering and fierce.

The prince finally emerged from the dark park, in which he had been wandering for a long time, just as he had the day before. The light, transparent night seemed even brighter than usual; “could it be this early?” he thought. (He had forgotten to take his watch). Somewhere in the distance, it seemed to him, faint music was playing; “must be at the station,” he thought again, “they certainly didn’t go there today.”  Having realized this, he saw that he was standing right in front of their dacha; he knew all along that he would inevitably end up here, and, his heart pounding, he stepped onto the terrace.  No one met him, the terrace was empty. He waited a moment and opened the door into the hall. “That door was never locked by them,” flashed through his mind, but the hall was also empty; it was almost completely dark. He stood in the middle of the room, bewildered. Suddenly, the door opened, and Alexandra Ivanovna entered with a candle in her hand. Seeing the prince, she was surprised and stopped in front of him, as if asking. Apparently, she was just passing through the room, from one door to another, not at all expecting to encounter anyone.

Time flew by. One day, Liu Hong went far on official business, and the young mistress, missing her mother-in-law and husband, lamented on the flower pavilion. Suddenly, she felt weary and a pain seized her belly, causing her to faint. As she was overcome, a voice spoke, "Full-Chamber Beauty, listen to my words. I am the Star Jun of the South Pole, sent by the Bodhisattva Guanyin. I have brought this child to you. In the future, he will achieve great renown, surpassing ordinary people. If Liu the Rogue returns, he will surely harm this child, so protect him with all your heart. Your husband has been saved by the Dragon King, and in the future, you will be reunited with him, and mother and child will be together. You will avenge yourselves. Remember my words, wake up quickly, wake up quickly!" Then the voice vanished. The young mistress awoke, remembering every word. She held the child close, but felt helpless. Just then, Liu Hong returned. Seeing the child, he wanted to drown him. The young mistress said, "The day is late. I will dispose of him tomorrow in the river." Fortunately, the next morning Liu Hong was urgently summoned away on business. The young mistress thought, "If the scoundrel returns, this child will be finished. It's better to abandon him in the river early on. Perhaps the heavens will take pity, and someone will rescue him and raise him. We might be reunited someday." But she feared they wouldn't recognize him, so she bit her finger and wrote a blood letter on a piece of paper, detailing the names of her parents, the reason for their plight, and the child's lineage. She then bit off a small fingernail from his left foot as a token. Taking a sweat-soaked undershirt, she wrapped the child inside, and secretly carried him out of the government office. Fortunately, the office was near the river. Arriving at the riverbank, the young mistress wept bitterly. Just as she was about to throw the child away, she saw a piece of driftwood floating ashore. She bowed to heaven and placed the child on the board, securing him with a rope and attaching the blood letter to his chest. The newcomer seemed to avoid speaking much about himself; if he did speak, it was with general platitudes, marked by considerable humility, and his conversation took on a somewhat bookish tone. He spoke of himself as an insignificant worm of the world, unworthy of much concern; he had experienced much in his lifetime, endured hardships in service for the sake of truth, had many enemies who had even attempted his life, and that now, desiring peace, he sought a place to settle. Having arrived in this city, he considered it his duty to pay his respects to its first dignitaries. This was all the city learned about this new arrival, which very soon made its appearance at the governor's soirée.

Preparation for this soirée took over two hours, and the newcomer displayed such meticulous attention to his toilette as is rarely seen. After a short post-lunch nap, he ordered himself to be washed, washing his cheeks thoroughly with soap, pressing them against his tongue from within. Then, taking a towel from the innkeeper’s shoulder, he wiped his entire face with it, starting behind his ears and letting out two sharp snorts directly into the innkeeper’s face. After putting on his shirt before a mirror, he plucked out two hairs from his nose and immediately found himself in a blueberry-colored frock coat with a spark of finery. Thus dressed, he set off in his own carriage down the infinitely wide streets, illuminated by meager lighting from the occasional flickering street lamps. 

However, the governor’s house was well-lit, even for a ball; the carriage with its lanterns, two gendarmes at the entrance, the cries of footmen in the distance - in a word, everything was in order. Entering the hall, Chikchov had to momentarily squeeze his eyes shut, for the brilliance of the candles, lamps, and ladies’ dresses was blinding. Everything was bathed in light. Black frock coats darted and swirled hither and thither like flies buzzing on a gleaming, white piece of sugar in the heat of a July afternoon, when an old housekeeper hacked and divided it into sparkling fragments before an open window; children, all gathered around, watched with curious eyes the movements of her stiff hands as she lifted the mallet, and the aerial squadrons of flies, lifted by a gentle breeze, boldly entered, behaving as though they were the masters of the house. They took advantage of the old woman’s nearsightedness and the sun, dazzling her eyes, and showered the sugary morsels, wherever they were hacked or gathered in clusters, with renewed energy.  Satiated with the abundance of the summer, and with tempting dishes laid out at every step, they had flown in not to eat, but simply to show themselves, to strut back and forth across the sugar pile, rub their hind legs or front legs against each other, or, extending both front legs, to scratch under their wings, turn around, and fly away again, only to return with new, annoying squadrons. Before Chikchov could take in the scene, he was already seized by the hand by the governor, who immediately presented him to the governor’s wife. The newcomer did not disappoint himself in this situation either; he uttered some compliment quite fitting for a man of middle years, holding a modest position. When the established dancing couples pressed everyone against the wall, he stood with his arms behind his back, observing them attentively for a couple of minutes. Many ladies were well-dressed and fashionable, others had dressed in whatever they had found in their provincial wardrobes. The men were, as everywhere, divided into two types: some were slender, constantly swirling around the ladies; some of them were such that it was difficult to distinguish them from those in St. Petersburg; they had just as meticulously and tastefully trimmed mustaches or simply well-groomed, smooth-shaven oval faces, they lounged casually next to the ladies, spoke French, and entertained them just as in Petersburg. The other type of men were stout or, like Chikchov, not particularly stout, but not slender either. These, on the contrary, peered at the ladies from afar and only looked around, wondering if the governor's steward was setting up a green table for whist. Their faces were full and round, some even had warts, some were red-haired, their hair was either cut short, or slicked back, and their features were more rounded and robust. These were the respected officials of the city. Alas! the stout know how to get things done in this world better than the slender. The slender serve mainly on special assignments or simply exist, flitting about; their existence is somehow too easy, airy, and unreliable. The stout, however, never occupy indirect positions; they always take the direct ones, and if they sit down somewhere, they sit down securely and firmly, so that the place is more likely to crack and bend under them than they will move. They are not fond of external brilliance; their frock coats are not as well-tailored as those of the slender, but their trunks contain true riches. A slender man has no soul left by the age of three that hasn't been pawned; a stout man has peace of mind; look, there's a house bought in his wife’s name at the end of the town, then another at the other end, then a village nearby, then a whole estate with all its land. Finally, a stout man, having served God and the state, having earned general respect, leaves service, becomes a landowner, a glorious Russian lord, a generous host, and lives, and lives well. And after him, the slender heirs, according to Russian custom, descend on the estate by courier. 

It is impossible to deny that these kinds of thoughts occupied Chikchov's mind as he observed the society, and the consequence was that he eventually joined the stout, where he met most of the familiar faces: the prosecutor with very dark, thick eyebrows and a slightly squinting left eye as if saying, "Come, brother, let's go to another room, I have something to tell you," - a man, however, serious and taciturn; the postmaster, a short man, but witty and a philosopher; the chairman of the board, a very sensible and pleasant man, - all of whom greeted him as an old acquaintance, to which Chikchov bowed slightly, not without pleasure. He also met the very courteous and polite landowner Manilov and the somewhat clumsy Sobakevich, who, from the first moment, stepped on his foot, saying, "Excuse me."  They immediately handed him a card for whist, which he accepted with an equally polite bow. They sat down at the green table and did not rise until dinner. All conversation ceased, as always happens when they finally devote themselves to a serious occupation. Even the postmaster, who was very talkative, covered his lower lip with his upper one as soon as he took the cards in his hands and assumed a thoughtful expression throughout the game.

As he played, he hit the table hard with his hand, saying, "Go away, old hag!" if it was a queen, and "Go away, Tambov peasant!" if it was a king. And the chairman would exclaim, "I'll get you by the whiskers! I'll get you by the whiskers!" Sometimes, with the sound of the cards on the table, expressions like "Was it or wasn't it, if not for the drum!" or simply exclamations like "Worms! Vermin!  Pik!" or "Pikendra! Pikuru shuk! Pikura!" and even just "Pik!" - names by which they designated the suits in their company. At the end of the game, they argued, as usual, rather loudly. The newcomer also argued, but very skillfully, so that everyone saw that he was arguing, but pleasantly. He never said, "You went," but "You were pleased to go," "I had the honor to cover your pair," and so on. To further reconcile his opponents, he offered them all his silver snuffbox with enamel, on the bottom of which two violets were placed for fragrance. The newcomer's attention was particularly drawn to the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, about whom he had already been mentioned. He immediately inquired about them, calling the chairman and the postmaster aside.
