They don’t like outward splendor; their frock coats aren’t as cleverly tailored as those of the thin ones, but in their chests of drawers, they have the blessing of God. A thin man in three years doesn’t have a single soul pledged in a pawn shop; a stout man is calm, look – and there appears somewhere at the end of the city a house bought in his wife’s name, then another one in another end of the town, then a village near the city, then a whole estate with all its holdings. Finally, the stout man, having served God and the state, having earned universal respect, leaves the service, moves away, and becomes a landowner, a glorious Russian gentleman, a generous host, and lives well and happily. And after him, his thin heirs, as is the Russian custom, collect all their father's property by courier. 

It cannot be denied that Chichikov was occupied with this sort of reasoning at that time, as he observed the society around him, and as a result, he eventually joined the stout men, where he met almost all familiar faces: the prosecutor with very black thick eyebrows and a somewhat winking left eye, as if to say: "Come, brother, let's go to another room, there I'll tell you something," – a man, however, serious and taciturn; the postmaster, a short man, but a witty and philosophical fellow; the chairman of the chamber, a very reasonable and amiable man, – who all greeted him as an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov bowed slightly, though not without pleasure.  There he also met the very courteous and polite landowner Manilov and the rather clumsy-looking Sobakevich, who, on the first occasion, stepped on his foot, saying, "Forgive me."

He was then immediately handed a card for whist, which he accepted with the same polite bow. They sat down at the green table and did not get up until dinnertime. All conversation completely ceased, as always happens when people finally devote themselves to a serious occupation. Even though the postmaster was very talkative, the moment he took the cards in his hands, an expression of thoughtfulness appeared on his face, he covered his lower lip with his upper one, and kept it in that position throughout the game. When playing his cards, he struck the table firmly with his hand, saying, if it was a lady, "Go away, old hag!" and if it was a king, "Go away, Tambov peasant!" And the chairman would say, "I’ll get you by the whiskers! I’ll get her by the whiskers!" Sometimes, with a strike of the cards on the table, expressions would be let out like, "Well, that was that, no reason to, so on a drum!" or simply exclamations like "Worms! Wormholes! Picquet!" or: "Picquet! Pichu-hu! Pichu-huh!" and even just: "Pich!" - names with which they christened the suits in their company.

At the end of the game, they argued, as usual, quite loudly. The newcomer also argued, but so skillfully that everyone saw he was arguing, and yet pleasantly so. He never said, "You went," but: "You graciously agreed to go," "I had the honor to cover your double," and the like. To further convince his opponents, he always offered them his silver snuffbox with a finial, the bottom of which contained two violets, laid there for fragrance.

The visitor’s attention was particularly drawn to the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, about whom he had already been informed. He immediately inquired about them, addressing a few questions to the chairman and the postmaster.  A few questions, made to them, showed in the guest not only curiosity but also earnestness; for first of all, he asked how many peasant souls each of them had and what state their estates were in, and then he inquired about their first and patronymic names. In a short time, he had completely managed to charm them. The landowner Manilov, still quite a young man, with eyes sweet as sugar and squinting whenever he laughed, was utterly smitten with him. He shook his hand for a very long time and earnestly requested him to do him the honor of visiting his estate, which, according to him, was only fifteen versts from the city gate. To which Chichikov, with a very polite inclination of his head and a sincere handshake, replied that he not only would gladly do so but would consider it his sacred duty. Sobakevich also said rather laconically, "And you are welcome too," shuffling his foot, which wore a boot of such an enormous size that one could hardly find a foot to fit it nowadays, especially in this time when even in Russia, heroes are starting to appear.

About himself, the traveler seemed to avoid talking much; when he did speak, it was with general platitudes, with a noticeable modesty, and his conversation in these cases took on a somewhat bookish turn. He spoke of himself as a insignificant worm in this world and unworthy of much concern, that he had experienced much in his life, endured much in service for the truth, had many enemies who had even tried to take his life, and that now, wishing to settle down, he sought to find a place to live and, having arrived in this city, considered it his duty to pay his respects to its first dignitaries. This was all that was learned about this new arrival, which very soon made itself known at the governor's soirée. 

The preparations for this soirée took more than two hours, and in the traveler’s toilette there was an attentiveness to detail that was rarely seen. After a short afternoon nap, he ordered himself to be washed and washed his cheeks with soap for an extraordinarily long time, pressing his tongue against them from the inside. Then, taking a towel from the innkeeper's shoulder, he wiped his entire face, starting behind his ears and letting out a snort or two right into the innkeeper's face. Then he donned a waistcoat in front of the mirror, plucked out two hairs that had sprouted from his nose, and immediately found himself in a frock coat the color of cranberry with a sparkle. Thus dressed, he rolled off in his own carriage through the infinitely wide streets, illuminated by feeble light from the occasional lanterns. 

However, the governor’s house was brightly lit, even for a ball; carriages with lanterns, two gendarmes at the entrance, the shouts of footmen in the distance – in a word, everything was as it should be. Suddenly she stopped, placed her hand on K.'s, as if to soothe him, and whispered, "Quiet, Berthold is looking at us." K. slowly lifted his gaze. In the doorway of the sitting room stood a young man, small in stature, with slightly crooked legs, who searched for dignity in a short, thin, reddish full beard, constantly running his fingers through it. K. looked at him curiously; it was the first student of the unknown legal science that he had encountered, in a manner of speaking, as a human being, a man who would probably also ascend to higher positions in the civil service. The student, however, seemed not to care about K. at all. He only beckoned with a finger, which he drew out of his beard for a moment, to the woman and went to the window. The woman leaned toward K. and whispered, "Don't be angry with me, I beg you, don't think badly of me either, I must go to him now, to that horrible man, look at his crooked legs. But I'll be right back, and then I'll go with you, if you'll take me. I'll go anywhere you want, you can do anything you want to me, I'll be happy if I can leave here for as long as possible, preferably forever." She stroked K.'s hand again, jumped up, and ran to the window. Unconsciously, K. reached after her hand into the void. The woman was truly tempting him; despite all his deliberation, he couldn't find a solid reason why he shouldn't give in to the temptation. The fleeting thought that the woman would turn him in to the court, he easily dismissed. How could she possibly arrest him? Wasn't he always so free that he could shatter the entire court, at least as far as it concerned him, immediately? Couldn't he have that much confidence in himself? And her offer of help sounded sincere and was perhaps not without value. And perhaps there was no better revenge on the examining magistrate and his entourage than to take this woman away from them and make her his own. Perhaps one day the examining magistrate, after laborious work on false reports about K., would find the woman's bed empty in the late night. And empty precisely because she belonged to K., because this woman at the window, this lush, supple, warm body in the dark dress of coarse, heavy material, completely belonged to K.

As the行者 accompanied the Tang monk westward, several days into their journey, it was the heart of winter. The wind was icy and fierce, and the ground was slippery with frost. They traveled along rugged cliffs and treacherous mountain passes, their route winding through steep ridges and valleys. 

As they rode, the Tang monk heard a loud roaring sound and called out, "Sun Wukong, what is that sound?"  Sun Wukong replied, "I recall this place is called Shepan Mountain, Yingchou Gorge. It must be the sound of water from the gorge."  

They soon arrived at the edge of the gorge.  The Tang monk reined in his horse and looked around. He saw a stream of icy water rushing through the clouds, its clear waves reflecting the scarlet hues of the setting sun. The sound echoed through the deep valley like the drumming of night rain, while rays of dawn light shimmered across the vast expanse of sky. Water cascaded down the thousand-zhang cliff, shattering into jade-like fragments, roaring like the wind. The water flowed back into the vast expanse of water, and the gulls and herons flew about, oblivious to the presence of fishermen.

As the master and apprentice were watching, a sudden sound erupted from the depths of the gorge. A dragon emerged, churning the water and sending waves crashing against the cliffs. It lunged at the Tang monk.  Sun Wukong dropped his luggage and quickly pulled his master off his horse, turning to flee. The dragon was unable to catch up, swallowing the white horse, saddle and bridle in one gulp, before disappearing beneath the water. Sun Wukong led his master to a high hill and sat him down. Then he went back to retrieve his luggage, but only one load remained; the horse was gone.  

He carried the remaining load to the Tang monk and said, "Master, the dragon has disappeared, but my horse is gone."  The Tang monk said, "How will we find our horse, disciple?"  Sun Wukong reassured him, "Don't worry, master, I'll go find it."

As he sat there in his stiff chairs, troubled by thoughts and insomnia, and diligently entertaining Nozdryov and his entire family, and before him a tallow candle flickered, its lampshade long since blackened by the soot and threatening to go out at any moment, and outside the window, a blind, dark night looked in, ready to turn a sickly purple from the approaching dawn, and roosters crowed in the distance, and in the completely asleep city, perhaps somewhere a frusky coat, a wretched soul of unknown rank and station, knowing only one too well-worn path, familiar to the Russian throng—at that very moment, on the other side of town, an event was unfolding that was poised to worsen the predicament of our hero.  

Indeed, in the distant streets and back alleys of the city, a very strange carriage rattled along, raising bewilderment as to its name. It wasn't like a tarantass, nor a chaise, nor a gig, but rather resembled a thick-cheeked, protruding watermelon, set upon wheels. The cheeks of this watermelon, that is, the doors, bearing the remnants of yellow paint, closed very poorly due to the poor condition of the handles and locks, haphazardly bound together with ropes. The watermelon was crammed with calico cushions in the shape of pouches, rolls, and pillows, stuffed with bags of breads, pastries, buns, sweet breads, and twisted dough rings. Pies-coffins and pies-borscht peeked out even to the top. The rear was occupied by a face of a liveryman's origin, in a jacket of motley fabric, with an unshaven beard, dusted with a hint of gray—a face known as “the little one.” The screech and clang of iron clamps and rusty bolts awakened the baker on the other side of town, who, raising his halberd, cried out sleepily, “Who’s there?” But, seeing that no one was coming, and only the distant rattling could be heard, he caught some creature on his collar and, approaching the lamppost, executed it right there on his fingernail. After which, putting aside his halberd, he fell asleep again, according to the customs of his knighthood. 

The horses kept collapsing onto their front knees because they weren't shod, and, apparently, the deceased city cobblestones were unfamiliar to them. The cart, after making several turns from street to street, finally veered into a dark alley past the small parish church of Nicholas at Nedotyk and stopped at the gates of the provost’s house.  A maid, with a headscarf on her head, in a quilted jacket, emerged from the carriage and hit the gates with both fists so hard that it would have been enough to make a man (the liveryman in the motley jacket was already dragged out by the legs, for he was sleeping like the dead). The dogs barked, and the gates, finally gaping open, swallowed, though with great effort, this clumsy road vehicle. 

The carriage entered the cramped yard, cluttered with firewood, chicken coops, and all sorts of cages; a lady emerged from the carriage: this lady was a landowner, the collegiate secretary Korobochka. 
The old woman, shortly after our hero’s departure, had come to such distress about the possibility of his deceit that, having not slept for three nights in a row, she decided to go to the city, despite the fact that the horses were unshod, and to find out for certain what dead souls were worth and whether she, God forbid, had not blundered, perhaps selling them for a third less. What consequence this arrival had, the reader can learn from a conversation that took place between two ladies. This conversation… but let it be in the next chapter.

Nozdrev was a man of a certain historical type. No gathering he attended was complete without a story. Some sort of story would inevitably unfold: either gendarmes would escort him out, or his own companions would feel compelled to shove him away. If that didn't happen, something else would occur, something that wouldn't happen with anyone else: he might find himself in the buffet somehow, becoming the subject of laughter, or he might weave such a cunningly awful lie that he himself would finally feel shame. And he would lie, completely without need, suddenly claiming he owned a horse of blue or pink wool, or some such nonsense, until the listeners would finally depart, muttering, "Well, friend, it seems you've started spitting bullets." There are people with a peculiar penchant for ruining someone else's day, sometimes for absolutely no reason. Take, for example, a man in uniform, with an aristocratic bearing, a star on his chest. He might shake your hand, engage you in conversation about profound subjects, prompting reflection, and then, right before your eyes, he'll do the unthinkable: he'll muck it all up, like an ordinary junior clerk, not at all like a man with a star on his chest discussing thought-provoking matters. You just stand there, shaking your head, speechless. Nozdrev possessed this very strange affliction. The closer someone got to him, the more he would relish in ruining them. He'd spin out a fabrication so absurd it was hard to imagine, he'd disrupt a wedding, a business deal, and wouldn't consider himself an enemy. On the contrary, if circumstance brought them together again, he'd treat them amicably, even saying, "You're such a scoundrel, you never come to visit me."

Nozdrev was a multi-faceted man in many ways, a jack-of-all-trades. In an instant, he'd offer to take you anywhere, to the ends of the earth, to join any venture, to trade anything for anything. A gun, a dog, a horse – everything was up for barter, but not with the intention of winning: it was simply a manifestation of his restless, vivacious nature. If he got lucky at the fair and bested a gullible mark, he'd buy up a mountain of whatever he'd seen in the shops: halters, candles for smoking pipes, handkerchiefs for nannies, a colt, raisins, a silver wash basin, Dutch canvas, coarse flour, tobacco, pistols, sprats, paintings, sharpening tools, pots, boots, porcelain dishes – as long as his money allowed. However, it rarely reached his home. Almost the same day, it would all be passed on to another, more fortunate gambler, sometimes even including his own pipe with a pouch and mouthpiece, and on another occasion even the entire lot: carriage and coachman, leaving the original owner to set out in his short coat or frock coat in search of a friend to borrow a carriage from.  That was Nozdrev! Perhaps they'll say he's a clichéd character, that there are no more Nozdrevs. Alas, they'll be wrong. Nozdrev will be around for a long time to come. He's everywhere among us, and perhaps he just walks around in a different coat. But people are insouciantly oblivious, and a man in a different coat seems like a different person to them.

But did it confirm itself? But was it justified? Why is there again that tremor, that cold sweat, that mental gloom and coldness? Is it because he saw those eyes again? That was the basis of his “sudden idea.” He ardently wanted to see those “recent eyes,” to be completely sure that he would inevitably meet them there, at that house. It was a spasmodic desire of his, and why is he so crushed and struck now that he has really seen them? He certainly didn’t expect it! Yes, it was those very eyes (and there is now absolutely no doubt about that!), the ones that flashed at him this morning, in the crowd, when he was leaving the Nikolaev Railway Station; those very ones (completely the same!), whose gaze he had caught the other day, behind him, as he sat down on the chair by Rogozhin. Rogozhin had denied it the day before: he asked with a distorted, chilling smile: “Whose eyes were they?” And the prince desperately wanted, even recently, at the Tsarskoye Selo Railway Station, – when he was getting into the carriage to go to Aglaya, and suddenly saw those eyes again, for the third time that day – to approach Rogozhin and say to him, “Whose were those eyes!” But he ran out of the station and only woke up in front of the butcher’s stall the moment he was standing there, assessing a thing with an elk handle for sixty kopecks. A strange and terrible demon had attached itself to him finally and no longer wanted to leave him. This demon whispered to him in the Summer Garden, when he was sitting, lost in thought, under the linden tree, that if Rogozhin had to watch him so closely from morning and catch him at every turn, then, having learned that he would not go to Pavlovsk (which was, of course, a fatal piece of information for Rogozhin), Rogozhin would inevitably go there, to that house on Petersburg Street, and would inevitably guard him there, the prince, who had given him a sincere promise that morning that he “would not see her” and that “he had not come to Petersburg for that reason.” And here the prince was frantically rushing towards that house, and what’s wrong with the fact that he really meets Rogozhin there? He was completely in the open now and, it seemed, deliberately wanted to be seen. He stood like an accuser and a judge, and not as… And not as who?

Yes, it was those very eyes (and there is now no doubt about it being those very ones!) that flashed at him this morning, in the crowd, when he was leaving the Nikolaev Railway station; those very ones (exactly those!), whose gaze he had caught earlier, behind him, as he sat down on a chair by Rogozhin's. Rogozhin had denied it earlier: he asked with a distorted, chilling smile: "Whose eyes were they?" And the prince had desperately wanted, earlier, at the Tsarskoye Selo Railway station, when he was getting into the carriage to go to Aglaya, and suddenly saw those eyes again, for the third time that day, to approach Rogozhin and say to him, "Whose eyes were those!" But he had dashed out of the station and only came to his senses in front of a scythe seller's stall at the moment when he was examining an item with a deer handle for sixty kopecks. A strange and terrible demon had attached itself to him finally and no longer wanted to leave him. This demon whispered to him in the Summer Garden, when he was sitting, lost in thought, under the lime tree, that if Rogozhin had to watch him so closely from morning till night and catch him at every turn, then, learning that he was not going to Pavlovsk (which, of course, was a fateful piece of information for Rogozhin), Rogozhin would certainly go there, to that house on Petersburg Street, and would certainly watch him there, the prince who had given him an honest word that morning that he "would not see her" and that "he did not come to Petersburg for that reason." And so the prince rushes convulsively towards that house, and what's wrong with the fact that he really meets Rogozhin there? He saw only a miserable man, whose mood was gloomy, but very understandable. This unhappy man was not even trying to hide himself now. Yes, Rogozhin had hidden himself and lied yesterday, but at the station he stood almost in the open. It was rather he, the prince, who was hiding, and not Rogozhin. He was completely in the open now and, it seemed, deliberately wanted to be seen. He stood like an accuser and judge, and not like... And not like who?

K. was interrupted from the end of the hall by a scream. He shielded his eyes to see, for the dim daylight made the haze appear white and blinding. It was the laundress, whom K. had recognized immediately upon her entry as a significant disturbance. Whether she was guilty or not was unclear. K. only saw that a man had pulled her into a corner by the door and was pressing against her. But it wasn't her who was screaming, but the man. He had his mouth wide open and was looking at the ceiling. A small circle had formed around the two of them, the gallery attendees near seemed delighted that the seriousness with which K. had introduced himself to the assembly was interrupted in this way. K. wanted to run towards them immediately, and he thought everyone would be concerned about establishing order and at least ushering the couple out of the hall, but the first rows in front of him remained completely still, no one moved, and no one let K. through. On the contrary, they hindered him, old men held out their arms, and some hand – he didn't have time to turn around – grasped him by the collar. K. no longer really thought about the couple; it felt as though his freedom was being restricted, as if he were being arrested, and he jumped recklessly from the podium. Now he stood face to face with the crowd. Had he misjudged the people? Had he given his speech too much impact? Had they been pretending while he spoke, and were they now, as he came to his conclusions, satisfied with the pretense? What faces surrounded him! Small, black eyes darted around, cheeks hung down, as if with those who had drunk too much, the long beards were stiff and sparse, and if you reached into them, it was as if you were touching claws, not beards. But under the beards – and that was the actual discovery K. made – insignia of various sizes and colors shimmered on the collar. Everyone had these insignia, as far as one could see. They all belonged together, the apparent parties on the right and left, and as he suddenly turned around, he saw the same insignia on the collar of the examining magistrate, who, with his hands in his pockets, looked down calmly. "So," K. exclaimed, throwing his arms into the air, the sudden realization needed space, "you are all officials, as I see it, you are the corrupt band I spoke against, you have gathered here as listeners and spies, you have formed apparent parties, and one has applauded to test me, you wanted to learn how to seduce the innocent! Well, you haven't been useless here, I hope, either you have discussed among yourselves that someone expected the defense of innocence from you, or – let me go, or I'll hit," K. shouted to a trembling old man who had pushed himself particularly close to him – "or you have really learned something. And with that, I wish you luck in your profession." He quickly grabbed his hat, which lay on the edge of the table, and, under a complete and absolute silence, forced his way to the exit. The examining magistrate, however, seemed to have been even quicker than K., for he awaited him at the door. "A moment," he said. K. stopped, but did not look at the examining magistrate, but at the door, whose handle he had already grasped. "I just wanted to point out to you," said the examining magistrate, "that you have deprived yourself today – it may not have occurred to you yet – of the advantage that an interrogation for the arrested always entails." K. laughed at the door. "You scoundrels," he cried, "I give you all the interrogations," opened the door, and hurried down the stairs. Behind him, the noise of the revived assembly rose, which probably began to discuss the events in the manner of students.

K. found himself, without wanting to, drawn into a conversation of glances with Franz, but then he slammed down on his papers and said: "Here are my identification papers." "What do we care about those?" exclaimed the big guard. "You're acting more childish than a child. What do you want? Do you want to bring your big, damned trial to a quick end by discussing identification and arrest warrants with us, the guards? We are low-level employees who barely understand anything about identification papers and have nothing to do with your case except that we stand guard here for ten hours a day and are paid for it. That's all we are, yet we are capable of seeing that the higher authorities, in whose service we stand, before issuing such an arrest warrant, inform themselves very carefully about the reasons for the arrest and the person being arrested. There's no mistake there. Our agency, as far as I know it, and I only know the lowest ranks, does not seek out guilt in the population, but is, as the law states, drawn to guilt and must send us guards. That's the law. Where could there be a mistake?" "I don't know that law," said K. "All the worse for you," said the guard. "It probably only exists in your heads," said K., he wanted to somehow insinuate himself into the thoughts of the guards, to win them over to his side or to naturalize himself there. But the guard only replied dismissively: "You'll feel it." Franz intervened and said: "Look, Willem, he admits he doesn't know the law, and at the same time claims to be innocent." "You're right, but you can't make anything clear to him," said the other. K. said nothing more; must I, he thought, be further confused by the babbling of these lowest organs - they even admit it themselves - they are talking about things they don't even understand. Their security is only possible through their stupidity. A few words with a person who is my equal will make everything incomparably clearer than the longest speeches with these. He paced back and forth several times in the free space of the room, over there he saw the old woman who had dragged a much older man to the window, whom she held in her arms. K. had to put an end to this display: "Take me to your superior," he said. "If he wants to see me; not sooner," said the guard, who had been called Willem. "And now I advise you," he added, "to go back to your room, behave yourself calmly and wait for what will be decided about you. We advise you, don't let yourself be distracted by useless thoughts, but gather yourself, great demands will be made of you. You haven't treated us as our helpfulness deserves, you have forgotten that we, whatever we may be, are at least free men towards you now, which is no small advantage. Nevertheless, we are willing, if you have money, to bring you a small breakfast from the coffee house across the street."

Ba Ching recounted the dreams of the three young children to San Zang, who was pleased.  After they had received the plain vegetarian meal, Ba Ching offered a silver tael in thanks. San Zang refused it. The family persisted in their pleas, and San Zang, though he still refused any payment, said, "Your kindness in offering me this journey is enough to touch my heart." Ba Ching and his wife, unable to convince him otherwise, hastily made some coarse steamed buns and dried rations, and had Ba Ching see San Zang off. San Zang was happy to receive them. 

Tai Bao, having received his mother's orders, also called for two or three house servants, each with their hunting implements, and they went together along the main road, marveling at the mountain scenery and the views from the ridges. After traveling for half a day, they came to a mountain across the way, which truly reached up to the heavens, its peak lofty and perilous. San Zang, however, did not hesitate and quickly reached the front. For Tai Bao, ascending this mountain was like walking on level ground.  As they walked halfway up, Ba Ching turned around and stood at the foot of the road, saying, "Elder, please go ahead. I shall return." San Zang, hearing this, dismounted and said, "Please, do not trouble Tai Bao to accompany me any further!" Ba Ching replied, "Elder, you don't know, this mountain is called Liang Jie Shan. The eastern half belongs to the territory of our Tang Dynasty, but the western half is the territory of the Tatars. The wolves and tigers over there don't submit to my authority, so I cannot cross the border. You go on." San Zang was startled, his hands trembling, he clasped his robe and wept tears that he could not contain.  Just as he was saying farewell, a thunderous shout came from the foot of the mountain, "My master is here! My master is here!" This startled San Zang, causing him to become dumbfounded. Ba Ching struggled to defend himself. In the end, he didn't know who was shouting, so listen to the next installment.

Master Chen was told of the three young boys' dream narratives by Master Bao. Master Chen was pleased. He had already received the vegetarian meal, and he was then presented with one tael of silver as a thank you. Master Chen refused to accept any money. The family repeatedly pleaded with him, but Master Chen still refused, saying, "It is enough for you to have shown your kindness and compassion by sending me this far."

Master Bao and his wife, with no other choice, hastily prepared some coarse flatbread and grain, and had Master Bao escort him far away. Master Chen was happy to accept them. Master Bao's steward, having received his master's orders, summoned two or three house servants, each carrying hunting gear, and they all set out on the main road, unable to tire of the wild scenery of the mountains and the vistas from the ridges.

After half a day of travel, they came upon a towering mountain across the road, its peak touching the sky, its sides steep and precipitous. Master Chen, unhesitating, reached the foothills. It was as if Master Bao was walking on flat ground as he ascended the mountain. When they reached halfway up, Master Bao turned around and stood at the foot of the road, saying, "Elder, please go on ahead. I must turn back now."

Master Chen, hearing this, dismounted and said, "Please do not trouble Master Bao any further!" Master Bao said, "Elder, you don't know, this mountain is called the Two Realms Mountain. The eastern half belongs to the Tang Dynasty, while the western half belongs to the Tatars. Those wolves and tigers there do not submit to my authority, and I cannot cross the border. You should proceed on your own." 

Master Chen was startled. He opened his hands, clutched his robes, and tears streamed down his face. As they were saying their goodbyes, a booming shout echoed from the foot of the mountain, "My master is here! My master is here!"

Master Chen was so startled that he froze, Master Bao struggling to regain his composure. He had no idea who was shouting, but he listened as the story continued.

The poem says: Great Tang King issued an edict, sending Xuanzang to inquire about the Chan school. With a resolute heart, he sought the Dragon's Cave, diligently practicing on Mount Shoushi. He journeyed through many countries beyond the border, across thousands of mountains and clouds. From now on, the noble scholar is going westward, carrying the teachings and attaining great emptiness.

Let me tell you that on the third day of the ninth lunar month of the thirteenth year of Emperor Taizong's reign, Sanzang was sent out beyond Chang'an Gate by the Tang King and many officials. After a few days of tireless travel, he arrived at the Fa Men Temple. The resident abbot, Shangfang Elder, led over five hundred monks, lining both sides, to welcome him inside and present him with tea. After tea, they entered the hall, and after the meal, they didn't realize it was late. It was truly as if:

Stars near, river of light in motion,
The moon bright, without a speck of dust.
Geese call far across the Han,
Clamor of the wooden mallet from the western neighbor.
Birds return to roost in withered trees,
Monks discourse in the sound of Sanskrit.
On a mat, upon a single bed,
Sitting till night is about to part.

The monks discussed the matter of Buddha's decree and the reason for Sanzang's journey to the west to retrieve scriptures, speaking under the lamps. Some said the water was far, the mountains high; some said the road was treacherous with tigers and leopards; some said the steep cliffs and ridges were hard to traverse; and some said the demonic and monstrous creatures were hard to subdue. Sanzang kept silent, but pointed to his heart and nodded several times. The monks, unable to understand his meaning, clasped their hands and asked, "Master, what does it mean to point at your heart and nod?"

Sanzang replied, "When the mind arises, all kinds of demons arise; when the mind perishes, all kinds of demons perish. I, your disciple, made a great vow to Buddha at the Hua Sheng Temple, and it is not something I can avoid. This time, I must go west to see Buddha and seek the scriptures, to enable the cycle of Dharma to turn, and may the prosperity of the Holy Master's lineage endure forever."

Hearing this, the monks all expressed their admiration, praising him one after another as "the loyal, courageous, and truly enlightened master" and urged him to rest in the bed.

A poem says: Emperor Taizong of the Tang Dynasty issued an edict, sending Xuanzang to seek teachings from the Zen sect. With a steadfast heart, he sought the Dragon's Lair, diligently cultivating on Mount Shuangfeng. He journeyed far beyond borders, through countless countries and mountains. 

Now he sets out west, entrusted with the teachings, and attains enlightenment in the great emptiness.

It is said that in the tenth year of the Zhenguan era, on the third day before the full moon of September, Xuanzang was sent out of Chang'an Pass by Emperor Taizong and many officials.  For days, his horse didn't stop, arriving at the Famen Temple early.

The head abbot, Elder Shangfang, led over five hundred monks, lining the sides, to welcome him inside. They greeted him with tea, which they served and then, after the meal, they realized it was already late at night.  The stars were close to the moving shadows, the moon shone bright without a speck of dust. 

The cries of geese echoed from afar, the sound of a pounding mortar came from a neighboring house. Returning birds nested in withered trees, while monks chanted scriptures. On a single mat, they sat until nightfall. 

The monks discussed under the lamplight the Buddhist decree and the reason behind Xuanzang's journey to the west to retrieve the scriptures. Some said the distance was vast and the mountains high, others said the road was fraught with tigers and leopards, while others pointed to the dangerous cliffs and slopes. Still others mentioned the formidable demons and evil spirits. 

Xuanzang kept silent, merely pointing at his heart and nodding several times.  The monks couldn't understand, so they bowed and asked, "Master, what does pointing at your heart and nodding signify?"

Xuanzang replied, "When the heart arises, all manner of demons arise; when the heart ceases, all manner of demons cease. I, a disciple, made a great vow before Buddha at Huasheng Temple, and I cannot go back on my word. This journey is for sure, I will reach the West Heaven, see Buddha, and retrieve the scriptures, turning the wheel of the Dharma. My wish is for the sacred reign of the emperor to endure forever." 

Hearing these words, the monks were filled with admiration and respect, praising him with "Honest and Bold Master Xuanzang," and invited him to rest.

K. turned around, the merchant hardly noticing as he immediately stood up. “Please stay seated,” said K. and pulled a chair next to him. “Have you been an old client of the lawyer for a long time?” asked K. “Yes,” said the merchant, “a very old client.” “How many years has he been representing you?” asked K. “I don’t know how to tell you,” said the merchant, “in business legal matters – I have a grain business – the lawyer has represented me since I took over the business, so about twenty years. In my own case, the one you’re probably referring to, he’s been representing me since the beginning, it’s been longer than five years. Yes, well over five years,” he added, then pulled out an old wallet, “I have everything written down here; if you want, I’ll tell you the exact dates. It’s hard to keep track of everything. My case has probably been going on for much longer, it began shortly after my wife died, and that’s been longer than five and a half years.” K. moved closer to him. “So the lawyer also takes on ordinary legal matters?” he asked. This connection of the courts and legal matters seemed immensely reassuring to K. “Certainly,” said the merchant, and then whispered to K., “they even say that he is better at these matters than the others.” But then he seemed to regret it, placed a hand on K.’s shoulder and said, “Please, don’t betray me.” K. patted him on the knee reassuringly and said, “No, I’m not a betrayer.” “He is vindictive, though,” said the merchant. “He won’t do anything to such a loyal client,” said K. “Oh, but,” said the merchant, “when he’s upset, he makes no distinctions, by the way, I’m not actually loyal to him.” “Why not?” asked K. “Should I confide in you?” asked the merchant doubtfully. “I think you may,” said K. “Well,” said the merchant, “I’ll confide in you partly, but you must also tell me a secret so that we can support each other against the lawyer.” “You’re very cautious,” said K., “but I will tell you a secret that will completely reassure you. What is your disloyalty to the lawyer then?” “I have,” said the merchant hesitantly, in a tone as if confessing something dishonorable, “I have other lawyers besides him.” “That’s not so bad,” said K., a little disappointed. “Here, yes,” said the merchant, who was still breathing heavily from his confession but became more confident due to K.’s remark. “It’s not allowed. And it’s especially not allowed to have corner lawyers in addition to a so-called lawyer. And that’s exactly what I’ve done, I have five corner lawyers besides him.” “Five!” exclaimed K., the number first put him in astonishment, “five lawyers besides this one?” The merchant nodded: “I’m still negotiating with a sixth.” “But why do you need so many lawyers?” asked K. “I need them all,” said the merchant. “Don’t you want to explain that?” asked K. “Certainly,” said the merchant. “Above all, I don’t want to lose my case, that’s self-evident. Consequently, I can’t ignore anything that could be of benefit to me, even if the hope of benefit in a particular case is only very small, I can’t discard it. That’s why I’ve put everything I own into the case. For example, I’ve withdrawn all the money from my business, before it filled almost an entire floor of the building, now I only have a small room in the back where I work with an apprentice. This decline hasn’t only been caused by the withdrawal of the money, but even more so by the withdrawal of my working capacity. When you want to do something for your case, you can’t really focus on anything else.” “So you’re also working at court yourself?” asked K. “That’s precisely what I’d like to know more about.” “I can’t tell you much about that,” said the merchant, “at first, I probably tried it too, but I soon gave up. It’s too exhausting and doesn’t bring much success. Even working and negotiating there has proven to be impossible for me. It’s hard enough just sitting and waiting there. You know the heavy atmosphere in the offices.” “How do you know that I was there?” asked K. “I was just in the waiting room when you went through.” “What a coincidence!” exclaimed K., completely absorbed and forgetting the merchant’s former ridicule. “You saw me! You were in the waiting room when I went through. Yes, I did go through there once.” “It’s not such a big coincidence,” said the merchant, “I’m there almost every day.” “I’ll probably have to go there more often now,” said K., “but I won’t be received so honorably anymore, I’m sure. Everyone stood up. They probably thought I was a judge.” “No,” said the merchant, “we greeted the court officer then. We knew you were the defendant.” “You knew that already,” said K., “then my behavior probably seemed arrogant.” “No,” said the merchant, “on the contrary. But that are foolish things.” “What kind of foolish things?” asked K. “Why are you asking about that?” said the merchant irritably. “You don’t seem to know the people there and might misunderstand. You have to remember that many things come up in this process that are beyond the mind, you’re simply too tired and distracted for a lot, and as a substitute, people resort to superstition. I’m talking about the others, but I’m no better myself. One such superstition is that many people, especially from the defendant’s lips, can see the outcome of the trial. These people claimed that, according to your lips, you would definitely and soon be convicted. I repeat, it’s a ridiculous superstition and in most cases completely refuted by the facts, but when you live in that society, it’s hard to escape these opinions. Think about how strong this superstition can be. You did speak to one of them, didn’t you? He could barely answer you. There are many reasons why he might have been confused, but one was the sight of your lips. He later said that he even believed he saw the sign of his own condemnation on your lips.” “My lips?” asked K., pulled out a pocket mirror and looked at himself. “I can’t see anything special about my lips.” “Me neither,” said the merchant, “nothing at all.” “How superstitious these people are!” exclaimed K. “Didn’t I tell you?” asked the merchant. “Do they interact with each other so much and share their opinions?” asked K. “I’ve mostly kept to myself,” said the merchant. “Generally, they don’t interact,” said the merchant, “it wouldn’t be possible, there are so many. There are also few common interests. When sometimes a belief in a common interest appears in a group, it soon turns out to be a mistake. Together they can’t achieve anything against the court. Each case is examined individually, it is the most careful court after all. Together you can’t achieve anything, only an individual can sometimes achieve something in secret; only when it is achieved, do the others find out; no one knows how it happened. So there’s no unity, although they come together in the waiting rooms now and then, but little is discussed there. The superstitious opinions have existed for ages and multiply almost by themselves.” “I saw the gentlemen there in the waiting room,” said K., “their waiting seemed so pointless to me.” “Waiting is not pointless,” said the merchant, “it’s only independent action that is pointless. I said that I now have five lawyers besides this one. One would think – and I myself thought so at first – now I could leave it all to them. But that would be completely wrong. Chichikov's spirits sank entirely, and he flung his saber onto the floor—the one he carried on his journey to inspire the necessary fear in the appropriate people. No matter how heatedly he protested, calling them swindlers, robbers, plunderers of travelers, even hinting at the terrible judgment to come, the blacksmiths remained unmoved: they held their ground firmly—not only did they not lower their price, but they dragged out the work instead of the two hours it should have taken, taking a full five and a half.

During this time, he had the pleasure of experiencing those pleasant moments familiar to every traveler, when one's trunk is unpacked and all that remains in the room are strings, scraps of paper, and miscellaneous items, when a man belongs neither to the road nor to his seat, and from the window he sees people shuffling by, chattering about their grivna coins, and with a peculiar curiosity lifting their eyes to glance at him, then returning to their path, which only further aggravates the bad mood of the poor, non-traveling traveler. Everything he sees, everything that comes to his eyes—the little shop opposite his window, the head of the old woman in the opposite house approaching the window with her short curtains—it all seems loathsome to him, and yet he doesn't move away from the window. He stands, sometimes lost in thought, then turning his attention once more to everything that moves and doesn't move before him, crushing a fly with his finger that buzzes and flutters against the glass. But all things come to an end, and the longed-for moment arrived: everything was ready; the cart was properly arranged, the wheel was fitted with a new tire, the horses were brought from the watering trough, and the robbers—the blacksmiths—having counted the received rubles, wished him good fortune. Selyfan cracked his whip; Petrukha, after hanging on the footboard for a moment, finally clambered up; and our hero, settling himself more comfortably on the Georgian rug, leaned back on a leather cushion, tucked two hot buns, and the carriage started to bounce and sway thanks to the uneven cobbles.

He looked at the houses, walls, fences, and streets with some vague feeling as they also, as if in response, slowly receded behind him, and who knows if fate would ever allow him to see them again during the course of his life.  As they turned onto one of the streets, the carriage had to stop because a seemingly endless funeral procession stretched the whole length of the road. Chichikov, leaning out, ordered Petrukha to ask who was being buried, and learned that the prosecutor was being buried. Filled with unpleasant sensations, he immediately hid in a corner, covered himself with a cloak, and pulled the curtains. At this time, while the carriage was thus detained, Selyfan and Petrukha, having removed their hats in a respectful gesture, were watching, counting, and noting who, how, in what, and on what was riding and walking. The master, having instructed them not to acknowledge or bow to any of the familiar footmen, also peered out timidly through the little panes in the leather curtains. The procession of officials, having removed their hats, followed the coffin. He began to fear that they might recognize his carriage, but they seemed not to notice him at all. They didn't even engage in the usual everyday conversations that people have while accompanying a deceased person. All their thoughts seemed to be directed inward: they were thinking about what kind of new governor-general would arrive, how he would take up his duties, and how he would treat them. Behind the officials, who were walking on foot, came carriages, from which ladies in mourning bonnets could be seen, their lips and hands moving, indicating lively conversation. Perhaps they were also discussing the arrival of the new governor-general, making conjectures about the balls he would give, and gossiping about their eternal fringes and embroidery. He began to be afraid that they might recognize his carriage, but they were not interested in that. They didn't even engage in the usual everyday conversations that accompany those accompanying the deceased. All their thoughts were absorbed in themselves: they were thinking about what kind of a new governor-general it would be, how he would take over, and how he would treat them. Behind the officials, walking on foot, followed carriages, from which ladies in mourning head-wraps peered out. From the movements of their lips and hands, it was clear that they were engaged in lively conversation; perhaps they were also talking about the arrival of the new governor-general and making assumptions about the balls he would give, and worrying about their eternal frills and trimmings. Finally, a few empty carriages followed, stretching out in a row, and nothing remained. The hero could now go on. Opening the leather curtains, he sighed and said from the bottom of his heart, "Well, so goes the prosecutor! He lived, lived, and then he died! And now they will print in the newspapers that a respected citizen, a rare father, a model husband, has passed away to the grief of his subordinates and all mankind, and they will write all sorts of things; perhaps they will add that he was accompanied by the weeping of widows and orphans; but if you look closely, it turns out that you only had thick eyebrows after all." Then he ordered Selifan to drive faster, and in the meantime thought to himself, "Well, it's good that we met the funeral; they say it's a good omen to meet a deceased."

They say the ancients held elections in secret, hiding like thieves; some of our historians even claim they attended election festivals disguised (I imagine it as a fantastically gloomy spectacle: night, a square, figures creeping along the walls in dark cloaks; a flickering, blood-red torch flame bending in the wind...). Why all this secrecy is still not entirely clear; most likely, elections were connected with some mystical, superstitious, perhaps even criminal rituals. We have nothing to hide or be ashamed of: we celebrate elections openly, honestly, in the daylight. I see how everyone votes for the Benefactor; everyone sees how I vote for the Benefactor – and can it be otherwise, since "all" and "I" are a single "We". How uplifting, sincere, how much higher than the cowardly "secret" of the ancients. Besides, how much more practical. After all, even if we imagine the impossible, that is, some dissonance in the usual monophonic chorus, the Invisible Guardians are right here, among us: they can immediately identify those who have strayed from the path and save them from further false steps, and the United State – from themselves. And finally, one more thing...

News of the adventure reached the church with extraordinary speed. As Keller approached the prince, a multitude of people, completely unknown to him, swarmed around him, peppering him with questions. There was loud chatter, head-shaking, even laughter; no one left the church, everyone waited to see how the groom would receive the news. He paled, but took it calmly, barely audible, saying: “I was afraid; but I didn’t think it would be like this…” and then, after a moment's pause, added: “However… given her condition… it's perfectly understandable.” Keller later called this response “unparalleled philosophy.” The prince emerged from the church seemingly calm and composed; at least that's how many noticed and later recounted it. It seemed he was very eager to get home and be alone, but this was not allowed.  

Some of the invited guests, including Ptcyin, Gavrila Ardalionovich, and the doctor, who also wasn't inclined to leave, followed him into the room. Moreover, the whole house was besieged by idle curiosity-seekers. Even from the terrace, the prince heard Keller and Lebedev engage in a heated argument with some, completely unknown, though seemingly official-looking individuals, who were determined at all costs to get onto the terrace. The prince approached the disputants, inquired about the matter, and, politely setting Lebedev and Keller aside, delicately addressed a rather elderly and stout gentleman standing on the steps at the head of several others, and invited him to honor him with his presence. The gentleman was embarrassed, but nonetheless went in, followed by another, then another. Out of the whole crowd, about seven or eight visitors managed to enter, trying to do so as casually as possible; but no more eager guests appeared, and soon, within the crowd, they began to criticize the "jumpers". 

Those who had entered were seated, the conversation started, tea was served — all of this was extremely decent, modest, to the surprise of some of the guests. There were, of course, a few attempts to lighten the conversation and steer it towards the "proper" topic; some impertinent questions were asked, some "bold" remarks were made. The ladies immediately surrounded him, a brilliant garland, and carried with them whole clouds of all sorts of perfumes: one breathed roses, from another one could smell spring and violets, the third was completely infused with  mint; Chikchkov only raised his nose and sniffed. Their taste in attire was appalling: muslins, satins, chiffons were such pale fashionable colors that they couldn't even be named (the refinement of taste had reached such a degree). Ribbon bows and flower bouquets fluttered there and there on the dresses in the most picturesque disorder, although a considerable head had worked over this disorder.  A light headwear held only on the ears and seemed to say: "Hey, I'll fly away, it's a pity that I won't take the beauty with me!" The waists were belted and had the most firm and pleasant for the eye forms (it should be noted that generally all the ladies of the city N. were somewhat full, but they were laced so skillfully and had such a pleasant demeanor that their fullness could not be noticed at all). Everything was devised and foreseen with extraordinary meticulousness; the neck, shoulders were open just as much as necessary, and no further; each one revealed her possessions to the extent that she felt, according to her own conviction, that they were capable of destroying a man; the rest was hidden with extraordinary taste: either a light ribbon tie or a scarf lighter than a pastry known as “a kiss”, ethereally enveloped the neck, or small, jagged walls of thin batiste, known as “modesty,” peeked out from behind the shoulders, from under the dress; these “modest” things concealed what could no longer harm a man, and at the same time made one suspect that precisely there was the most danger. Long gloves were not worn up to the sleeves, but thoughtfully left bare the exciting parts of the hands above the elbow, which at many, breathed temptingly full; at others even the silk gloves burst, urged to be pulled further – in a word, it seemed as if everything was written: no, this is not a province, this is the capital, this is Paris itself! Only occasionally some unheard-of cap or even some almost peacock feather would suddenly protrude in defiance of all fashion, according to one’s own taste. But without this it is impossible, such is the property of a provincial town: somewhere it must necessarily break off. Chikchkov, standing before them, thought: "Which one, however, is the writer of the letter?" – and he stuck his nose forward; but his nose was tugged by a whole row of elbows, cuffs, sleeves, ends of ribbons, fragrant chemises, and dresses. The cavalcade galloped at full speed: the postmaster's wife, the captain of the militia, the lady with the blue feather, the lady with the white feather, the Georgian prince Chipkhaidze, a civil servant from St. Petersburg, a civil servant from Moscow, the Frenchman Kuk, Perkhunovsky, Berebenovsky – everyone rose and rushed.

His appearance at the ball produced an extraordinary effect.  Everything that was, turned towards him. Some with cards in their hands, others in the middle of a conversation, interrupting with "and what does the lower magistrates' court say about this…" But what the magistrates' court says—he simply cast that aside, rushing forward with greetings to our hero. "Pavel Ivanovich! My God, Pavel Ivanovich! Dear Pavel Ivanovich! Respected Pavel Ivanovich! Soul of my soul, Pavel Ivanovich! Here you are, Pavel Ivanovich! Here is our Pavel Ivanovich! Allow me to embrace you, Pavel Ivanovich! Let us take him here, I shall kiss my dear Pavel Ivanovich more thoroughly!" Chivchkov all at once found himself in several embraces. Before he could quite wriggle free from the governor's embrace, he was already in the arms of the police chief; the police chief handed him over to the inspector of the medical administration; the inspector—to the tax collector; the tax collector—to the architect… The governor, who was standing near the ladies at the time, holding a confectionary ticket in one hand and a half-bottle of wine in the other, saw him and threw both the ticket and the bottle on the floor—only a little dog barked; in a word, he spread extraordinary joy and merriment. In my explanation here, I note all these figures and numbers. Of course, it will be all the same to me, but now (and perhaps only at this very moment) I want those who judge my actions to clearly see what logical chain of conclusions led to my “final conviction.” I wrote above that the final resolve, which I lacked to carry out my “final conviction,” arose in me, it seems, not from a logical deduction, but from some strange impulse, some strange circumstance, perhaps entirely unconnected with the course of events. Ten days ago, Rogozhin came to me on one of his own affairs, which is extraneous to mention here. I had never seen Rogozhin before, but I had heard a great deal about him. I gave him the necessary information, and he soon left, and since he had only come for information, that would have been the end of our business. But he interested me too much, and the whole day I was under the influence of strange thoughts, so much so that I decided to visit him the next day myself. Rogozhin was obviously not pleased to see me and even “delicately” hinted that we had nothing more to continue our acquaintance. But still, I spent a very interesting hour, as, probably, he did too. There was such a contrast between us, which could not but affect us both, especially me: I was a man who had already counted his days, and he — living the fullest, most immediate life, the present moment, without any concern for “final” conclusions, figures, or anything that did not concern what… what… well, at least what he was obsessed with; let me apologize for this expression, Mr. Rogozhin, perhaps even to a bad writer who was unable to express his thought. Despite his unfriendliness, I thought he was a man of intellect and capable of understanding much, though little interested him from outside. I did not hint to him about my “final conviction,” but for some reason it seemed to me that he, listening to me, guessed it. He remained silent, he is terribly taciturn. I hinted to him, leaving, that despite all the difference between us and all the contradictions — les extrémités se touchent [20] (I explained this to him in Russian), so that, perhaps, he himself is not so far from my “final conviction” as it seems. To this he replied to me with a very sullen and sour grimace, stood up, himself found my cap, pretending as if I was leaving myself, and simply escorted me out of his gloomy house as if out of politeness. His house struck me; it resembled a graveyard, and he, it seems, likes it, which is understandable, of course: such a full, immediate life, which he lives, is too full by itself to need any setting.

"Understand ("p" – fountain) – an ancient legend about paradise… This is about us, about now. Yes! Think about it. Those two in paradise – were given a choice: happiness without freedom – or freedom without happiness; there is no third option. They, fools, chose freedom – and what do you know – they yearned for their shackles for centuries afterward. For shackles – you understand – that's what world sorrow is about. Centuries! And only we have figured out how to bring back happiness… No, listen further – further! The Ancient God and we – we are together, at the same table. Yes! We helped God finally defeat the devil – it was he who tempted people to break the prohibition and taste the poison of freedom, he – the sly serpent. And we – with a kick to his head – thwack! And that's it: paradise again. And we are again simple, innocent, like Adam and Eve. No more this confusion about good and evil: everything is very simple, paradisiacal, childishly simple. The Benefactor, the Machine, the Cube, the Gas Bell, the Guardians – all this is good, all of it – magnificent, beautiful, noble, sublime, crystal-clear. Because it protects our lack of freedom – that is, our happiness. The ancients would start judging here, sorting things out, racking their brains – ethics, non-ethics… Well, forget it; in short, here's a little paradise poem, eh? And with a serious tone, you understand? A masterpiece, eh?"

Our hero, though, was already middle-aged and possessed of a cautious, cool temperament. He too pondered, but in a more positive light, his thoughts less impulsive and even partly quite substantial. "A fine young woman!" he said, opening his tobacco pouch and sniffing the tobacco. "But what, above all, is good about her? What's good is that she's clearly just emerged from some kind of boarding school or institute, that she hasn't yet, as they say, acquired any 'womanly' traits, that is, precisely what is most unpleasant about them. She's now like a child, everything about her is simple, she'll say whatever comes to mind, she'll laugh where she pleases. You can make anything of her, she could be a wonder, or she could turn into a real disaster, and she will become a disaster! So let the mothers and aunts take over now. In a year, they'll fill her with all kinds of feminine things that even her own father won't recognize.  Where will the inflated airs and the stiff formality come from? She'll start behaving according to rote instructions, she'll rack her brains trying to figure out whom to speak to, how, and for how long, what look to give to whom; every minute she'll be afraid of saying too much, she'll eventually get entangled, and will end up telling lies her whole life, and become something truly monstrous!" He paused for a moment and then added: "It would be interesting to know who her parents are. What kind of man is her father? A wealthy landowner of honorable character, or simply a decent man with a capital earned in service? If, let's say, this girl were given two hundred thousand rubles in dowry, she could become a very, very desirable catch. This could be, so to speak, the happiness of a respectable man." Two hundred thousand rubles began to take shape so alluringly in his mind that he inwardly started to resent himself for not finding out from the coachman or the stablehand during his errands around the carriages who the travelers were.  Soon, however, the village of Sobakevich, which appeared on the horizon, dispersed his thoughts and forced them to return to their constant subject.

Yesterday morning the prince was here; among other things, he persuaded me to move to his dacha. I knew he would insist on this, and I was sure he would blurt out to me that it would be "easier to die among people and trees" on the dacha, as he puts it. But today he didn't say "die," but "it will be easier to live," which, however, is almost the same for me, in my situation. I asked him what he meant by his constant "trees" and why he was imposing them on me so, and I was surprised to learn that I had supposedly said that evening that I was coming to Pavlovsk for the last time to look at the trees. When I pointed out to him that it makes no difference whether you die under the trees or looking out the window at my bricks, and that there's no need to make such a fuss for two weeks, he immediately agreed; but, in his opinion, the greenery and fresh air would certainly produce some physical change in me, and my agitation and my dreams would change and perhaps ease. I again remarked to him, laughing, that he speaks like a materialist. He replied to me with his smile that he had always been a materialist. Since he never lies, these words mean something. His smile is beautiful; I saw him more attentively now. I don't know if I love him or not now; I don't have time for that now. My five-month-long hatred for him, it should be noted, has been waning completely in the last month. Who knows, perhaps I came to Pavlovsk, primarily, to see him. But... why did I leave my room then? A condemned man should not leave his corner; and if I had not made a final decision now, and had decided instead to wait until the last moment, then, of course, I would not have left my room for anything and would not have accepted his offer to "die" with him in Pavlovsk.

When I pointed out to him that it's all the same to die under trees or looking out the window at my bricks, and that for two weeks there's no need for such ceremony, he immediately agreed; but, in his opinion, the greenery and fresh air would inevitably produce some physical change in me, and my agitation and dreams would change and, perhaps, ease. I again remarked to him, laughing, that he speaks like a materialist. He replied to me with his smile that he had always been a materialist. Since he never lies, these words must mean something. His smile is lovely; I saw him more closely now. I don't know if I love him or not now; now I haven't time to deal with this. My five-month-old hatred for him, it should be noted, has dwindled considerably in the last month. Who knows, maybe I came to Pavlovsk mainly to see him. But... why did I leave my room then? A condemned man shouldn't leave his corner; and if I hadn't made a final decision now, and had decided instead to wait until the last hour, I certainly wouldn't have left my room for anything and wouldn't have accepted his offer to move to "die" with him in Pavlovsk.

Suddenly, a macaque leapt out from the group, calling out in a loud voice, "Your Majesty, if you are thinking so far ahead, it is truly a display of an enlightened mind! Nowadays, among all living creatures, there are only three who are beyond the control of Yama, the King of Hell." The Monkey King said, "Do you know who these three are?" The macaque replied, "They are the Buddha, the Immortal, and the Divine. They have escaped the cycle of reincarnation and are neither born nor destroyed, living as long as heaven, earth, mountains, and rivers." The Monkey King said, "Where do these three reside?" The macaque answered, "They are only in the world of Jambudvipa, within the ancient caves of Mount Xumi." Hearing this, the Monkey King was filled with joy and said, "Tomorrow, I shall bid you farewell and descend the mountain. I will travel to the ends of the earth, venturing far and wide to seek out these three, and learn the secret of eternal life and immortality, so as to forever evade the clutches of Yama." Ah! That very sentence shattered the net of reincarnation, leading to the becoming of the Great Sage, Equalling Heaven. All the other monkeys clapped their hands in praise, saying, "Well done! Well done! We shall climb the mountain tomorrow to gather fruits and prepare a grand feast to send off our Great King!"

"But he is loyal to me and the dynasty," Napoleon would say of him. One day, I was terribly pained, and suddenly he noticed the tears in my eyes; he looked at me with tenderness: "You pity me!" he exclaimed, "You, my child, and perhaps another child, my son, le roi de Rome,[27] will also pity me; all the rest, all of them hate me, and my brothers will be the first to sell me in my misfortune!" He immediately sat down and wrote that letter to Josephine, which the next day was sent off with Constant.

Thousand officials with jeweled ornaments surround the throne, the five guards' banners stand guard on both sides. Holding gold gourds and axes, they stand in pairs; red silk candles and incense from royal censors fill the hall with a magnificent aroma. Dragons soar and phoenixes dance, falcons and eagles ascend; the holy emperor's presence shines, loyal and righteous ministers gather close. 

Passing over millennia to surpass Shun and Yu, ascending to a thousand generations to rival Yao and Tang. I see the royal scepter and the dragon robes, their brilliance intermingling; jade bracelets and jeweled fans, auspicious clouds gently wafting. Crowns of jewels, belts of jade, purple sashes and gold emblems.  A thousand troops guard the imperial carriage, with two lines of courtiers attending. The emperor bathes, devoutly respecting the Buddha, converting to the good fruit, joyfully taking incense.

King Tang, in his grand procession, arrives early at the temple gates, silencing the music and ceremonial instruments, disembarks from his carriage, and leads his retinue of officials. They bow and take incense before the Buddha. After three circumambulations, he lifts his head to admire the beautiful sacred grounds. Look! The banners flutter and the jeweled canopy shines. Banners flutter and sway, condensing the emptiness, a rainbow cascade of colors; the jeweled canopy shines, reflecting the sun, red sparks flash with brilliance. 

The Buddha’s golden image, majestic, the Arhats' jade faces, awe-inspiring.  Bottles of fragrant flowers stand, sandalwood incense smolders, incense permeates the sky. Fresh fruits are arranged on a vermilion platter, exotic candies piled on colorful trays. Great monks recite scriptures, hoping to liberate wandering souls from suffering.

Emperor Taizong, with his ministers, both civil and military, take incense and bow before the Buddha's golden body, then venerate the Arhats.  I see the eminent Master Xuanzang, master of the great hall, leading the monks and bowing to King Tang. After the ceremony, they disperse to meditate, the master presents the Emperor with a scroll titled "Liberating the Perishing" saying:

"Vast virtue, deep and boundless, Zen stillness, utterly silent. Purity, clear and luminous, flowing through the three realms. Infinite transformations, encompassing yin and yang. True nature, boundless and eternal. Observing these lost souls, compassion is deeply called for.

By imperial mandate, I have assembled these monks, to meditate and teach dharma. To widely open the doors of convenience, to launch a great vessel of compassion, to ferry across the suffering sea of life, to liberate all beings from the illness of the six realms. Guide them back to the true path, where freedom reigns in the vastness of creation.

Neither action nor inaction; all is perfectly pure. Relying on this opportune moment, invite the blessings of the grand, pure jade palaces. Utilize this auspicious assembly, to escape the prison of hell and rebirth.

Ascend to the Pure Land and enjoy boundless freedom, traveling to the West at will.

Poetry:

One eternal incense burner, several scrolls of transcendence.

Infinite wondrous dharma proclaimed, limitless divine grace received.

All grudges and entanglements disappear, all wandering souls are liberated.

May my kingdom be blessed with peace and prosperity for ten thousand years."

Emperor Taizong read with great joy and said to the monks, "May you all maintain your pure intentions and never neglect these sacred rituals. When the work is completed, I will bestow great rewards, ensuring your labors are not in vain." 

The twelve hundred monks bowed in unison, expressing their gratitude.

Thousand officials surrounded the Emperor, their emblems fanning out before and behind. The guards stood in rows on either side, swords and axes gleaming, in pairs facing each other.  Red silk candles flickered, while incense burned in ornate censers, filling the hall with a rich, palpable fragrance. Dragons soared and phoenixes took flight, as eagles and falcons spread their wings. The divinely appointed Son of Heaven, the Emperor, sat upright, surrounded by loyal and righteous ministers. His virtues have surpassed those of Shun and Yu from a thousand years past, his rule will rival that of Yao and Tang, bringing prosperity for ten thousand generations.

A sight to behold! The jeweled handles of the parasols and the embroidered dragon robes shimmered, their light reflected in the jade ornaments and colorful peacock fans that rippled in the breeze. Crowned in jewels, adorned with jade belts and purple sashes, he was escorted by thousands of imperial guards and a line of dignitaries. The Emperor bathed in the devotion of these holy offerings, bowing in piety as he held the incense and worshipped.

The Tang King arrived early, arriving before the temple gates. He silenced the music, disembarked from his palanquin, and led a procession of officials. He too, bowed and held incense as he worshipped the Buddha, circling the altar three times. Then, raising his gaze, he beheld the magnificent sight before him: banners fluttered in the wind, and the jeweled canopy shone brightly. 

The banners danced, painted with rainbows across the sky; the canopy shimmered, reflecting the sun in a cascade of vibrant light. The image of the Buddha, majestic in his golden form, sat serenely alongside the Arhats, their jade faces radiating power.  Flowers in vases decorated the hall, and sandalwood incense perfumed the air.  The incense filled the room, its fragrant smoke reaching through the highest heavens. A platter of fresh fruits and delicate pastries adorned with sugar candy lay ready on a colorful table.

The high monks stood in a row, chanting the sacred scriptures, hoping to free the souls from their suffering. The Emperor, both civil and military officials, each lit incense and bowed to the Buddha's golden image, paying homage to the Arhats. 

Then, Master Xuanzang, chief abbot of the Grand Trinities Monastery, led the assembled monks in a bow before the Tang King. After the ceremony concluded, the monks returned to their meditation positions, and Xuanzang presented the Emperor with a scroll titled "The List for Liberating Souls," saying, "By the benevolence of Heaven, we have the path of Zen. Its purity and insight transcends the three realms. It embraces all transformations, uniting yin and yang. Its essence is true and eternal, infinite in its power. Observing these lonely souls, one must feel compassion. Thus, by command of the Emperor, we have gathered the monks to practice meditation and preach the Dharma. With open doors, we extend our compassionate embrace, offering salvation to all beings suffering in the sea of existence. We lead them to liberation from their mortal ailments, guiding them to the True Way, transcending the veil of illusion. By mastering stillness and movement, they achieve pure emptiness, free from all attachments.

Following this auspicious occasion, we celebrate the grandeur of the capital city, a shining beacon of civilization. Grasping this precious opportunity, we overcome the confines of the underworld and ascend to bliss. Soaring freely in the realm of Ultimate Happiness, we move back and forth freely,  free from the Western Pure Land. Poetry says:

One incense burner, a fragrance for eternal life,
A scroll of transcendent scriptures.
Infinite magical laws are proclaimed,
Unending heavenly grace pervades.

Every grievance is erased,
Each soul is freed from its prison.
May our kingdom prosper for ten thousand years,
Enjoy peace and tranquility.

The Emperor, overjoyed, addressed the assembled monks: "You hold true devotion in your hearts. Never neglect the practice of Buddhist teachings. When your efforts bear fruit and your aspirations are fulfilled, I shall reward you generously. I vow that your labor will not be in vain."

The 1,200 monks bowed in unison, expressing their gratitude.

They held golden gourds, axes, and halberds, facing each other in pairs; the red silk candles and incense burner filled the air with a sweet fragrance. Dragons danced and phoenixes soared, eagles took to the sky, hawks rising in pursuit.  The august emperor, a righteous and virtuous ruler, surpassed even Shun and Yu of old, his reign of peace would rival that of Yao and Tang.   Then came the sight of the curved-handle umbrella, the dragon-robed emperor, the light of the jewels reflecting; jade ornaments, and colored phoenix fans, auspicious clouds billowed around him.  Jewelled crowns, jade belts, purple sashes, and golden emblems adorned him.  Thousands of soldiers formed a protective escort, two rows of palanquins carried him. This emperor, bathed in a reverent devotion, respectfully bowed to Buddha, accepting the blessings of good fortune, offering incense.

After three circumambulations, he looked up and saw a truly magnificent gathering. Banners swayed in the wind, precious banners shone brightly. The banners danced and swayed,  casting dancing rainbows upon the sky; the banners shone, reflecting the sun, lightning flashed red. After the ceremony, each monk found their designated meditation spot. The master presented the "Jùgū Biǎng," a scroll with a proclamation, to the emperor.  The scroll declared: "Compassionate virtues are immeasurable, the Zen sect is eternal. Pure and clear understanding flows through the three realms. By imperial decree: we gather monks and nuns to practice Chan, to teach the Dharma, open wide the gates of convenience, set sail on the vast ocean of compassion, to save all living beings in the sea of suffering, and free them from illness and rebirth.  Guide them to the true path, liberate them from the confusion of chaos; inaction, yet moving, purity arises.  Depending on this opportunity, enjoy the blessings of the clear capital and magnificent palaces;  take advantage of this favorable gathering, break free from the prison of the realms of desire, quickly attain bliss, travel freely to the West, enjoy ultimate freedom. Opening the Door of Grace, Navigating the Boat of Compassion, Rescuing the Suffering Multitude from the Sea of Samsara, Freeing Them from Suffering and Rebirth. Guiding Them to True Paths, Experiencing the Cosmic Origin; Actionless Stillness, Transforming into Pure Being. Relying on this Auspicious Opportunity, Feasting in the Jade Palace of Our Capital; Riding on This Fortunate Convergence, Escaping the Hellish Cycle of Existence. Early Ascent to Blissful Joy, Freedom to Roam the West, Reunited with Nirvana.”

Emperor Taizong, filled with joy, addressed the monks: “You all possess righteous intentions; do not neglect Buddhist affairs. When your efforts are complete, each of you will find your reward.
