Thousands of officials surround the emperor, their belts adorned with jeweled ornaments, while five guards stand in formation on either side. One holds a golden mallet, the other an axe; the two stand in unison.

Red silk candles illuminate the room, incense from a burning brazier fills the air, creating an atmosphere of grandeur. Dragons and phoenixes dance, hawks and eagles soar. The holy sovereign, the enlightened emperor, is present; his loyal ministers are righteous. He surpasses the virtues of Yao and Shun by a thousand years, surpassing the peace of Yu and Tang by ten thousand.

And there, the emperor's staff shines, reflecting the splendor of his dragon-emblazoned robe. Jade rings and a fan decorated with colorful phoenixes radiate auspicious vibes. His jeweled crown, jade belt, purple sash, and gold insignia gleam. A thousand troops of imperial guards surround him, two lines of palanquin bearers follow close behind. The emperor, in a reverent and pious manner, bathes in the light of the Buddha, joyfully accepting the merit of incense offerings.

King Tang arrives early, approaches the temple, commands the musical instruments to be silenced, disembarks from his carriage, and leads his entourage of officials to bow before the Buddha, offering incense.

After three turns, he raises his head to gaze upon the magnificent temple. He sees banners fluttering, jeweled canopies radiating brilliance. The banners flutter and dance, painting the sky with colored clouds; the canopies shine, reflecting the sun's rays like crimson lightning. The Buddha's golden elephant form is truly magnificent, the Arhat's jade faces radiate divine power. 

Flowering immortal blossoms fill the vase, sandalwood incense fills the air.

Immortals blossoms fill the vase, illuminating the magnificent pagoda with their radiance; sandalwood incense fills the air, its fragrance permeates the clear skies. Fresh fruit, artistically arranged on a crimson platter, and unusual sugar pastries stacked on a colorful table are laid out.

High priests chant the true scriptures, hoping to liberate lone souls from suffering. Emperor Taizong, both civil and military, each offers incense, bows before the Buddha's golden statue, and pays homage to the Arhats.

Then, he sees the eminent Master Xuanzang, standing in front of the imperial court, leading the Buddhist monks in prostration before the Tang King.  

After the ceremony, the monks find their respective meditation spots. The master presents Emperor Taizong with a scroll titled "Pardoning the Destitute." The scroll reads: 

"Ultimate virtue is boundless, Zen Buddhism reaches its peak. Pure and illuminating, flowing through the three realms. Changing endlessly, unifying Yin and Yang. Its essence is eternal, infinite. Observing those lost souls, it is essential to show compassion.  Following the Holy Emperor's mandate, I have assembled these monks to practice Zen and preach the Dharma. We open wide the gates of convenience, navigate the vast vessel of compassion, and liberate all beings in the sea of suffering, freeing them from the affliction of the six realms.

Return to the true path, join the boundless cosmic dance; act and cease to act, unifying into pure nothingness. Relying on this good cause, we invite you to admire the celestial court of a clear and beautiful capital; ride this auspicious occasion, escape from the hellish realm of mortals.

Climb to the ultimate bliss freely, roaming the West as you please.

The poem says: 
One furnace of incense for everlasting life, 
Several scrolls of heavenly ascension talismans.

Infinite wonders of the Dharma are proclaimed,
Boundless grace of heaven envelops all. 
All grievances are removed,
All lost souls are released from prison.

May this protect our country, bringing a thousand years of peace and prosperity."

Emperor Taizong, overjoyed, says to the monks:

"You all possess unwavering sincerity, do not neglect Buddhist rituals. When your work is complete and everyone achieves their blessings, I will bestow generous rewards, never letting your efforts go unrewarded."

A thousand two hundred monks, all bow their heads in unison, expressing their gratitude.

This question came to my mind, as if on purpose, two hours ago (you see, prince, I do sometimes ponder serious matters); I have resolved it, but let us see what the prince has to say. We were just talking about ‘a particular case’. This word is very significant to us, we hear it often. Recently everyone has been talking and writing about that terrible murder of six people by this… young man and about the strange speech of his defender, where it is said that, given the defendant’s poverty, it was natural for him to kill these six people. Not literally, of course, but the sense, it seems, is about that. But in my personal opinion, the defender, by stating such a strange idea, was in complete conviction that he was saying the most liberal, the most humane and progressive thing that could be said in our time. Well, so, in your opinion, what will it be: is this a distortion of concepts and beliefs, this possibility of such a crooked and remarkable view of the matter, is it a particular or a general case?

Charges will inevitably be leveled against the author by those self-proclaimed patriots who sit placidly in their corners, occupied with their own extraneous affairs, amassing fortunes at the expense of others. But the moment something occurs, in their opinion, offensive to the fatherland, a book appears, perhaps one containing a bitter truth, they will emerge from their corners, like spiders who have seen a fly ensnared in their web, and raise their voices in cries: “Is it right to expose this, to make a public spectacle of it? After all, everything described here is ours – is this good? What will foreigners think? Isn't it painful to hear bad things said about oneself? Don’t they think we are patriots?” Such wise observations, especially about the opinion of foreigners, I must confess, are difficult to answer.  But consider this: in a remote corner of Russia lived two inhabitants. One was the head of the household, named Kipa Mokeevich, a meek man who had lived a careless life. He paid no attention to his family; his existence was more contemplative, preoccupied with what he called a philosophical question: "Take, for example, an animal," he would say, pacing the room, "an animal is born naked. Why, precisely, naked? Why not like a bird, why doesn't it hatch from an egg? How can you truly understand nature the more you delve into it!" That is how Kipa Mokeevich thought. But that's not the main point. The other inhabitant was Mokey Kipoevich, his own son. He was what is called a strongman in Russia, and while his father was pondering the birth of an animal, this twenty-year-old, muscular man was always ready to burst forth. He could not do anything lightly; everything would either result in someone's hand being broken or a blister appearing on someone's nose. Everyone in the house and the neighborhood, from the maidservant to the yard dog, would run away at his sight; he even broke his own bed in the bedroom. This was Mokey Kipoevich, though he was a good-hearted man. But that's not the main point either. The main point is this: "Please, master Kipa Mokeevich," the servants would say to his father, "what kind of Mokey Kipoevich do you have? No one gets any peace from him, he's a real menace!" "Yes, he's mischievous, mischievous," his father would usually reply, "but what can I do? It's too late to fight him, and besides, they would all accuse me of cruelty; he is an ambitious man, criticize him in front of someone else and he'll calm down, but the main problem is gossip – the town will hear and call him a dog. Don't they think it hurts me? Don't they think I'm his father? What, do you think I don't have a fatherly duty? Perhaps I spend my time on my philosophy, and sometimes I don't have time for fatherly duties, but I'm his father! By God, I am his father! I have Mokey Kipoevich right here, in my heart!" And, striking himself strongly on the chest with his fist, Kipa Mokeevich would become truly agitated. "If he remains a dog, then let him, but not let it be known by me, let them not think I raised him that way." And, having displayed such paternal affection, he would leave Mokey Kipoevich to continue his feats of strength, while he himself would return to his beloved subject, suddenly asking himself some similar question: "Well, if an elephant was born from an egg, the shell would have to be very thick, you couldn't shoot it with a cannon; you would need to invent some new kind of firearm." That's how these two inhabitants of a peaceful corner lived, who unexpectedly, like peeking out a window, appeared at the end of our poem, to humbly answer the accusations of certain fervent patriots who, until that moment, were calmly occupied with some philosophy or adding to their savings for the sake of their beloved fatherland, thinking not about not doing wrong, but about not being told that they were doing wrong. But no, it is not patriotism or first feelings that are the reasons for the accusations, something else lies beneath them. What need is there to conceal it? Who, if not the author, should tell the sacred truth? You are afraid of a deep gaze, you are afraid to direct your own gaze deeply at something, you prefer to glance at everything with unthinking eyes. You may even laugh heartily at Chivikov, perhaps even praise the author, saying: "However, he has hit on something cleverly, he must be a cheerful fellow!" And after such words, with doubled pride, you will turn to yourself, a self-satisfied smile will appear on your face, and you will add: "And indeed, people in some provinces are strange and even rascals!" But who of you, filled with Christian humility, not aloud, but in silence, alone, in moments of private conversations with oneself, will not delve deep into the depths of one's own soul with this weighty question: "Is there not a part of Chivikov in me too?" Yes, how could it be otherwise! But then, if at this time someone passes by, a fellow acquaintance of his, with a position neither too high nor too low, he will immediately nudge his neighbor and say, almost snorting with laughter: "Look, look, it's Chivikov, Chivikov is going by!" And then, like a child, forgetting all propriety due to rank and age, he will run after him, mocking him from behind and saying: "Chivikov! Chivikov! Chivikov!"

Why is it naked? Why not like a bird, why doesn't it hatch from an egg? How, really, you can't understand nature, the more you delve into it!" That's how Kipha Mokiyevich thought. But that's not the main point. The other inhabitant was Mokey Kipovich, his own son. He was what is called a hero on Russia, and at the time when his father was preoccupied with the birth of an animal, his twenty-year-old broad-shouldered nature was just bursting to unfold. He was incapable of doing anything lightly: either he would break someone's hand or make a welt appear on someone's nose. Everyone in the house and the neighborhood, from the maid to the yard dog, ran away at the sight of him; even his own bed in the bedroom he broke into pieces. Such was Mokey Kipovich, but he was a good-natured soul. But that's not the main point. The main point is this: “Lord, have mercy, my master, Kipha Mokiyevich,” the servants, both his own and others', would say to his father, “What have you got there in the form of Mokey Kipovich? No one has peace with him, such a troublemaker!”  “Yes, he's mischievous, mischievous,” his father would usually reply to this, “but what can be done: it's too late to fight him, and they'll accuse me of cruelty anyway. And he's an ambitious man, reprimand him in front of someone else, he will quiet down, but fame is the problem; the whole town will find out and call him a dog. What, do they think, is it not painful for me? Am I not his father? What, do they think, that I don't worry about him just because I'm busy with my philosophy? No, no! Father, damn them, I am his father! Here, in my heart!” And Kipha Mokiyevich would strike himself hard in the chest with his fist and become completely agitated. “Even if he remains a dog, let them not know it from me, let them not know it from me!" And, having shown such paternal affection, he would leave Mokey Kipovich to continue his heroic exploits, and would return to his beloved subject, suddenly posing himself another question of a similar kind: “Well, what if an elephant was born from an egg? After all, the shell would have to be very thick, you couldn't shoot it with a cannon; you would need to invent some new firearm.” Thus they lived two inhabitants of a peaceful corner, who unexpectedly, like peering out a window, appeared at the end of our poem, to humbly answer the accusations of some ardent patriots, who, up until then, quietly engaged in some philosophy or, perhaps, increasing their wealth at the expense of their beloved Fatherland, who were more concerned with not doing something wrong than with the fact that they might be accused of doing something wrong. But no, patriotism and not the first feeling are the reasons for the accusations, something else lies hidden beneath them. What need is there to hide the truth? Who, if not the author, should speak the holy truth? Do you fear a deep, penetrating gaze, are you afraid to direct your own gaze deeply at something? Do you prefer to glide over everything with unthinking eyes? You might even laugh heartily at Chikitov, perhaps even praise the author, saying: "However, he caught something cleverly, he must be a cheerful fellow!" And after such words, with doubled pride, you would turn to yourself, a self-satisfied smile would appear on your face, and you would add: "And indeed, strange and funny people live in some provinces, and there are quite a few scoundrels among them!" And which of you, full of Christian humility, not aloud, but in silence, alone, in moments of solitude with your own soul, would not delve deep into the recesses of your own heart with this heavy question: "Is there not a part of Chikitov in me?" Yes, as if not! But suppose, at this very moment, someone you know, with a rank neither too high nor too low, passes by, he would immediately nudge his neighbor and say, almost snorting with laughter: "Look, look, there goes Chikitov, Chikitov is walking!" And then, like a child, forgetting all propriety due to his rank and age, he would run after him, teasing him from behind and saying: "Chikitov! Chikitov! Chikitov!"

Charges will surely be leveled against the author by those self-proclaimed patriots who sit quietly in their corners, engrossed in their own affairs, amassing wealth at the expense of others. But the moment something occurs, something they deem an insult to the fatherland, the moment a book appears that dares to utter a bitter truth, they will emerge from their corners like spiders, spotting a fly tangled in their web. Suddenly, they'll raise their voices in a chorus: "Is it right to expose this, to proclaim it? After all, everything described here belongs to us, is it really good? What will foreigners think?  Isn't it painful to hear bad things said about ourselves? Don't we, too, consider ourselves patriots?" And these wise pronouncements, especially concerning the opinions of foreigners, I confess, are difficult to counter. 

Perhaps, for example, two men lived in a remote corner of Russia. One was the head of the household, named Kip Mokievich, a man of gentle disposition, who had led a life of idleness. He paid little attention to his family; his existence was more introspective, preoccupied with what he called a philosophical question: "For example," he would say, pacing his room, "an animal is born naked. Why exactly naked? Why not like a bird, why doesn't it hatch from an egg? One can hardly grasp the nature of things, the deeper one delves." This was Kip Mokievich's way of thinking.  But the most important thing was not this. The other inhabitant was Mokiy Kipkovich, his own son. He was a powerful man, a real hero, and at the age of twenty, his broad shoulders seemed to be straining to burst free.  He could never do anything gently; either he would break someone's hand or give them a welt on their nose. Everyone in the house and the neighborhood, from the maidservant to the stable dog, would flee at his approach; even his own bed in the bedroom he managed to smash to pieces. This was Mokiy Kipkovich, but despite all this, he was a good-natured soul. But the most important thing was not even this. "Yes, he's a mischievous fellow," the father would usually reply, "but what can I do? It's too late to discipline him, and besides, I'd be accused of cruelty. Mokiy Kipkovich is right here, in my heart!" And Kip Mokievich would strike himself repeatedly in the chest with his fist, overcome with a surge of paternal love. And, having shown such fatherly concern, he would leave Mokiy Kipkovich to continue his heroic exploits, while he himself would return to his beloved subject, suddenly asking himself a question like: "What if an elephant were born in an egg? The shell, of course, would have to be very thick, you couldn't pierce it with a cannon; you'd need some new kind of firearm." This is how these two inhabitants of a peaceful corner lived, unexpectedly appearing at the end of our poem, as if peering out a window, to humbly respond to the accusations of those certain passionate patriots who spent their time in peace, either lost in some philosophy or quietly increasing their wealth at the expense of their beloved fatherland, thinking not about not doing wrong, but about not being told that they are doing wrong. But no, it's not patriotism or the first impulse that is behind the accusations; something else lies beneath them. What need is there for pretense? You might even laugh heartily at Chichikov, perhaps even praise the author, saying: "Well, he's got some things right, he must be a lively fellow!" Ahead, they reached the City of Wrongful Deaths, only to hear a commotion, clearly shouting, “Li Shimin is here! Li Shimin is here!” Taizong, hearing this, trembled with fright. Seeing a group of ghosts, with broken waists, bent arms, some with feet but no heads, rushing forward to block him, they all cried, “Return our lives! Return our lives!” Terrified, Taizong hid and dodged, only crying, “Mr. Cui, save me! Mr. Cui, save me!” The Judge said, “Your Majesty, those people are the ghosts of sixty-four places of dust and seventy-two places of bandits, countless princes and leaders. They are all wrongful deaths, without redress or relief, unable to be reborn, and with no money or possessions, they are all impoverished ghosts.” Your Majesty, if you give them some money, then I can save them.” Taizong said, “This lowly one has come here empty-handed, where could I find money?” The Judge said, “Your Majesty, there is someone in the yang realm, with a large sum of gold and silver deposited here in my yin realm. Your Majesty can make a public pledge and I will guarantee it. Borrow it from him and give it to these ghosts, then they can pass.” Taizong asked, “Who is this person?” The Judge said, “He is a man from Kaifeng Prefecture in Henan, surnamed Xiang, given name Liang. He drafted a document with the Judge, borrowing a warehouse of gold and silver, and instructed the Grand Minister to distribute it. The Judge then instructed, “You can divide this gold and silver equally, let my grandfather of the Tang Dynasty pass, his yang lifespan is still long. The Judge ordered the Grand Minister to wave the soul-calling banner, leading Taizong out of the City of Wrongful Deaths, onto the Pingyang Road, drifting and swaying away. Around that same time, or thereabouts, when Surikov 'froze' the child, around the middle of March, I suddenly felt much better for some reason, and it lasted for about two weeks. I began to go out, more and more often at twilight. I loved March twilights, when it started to get chilly and they lit the gas; I sometimes walked far. One time, in Shestyalavochnaya, I was overtaken in the dark by some 'man of good breeding'; I didn't get a good look at him; he was carrying something wrapped in paper and wearing some shabby, unsightly coat – inappropriately light for the weather. When he evened up with the lamp, about ten paces ahead of me, I noticed that something had fallen out of his pocket. I hurried to pick it up – and it was timely, because someone else was already jumping up in a long coat, but, seeing the thing in my hands, he didn't argue, glanced at my hands briefly, and slipped by. The thing was large, a leather, old-fashioned wallet, tightly stuffed with paper; but for some reason, I guessed at first glance that it contained anything but money. The lost passerby was already about forty paces ahead of me and soon disappeared into the crowd. I ran and started shouting at him; but since I had nothing to shout besides 'hey!', he didn't turn around. Suddenly he darted left, into the gates of a house. When I burst into the gates, under which it was very dark, there was no one there. The house was enormous, one of those hulking buildings that swindlers build for tiny apartments; in some of these houses there are sometimes as many as a hundred apartments. When I passed through the gates, it seemed to me that in the right, rear corner of the vast courtyard someone was walking, although in the darkness I could barely make out anything. Reaching the corner, I saw the entrance to the staircase; it was narrow, extremely dirty, and completely unlit; but I could hear that someone was still climbing the stairs, and I started up the stairs, hoping that while he was being let in somewhere, I would catch up with him. And that's exactly what happened. The stairs were awfully short, and there were endless amounts of them, so I was terribly out of breath; the door was opened and closed again on the fifth floor, I guessed this three flights down. By the time I climbed up, caught my breath on the landing, and found the bell, several minutes had passed. Finally, a woman opened the door for me, who was blowing up a samovar in a tiny kitchen; she listened silently to my questions, of course understood nothing, and silently opened the door for me into the next room, also small, terribly low, with disgusting, necessary furniture and a wide, enormous bed under curtains, on which lay 'Terentyich' (that's what the woman called him), it seemed to me, drunk. On the table, a burnt-out ember smoldered in an iron candlestick and there stood a nearly empty half-bottle. Terentyich mumbled something to me lying down and gestured towards the next door, and the woman left, so I had no choice but to open that door. And that's what I did and entered the next room.

— It’s exactly a minute before death, — the prince began, with complete readiness, swept up in the memory, and seemingly forgetting everything else at once, — that very moment when he climbed the steps and had just stepped onto the scaffold. He glanced in my direction then; I looked at his face and understood everything... However, how to describe it! I would desperately, terribly like for you or someone to paint it! Better yet, if you! I thought at the time that the painting would be useful. You see, you need to imagine everything that preceded it, everything, everything. He had been in prison and awaited execution for at least another week; he somehow counted on the usual formalism, that the paper had to go somewhere and wouldn't come out for another week. But then, suddenly, for some reason, the case was expedited. At five in the morning he was sleeping. It was late October; at five it's still cold and dark. The prison guard entered, quietly, with the guards, and carefully touched him on the shoulder; he sat up, leaned, saw the light: “What is it?” — "Execution at ten o'clock.” He didn't believe from his sleep, began to argue that the paper would come out in a week, but when he fully woke up, he stopped arguing and fell silent, they said, then said: "Still, it's heavy to be like this suddenly..." and fell silent again, and no longer wanted to say anything. Then three or four hours passed on the usual things: the priest, breakfast, to which he was given wine, coffee, and beef (well, isn't it a mockery? After all, think, how cruel it is, but on the other hand, God bless them, these innocent people do it with a pure heart and are sure that it's compassion), then toilet (you know what a prisoner's toilet is), and finally, they drive him through the city to the scaffold... I think that here too it seems that there's still infinitely long to live, as long as they are driving. I imagine that he probably thought, "There's still a long way to go, three streets left to go; I'll get past this one, then there will be another one, then the one with the baker on the right; we'll get to the baker yet." There's a crowd all around, shouts, noise, ten thousand faces, ten thousand eyes, — all this has to be endured, and above all, the thought: "Here are ten thousand of them, and they won't be executed, but I will!" Well, here's all that preliminary stuff. The scaffold is approached by a staircase; there, before the staircase, he suddenly burst into tears, and this was a strong and courageous man, a big villain, they say. He was constantly accompanied by a priest, who rode with him in the cart and kept talking — he probably didn't hear; and he would start to listen, but from the third word, he wouldn't understand anymore. That's probably how it was. Finally, he began to climb the stairs; his legs were tied, and therefore he moved in small steps. The priest, probably a smart man, stopped talking and just kept giving him the cross to kiss. At the bottom of the steps he was very pale, and when he climbed up and stood on the scaffold, he suddenly became white as paper, completely like white writing paper. Probably his legs were weakening and stiffening, and he felt nausea, — as if something was squeezing him in his throat, and it tickled exactly, — have you ever felt this in fear or in very scary moments, when your whole mind remains, but you have no power anymore? It seems to me that, for example, if your inevitable death, a house is falling on you, then suddenly you will terribly want to sit down, close your eyes, and wait — whatever happens! Here, when this weakness began, the priest, quickly, with a swift gesture and silently, quickly put the cross to his lips, a small silver, four-pointed cross, — he kept offering it, every minute. And as soon as the cross touched his lips, he opened his eyes, and for a few seconds, he seemed to revive, and his legs went on. He kissed the cross with greed, rushed to kiss it, as if he was eager not to forget to grab something for later, just in case, but he probably wasn't aware of anything religious in this minute. And so it was until the very board... It's strange that rarely in these very last seconds do people faint! On the contrary, your head works incredibly hard and clearly, probably very, very, very hard, like a machine in motion; I imagine that all sorts of unfinished thoughts are rattling around, maybe even funny, extraneous ones: "Look, this one is looking — he has a wart on his forehead, look, the executioner's bottom button is rusty"... but all the same, you know and remember everything; there's one point that you can't forget, and you can't faint, and everything around it, around this point, revolves and spins. And to think that it's all the way to the very last quarter of a second, when the head is already on the chopping block, and it waits, and... knows, and suddenly it will hear, as the iron slips! This you will definitely hear! I would, if I were lying there, I would purposely listen and hear it! There, maybe, it's only a tenth of a moment, but you will definitely hear it! And imagine, they still argue about whether, maybe, when the head flies off, it still knows for a second that it has flown off, — what a concept! And what if it's five seconds!.. Paint the scaffold so that only the last step is clearly visible and close; the criminal has stepped on it: his head, face as white as paper, the priest extends the cross, he greedily stretches out his blue lips, looks, and — knows everything. The cross and the head — that's the picture, the face of the priest, the executioner, his two assistants, and a few heads and eyes from below, — all this can be painted as if on the third plan, in a haze, as an accessory... That's the picture.

The prison warden entered, quietly, with guards, and gently touched him on the shoulder; he lifted himself up, leaned against the wall, and saw the light: "What is it?" "At ten o'clock, death sentence." He didn't believe it from sleep, he started to argue that the papers would come out in a week, but when he finally woke up, he stopped arguing and fell silent, — so they said, — then said: "It's still hard to be executed like that..." and fell silent again, and no longer wanted to say anything. Then three or four hours passed on the usual things: the priest, breakfast, which they gave him wine, coffee, and beef (well, isn't that a joke? You think, how cruel, but on the other hand, by God, these innocent people do it with pure hearts and are convinced that it is humaneness), then personal hygiene (you know what the hygiene of a criminal is like?), and finally, they take him through the city to the scaffold... I think that even here it seems that there is still an eternity to live, as long as they are taking him. I imagine that he probably thought along the way: "Still a long way to go, still three streets left; I'll pass this one, then there will be another, then another one, where the baker is on the right; we'll get to the baker yet!". There is a crowd all around, shouting, noise, ten thousand faces, ten thousand eyes, — all this needs to be endured, and most importantly, the thought: "Here are ten thousand of them, and none of them will be executed, but they will execute me!" Well, that's all beforehand. The scaffold is reached by a ladder; here he burst into tears before the ladder, and this was a strong and courageous man, a big villain, they say. The priest was constantly with him, rode with him in the cart, and kept talking, — he probably didn't hear him; he might start listening, but from the third word he wouldn't understand. So it probably was. Finally, he started to climb the ladder; his legs were tied, and therefore he moved in small steps. The priest, probably a smart man, stopped talking and just kept giving him the cross to kiss. At the bottom of the ladder he was very pale, but as he climbed up and stood on the scaffold, he suddenly turned as white as paper, completely like a white writing sheet. Probably his legs were weakening and stiffening, and he felt nausea, — as if something was pressing on his throat, and from that it was exactly tickling, — have you ever felt this in fear or in very scary moments, when even your mind remains, but it has no power anymore? It seems to me that if, for example, inevitable death, the house is collapsing on you, then suddenly you would terribly want to sit down, close your eyes, and wait — whatever will be, will be!.. Here, at the very beginning of this weakness, the priest, quickly, with a quick gesture and silently, offered him the cross, right to his lips, a small silver cross, four-pointed, — he kept offering it, every minute. And as soon as the cross touched his lips, he opened his eyes, and for a few seconds as if revived, and his legs moved. He kissed the cross greedily, he hurried to kiss it, as if he was trying to grab something extra, just in case, but he probably didn't realize anything religious in this moment. And so it was until the very platform... Strange that rarely in these very last seconds do people faint! On the contrary, the head works incredibly hard, probably very, very, very hard, like a machine in motion; I imagine that different thoughts are clattering, all unfinished, and maybe even funny, extraneous thoughts: "Look, this one is looking — he has a wart on his forehead, the executioner has one lower button rusted..." but at the same time, you know everything and remember everything; there is one point that you can't forget, and you can't faint, and everything around it, around this point, goes and revolves. And imagine that this continues until the very last quarter of a second, when the head is already lying on the block, waiting, and... knows, and suddenly hears above it, how the iron has dropped! You will definitely hear it! If I were lying there, I would deliberately listen and hear! Here, perhaps, only one tenth of a moment, but you will definitely hear it! And imagine, they still argue that, perhaps, when the head flies off, it may still know for a second, maybe, that it has flown off — what a concept! What if it's five seconds?! Paint the scaffold so that only the last step is visible, clear and close; the criminal has stepped on it: his head, face pale as paper, the priest stretches out the cross, he greedily stretches his blue lips, and looks, and — knows everything. The cross and the head — that's the picture, the face of the priest, the executioner, his two assistants, and a few heads and eyes from below, — all this can be painted as if on the third plan, in a haze, as an accessory... That's the kind of picture.

Indeed, there is nothing more distressing than, for example, to be rich, from a respectable family, with an acceptable appearance, reasonably well-educated, not stupid, even kind, and at the same time to have no talent, no peculiarity, not even a quirk, not a single original idea, to be simply "like everyone else." You have wealth, but not Rothschild's; your family name is honest but has never distinguished itself in any way; your appearance is decent but lacks expressiveness; your education is respectable, but you don't know how to use it; you have intelligence, but without your own ideas; you have a heart, but without magnanimity, and so on, and so on, in every respect. There are an extraordinary number of such people in the world, and even more than it seems; they divide, like all people, into two main categories: the limited and the "much smarter." The former are happier. It is easier for a limited, "ordinary" person to imagine themselves an extraordinary and original person and to delight in that without any hesitation. All it took for some of our young ladies was to cut their hair, put on blue glasses, and call themselves nihilists to immediately convince themselves that, having donned the glasses, they instantly had their own "convictions." It only took someone to feel a flicker of some universal and good feeling in their heart to immediately believe that no one felt it as strongly as they did, that they were ahead of the pack in general development. It only took someone to accept a thought on the word or read a page of something with no beginning and end to immediately believe that it was "their own thoughts" and had originated in their own mind. The audacity of naiveté, if one can put it that way, reaches astonishing heights in such cases; it's all unbelievable, but it happens every minute. This audacity of naiveté, this unwavering belief of the foolish person in themselves and their talent, is wonderfully depicted by Gogol in the remarkable type of Poruchik Pyrov. Pyrov doesn't even doubt that he is a genius, even above all geniuses; he doesn't even doubt it to the point of asking himself the question; in fact, there are no questions for him. The great writer was forced, finally, to knock him down for the satisfaction of the offended moral feelings of his reader, but, seeing that the great man only shrugged and, to regain his strength after the torment, ate a layered pie, he spread his hands in amazement and left his readers that way. I always lamented that the great Pyrov was taken by Gogol in such a small rank, because Pyrov is so self-satisfied that it's easier for him to imagine himself, as the years and "by line" of epaulets thicken on him, an extraordinary, for example, general; he doesn't even need to imagine, he simply doesn't doubt it: they promoted him to general, how could he not be a commander? And how many such then make terrible blunders on the battlefield? And how many Pyrovs were there among our writers, scientists, propagandists? I say "there were," but, of course, there are still...

Chichikov bowed with gratitude. Having learned that he was going to the office to draw up a deed of sale, Manilov expressed his willingness to accompany him. The friends took each other's hands and went together. At every small rise, or hill, or step, Manilov supported Chichikov and almost lifted him up with his hand, adding with a pleasant smile that he would not allow Pavel Ivanovich to stub his toes. Chichikov felt embarrassed, not knowing how to thank him, for he felt he had been rather burdensome. In their mutual services they finally reached the square where the government offices were located: a large three-story stone building, all white as chalk, probably to depict the purity of the souls of those who worked there; the other buildings on the square did not compare in size to the stone building. These were: a guardhouse, where a soldier stood with a gun, two or three cab stands, and, finally, long fences with familiar fence inscriptions and drawings, scratched with charcoal and chalk; there was nothing else on this lonely, or, as we say, pretty square. Heads of the high priests of Themis appeared from the windows of the second and third floors and immediately disappeared again: probably, at that moment, the head official was entering the room. The friends did not climb, but raced up the stairs, because Chichikov, trying to avoid being supported by Manilov, quickened his pace, and Manilov, in turn, was flying forward, trying not to let Chichikov get tired, and so both were quite out of breath when they entered the dark corridor. Neither in the corridors nor in the rooms was their gaze struck by cleanliness. Then they did not yet care about it, and what was dirty remained dirty, without taking on an attractive appearance. Themis simply, as she is, in a nightgown and dressing gown, received her guests. It would be necessary to describe the office rooms that our heroes passed through, but the author has a strong aversion to all government offices. If he ever happened to pass through them even in a magnificent and ennobled form, with polished floors and tables, he tried to run as quickly as possible, humbly lowering and averting his eyes to the ground, and therefore he does not know at all how there everything prospers and flourishes. "So let her be your beloved then," said Leni, "You wouldn't miss her very much if you lost her, or exchanged her for someone else, say, for me."

"Certainly," said K. smiling, "that's conceivable, but she has one great advantage over you: she knows nothing of my trial, and even if she did, she wouldn't think about it. She wouldn't try to persuade me to be more accommodating."

"That's no advantage," said Leni. "If she has no other advantages, I won't lose heart. Does she have any physical flaw?"

"A physical flaw?" asked K.

"Yes," said Leni, "I have a small one, see." She spread her middle and ring finger of her right hand apart, between which the webbing stretched almost to the top joint of the short finger. K. couldn't make out in the dark what she wanted to show him, so she guided his hand towards it.

"What a curious quirk of nature," said K., and adding, as he took in the whole hand, "What a pretty claw!"

With a certain pride, Leni watched as K., full of wonder, repeatedly spread and closed her two fingers, until he finally kissed them fleetingly and let go.

"Oh!" she exclaimed, "You kissed me!" Eagerly, with her mouth open, she climbed onto his lap with her knees. K. looked at her almost in alarm; now that she was so close, a bitter, pungent smell like pepper emanated from her. She took his head, leaned over him, and bit and kissed his neck, even biting into his hair.

"You've exchanged me!" she cried from time to time, "See, now you've exchanged me!"

Suddenly her knee slipped, and with a little cry she almost fell onto the rug. K. grasped her to keep her from falling and was pulled down towards her.

"Now you belong to me," she said.

He dozed off on the bench, but his anxiety persisted even in his dreams. Right before falling asleep, he recalled that Hippolyte would kill ten people and chuckled at the absurdity of the thought. A beautiful, clear silence surrounded him, broken only by the rustle of leaves, which, it seemed, made the world around him even quieter and more secluded. He had many disturbing dreams, from which he would jolt awake every few moments. Finally, a woman came to him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could have named her and pointed her out any time — but strangely, she seemed to have a completely different face than the one he had always known, and he was agonizingly reluctant to recognize her as that woman. There was so much remorse and terror in her face that it seemed she was a terrible criminal who had just committed a horrific crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned him with her hand and pressed her finger to her lips, as if warning him to follow her more quietly. His heart stopped; he wouldn't, under any circumstances, acknowledge her as a criminal; but he felt that something terrible was about to happen, something that would affect him for the rest of his life. She seemed to want to show him something, right there, in the park. He stood up to follow her, and suddenly, a light, fresh laughter rang out beside him; a hand suddenly appeared in his, he grasped it tightly and woke up. Aglaya stood before him, laughing loudly.

The reader, I think, has already noticed that, despite his friendly appearance, Chichikov spoke with far more freedom than with Manilov, and indeed, showed no ceremony at all. One must say, in our Russia, if we haven't already fallen behind foreigners in something else, then we've certainly outstripped them in the art of address. It's impossible to count all the shades and nuances of our ways of speaking. A Frenchman or a German will never grasp all their intricacies and distinctions; he'd speak with the same voice and the same language to both a millionaire and a small tobacco merchant, though, of course, he'd inwardly fawn a little more before the first.  It's not the same with us: we have such wise men that with a landowner who owns two hundred souls, they'll speak quite differently than with one who owns three hundred, and with one who owns three hundred, they'll speak differently than with one who owns five hundred, and with one who owns five hundred, differently again than with one who owns eight hundred—in a word, even if you go up to a million, they'll always find shades. Let's say there exists a chancery, not here, but in a distant land, and in that chancery, let's say, there exists the head of the chancery.  Just observe him when he sits among his subordinates—you wouldn't be able to utter a word from fear! Doesn't his face express both pride and nobility? Just take a brush and paint him: Prometheus, resolute Prometheus! He peers like an eagle, moves gracefully and measuredly. Just take a brush and paint it: Prometheus, the resolute Prometheus! He surveys like an eagle, steps forth gracefully, measuredly. But that same eagle, as soon as he leaves the room and approaches his superior's office, scurries like a partridge, so fast with papers under his arm, that he has no strength left. In society and at a party, if everyone is of small rank, Prometheus remains just Prometheus, but as soon as he encounters someone of a slightly higher rank, such a transformation occurs with him that even Ovid wouldn't have imagined: he shrinks down to the size of an ant, nay, even smaller! "That's not Ivan Petrovich," you'd say, looking at him. "Ivan Petrovich is taller, and this one is short and thin; he speaks loudly, booms, and never laughs, and this one God knows what: he chirps like a bird and laughs all the time." You approach closer, you look - it is indeed Ivan Petrovich! "Eh, eh," you think to yourself... But, however, let us turn to our characters. Chichikov, as we have already seen, decided to dispense with any ceremony at all, and therefore, taking a cup of tea in his hand and adding some fruit juice to it, launched into the following speech:

"Do you see those lit-up first floors," said the general, "that's where all my comrades live, and I, I, the one who has served longest and suffered most, I'm walking to the Bolshoi Theatre to the apartment of a dubious woman! You don't believe it? A man with thirteen bullets in his chest... Yet it's true! Only I did Pirogov telegraph to Paris, and he even left the besieged Sevastopol for a while, and Nelatan, the Paris court physician, got a free pass for the sake of science and came to examine me in the besieged Sevastopol. The highest authorities know this: "Ah, that's Ivolgin, the one with thirteen bullets!" That's how they say it! Do you see that house, Prince? In the first floor apartment lives my old comrade, General Sokolovitch, with his noble and numerous family. That house, and three more on Nevsky and two on Morskoi — that's my entire current circle of acquaintances, or rather, my personal circle. Nina Alexandrovna has long since resigned herself to circumstances. I, however, continue to remember... and, so to speak, to rest in the educated circle of my former comrades and subordinates, who still adore me. This General Sokolovitch (though, it's been a while since I've been to his house, and I haven't seen Anna Fyodorovna)... you know, my dear Prince, when you don't participate yourself, somehow you involuntarily stop participating with others too. And yet... hm... you seem not to believe... Why, why not introduce my son to this charming family home? General Ivolgin and Prince Myshkin! You will see a remarkable girl, not just one, two, even three, adornment of the capital and society: beauty, education, direction... the woman question, poetry — all this coalesced into a happy, diverse mixture, not counting at least eighty thousand rubles of dowry, clean money, which never hurts, in any womanly or social question... in short, I absolutely, absolutely must and have to introduce you."

“What brings you here?” asked Jie Di.  “The monk Tang lost his horse in the Snake Pan Mountain Eagle Worry Ravine.  The Great Sage was in a predicament, unable to proceed or retreat. Upon inquiring of the local earth god, he learned that a dragon from the Bodhisattva had swallowed it.  Thus, the Great Sage sent this minor deity to beseech the Bodhisattva to subdue the dragon and return his horse.”

The Bodhisattva replied, “This one is the son of Ao Run from the West Sea.  He burned the hall’s luminous pearls, and his father accused him of disobedience. He committed a capital crime in Heaven, and I personally pleaded with the Jade Emperor to bring him down and tasked him to serve as a footman for Master Tang. How could he then have eaten Master Tang’s horse? I’ll attend to it personally.”  

Then the Bodhisattva descended on a lotus platform, leaving the fairy cave and, riding a radiant light alongside Jie Di, crossed the South Sea.  A poem attests to this, it goes:

The Buddha speaks the Great Vimalakirti Sutra,
The Bodhisattva spreads benevolence across the Great Wall.
Mahayana profound speech resonates through heaven and earth,
Prajna’s true words save all spirits.
This brings the golden cicada’s rebirth,
Hence, Xuanzang undergoes further cultivation.
But due to the obstruction of the Eagle Worry Ravine,
The dragon prince reverts to a horse form.

Soon, the Bodhisattva and Jie Di arrived at Snake Pan Mountain. There, they halted their auspicious clouds in mid-air, looking down. They saw the Monkey King shouting angrily by the ravine. The Bodhisattva told Jie Di to summon him. Jie Di landed on a cloud, bypassing Master Tang, and went to the Monkey King, saying, “The Bodhisattva has arrived.”  

Hearing this, the Monkey King leapt onto a cloud and roared, “You, my master who has the wisdom of seven Buddhas, the compassionate Supreme Leader! How dare you conspire against me!”

The Bodhisattva said, “You, you brazen and foolish monkey! I’ve gone to great lengths to save you. I’ve brought forth a pilgrim to take scriptures, and instructed him to save your life. Yet, you fail to thank me for this grace, and instead, you rant and rave at me?”

The Monkey King retorted, “You’ve caused me much trouble!  If you were to release me, let me roam free and enjoy myself, you could have simply beckoned me during the sea voyage, suggested I dedicate myself to serving Master Tang.  Why did you offer him a flower hat, and have me wear it to suffer? Why bind this iron hoop upon my head and have him chant the mantra endlessly? The pain it inflicts upon me is unbearable. You’ve only been tormenting me!”

The Bodhisattva laughed, “You, you impetuous monkey!  If you didn’t heed my instructions and accept your true destiny, if I hadn’t restrained you, you would surely stray further, deceive heaven, and be utterly clueless.  Were it not for this iron hoop, you’d be in the throes of yet another calamity.  It is only with this restriction that you are willing to enter my path of yoga!”

The Monkey King said, “This curse is my tormentor!  Why did you bring this wicked dragon, who committed crimes, to this place and turn him into a demon, allowing him to eat my master’s horse? You’ve allowed evil to thrive, this is most unkind!”

The Bodhisattva replied, “That dragon was brought here by me, pleading with the Jade Emperor. He is tasked to serve the pilgrims seeking scriptures.  Think, what earthly horse from the East could endure such arduous journeys across mountains and seas, could reach the Western Buddhist paradise?  Only this dragon horse can make the journey.”

The Monkey King said, “Such a fearsome creature as he, should be hiding, why does he dare show himself?”

The Bodhisattva instructed Jie Di, “Go to the ravine’s edge and call out, ‘Ao Run Dragon King, Yu Long, the third prince, emerge, for the South Sea Bodhisattva is here.’ He will come.”

Jie Di went to the ravine’s edge and called twice.  The dragon stirred the waters, leapt from the river, transformed into a human form, stepped onto a cloud, and bowed to the Bodhisattva, saying, “I thank the Bodhisattva for liberating and saving my life. I have been waiting here for a long time, but I have yet to hear news of the pilgrim seeking scriptures.”

The Bodhisattva pointed to the Monkey King and said, “This is Master Tang’s eldest disciple.”

The dragon said, “Bodhisattva, this is my nemesis. Yesterday, I was famished and devoured his horse. Because he possesses some strength, he drove me away and forced me back into hiding. He continues to berate me, and I dare not leave my abode. Not once has he mentioned anything about seeking scriptures.”

"What brings you here?" asked Jie Di.

"Tang Sanzang lost his horse at Shepan Mountain, Yingchou Diaojian. The situation left Sun Wukong in a bind. Upon inquiring of the local earth deity, he learned that a dragon had swallowed it. The Great Sage then sent this minor deity to implore the Bodhisattva to subdue the dragon and return the horse. 

The Bodhisattva replied, "This fellow is the son of Ao Run, of the West Sea. For setting fire to the celestial palace's luminous pearls, his father denounced him for defying Heaven. He committed a crime punishable by death in the Celestial Court. I personally petitioned the Jade Emperor on his behalf, bringing him down and assigning him to be a footman for Tang Sanzang. How could he have turned around and eaten Tang Sanzang's horse? Let me go deal with this."

The Bodhisattva descended on a lotus platform, departed the fairy cave, and, with Jie Di riding upon a radiant light, crossed the South Sea. There is a poem to attest to this:

The Buddha expounded the Sutra of Honeyed Words,
The Bodhisattva bestowed kindness throughout the Great Wall.
Mahamya words pervade Heaven and Earth,
Prajna's true sayings save ghosts and spirits.
Thus, Jin Chan was freed from his shell once more,
And Xuanzang was allowed to embark on a further pilgrimage.
Only because the path was obstructed at Yingchoujian,
The dragon prince returned to his true form, becoming a horse.

The Bodhisattva and Jie Di arrived at Shepan Mountain shortly thereafter. They paused their journey mid-air, lingering on a cloud, gazing downwards. They saw Sun Wukong berating the surrounding area.

The Bodhisattva instructed Jie Di to summon him. Jie Di landed upon the cloud, bypassing the three masters, and reached Sun Wukong, saying, "The Bodhisattva has arrived."

Hearing this, Sun Wukong leaped onto the cloud in the air and shouted, "You seven-Buddha disciple, compassionate teacher! What manner of trickery have you played on me!"

The Bodhisattva said, "You bold, foolish monkey! I have saved you from utter destruction, given you freedom from captivity, yet you refuse to express gratitude for the life I've spared. Instead, you berate me!"

Sun Wukong said, "You've done me great harm! If you simply released me and let me roam free, that would be enough. You accosted me at sea, belittling me and encouraging me to dedicate myself to serving Tang Sanzang wholeheartedly. But why did you place this flowery hat upon my head, forcing me to endure hardship? Why did you affix this tight-fitting circlet to my head, making the old monk endlessly recite the Tight-Ring Curse, causing me unceasing pain? You've done me a disservice!"

The Bodhisattva laughed, "You impudent monkey! You disobey orders, refuse to reap the proper rewards, and if I didn't bind you, you would surely deceive Heaven again, unaware of your transgressions. Had you caused further trouble, who could control you? Only with this yoke can you learn to enter my yogic path!"

Sun Wukong retorted, "I will be your yoke, but why did you bestow this blameworthy dragon, sent here to become a demon, upon this place? Why did you have him devour my master's horse?  This is blatant indulgence of evil!"

The Bodhisattva explained, "That dragon was personally rescued by me from the Jade Emperor, sent here specifically to serve the pilgrim. Do you think an ordinary horse from the Eastern Continent could traverse these countless waters and mountains, reach the holy land of Ling Shan? It had to be this dragon-horse to achieve it."

Sun Wukong said, "Such a fearsome creature, hiding from me, what can we do?"

The Bodhisattva instructed Jie Di, "Go to the edge of the chasm and call out, 'Ao Run, Dragon King of the South Sea, Yu Long, the Third Prince, emerge! The Bodhisattva of the South Sea is here.' He will appear."

Jie Di went to the edge of the chasm and called out twice. The young dragon, churning the waves, leaped from the water, transforming into a human-like figure. He rode upon a cloud and, reaching the air, bowed to the Bodhisattva, saying, "Thank you, Bodhisattva, for saving my life and granting me freedom. I have waited here for a long time, yet have heard no news of the pilgrim."

The Bodhisattva pointed to Sun Wukong and said, "This is the senior disciple of the pilgrim."

The young dragon said, "Bodhisattva, this is my adversary. Yesterday, driven by hunger, I devoured his horse. He, with his formidable power, drove me back, filled me with fear, and forced me to retreat into hiding. He never once mentioned anything about a pilgrim."

Sun Wukong exclaimed,

“What brings you here?” The Great Sage said: “Master Tang lost his horse at Snake Coil Mountain’s Eagle’s Sorrow Cliff and was in a great panic. I shall go myself.”

The Bodhisattva descended his lotus platform, left the fairy cave, and with Jie Di riding the auspicious light, crossed the South China Sea. There is a poem to attest to this:

Buddha spoke the Saddharma-pundarika Sutra,
The Bodhisattva spread virtue throughout the Great Wall.
Mahamaya words reach heaven and earth,
Prajna true sayings save spirits and ghosts.
Thus the Golden Cicada was reborn,
Therefore, Xuanzang must again practice.
Only due to the obstruction at Eagle’s Sorrow Cliff,
The dragon son reincarnated as a horse.

The Bodhisattva and Jie Di arrived at Snake Coil Mountain shortly. They halted their auspicious cloud in mid-air and looked down.

They saw the Great Sage shouting and cursing at the cliffside. The Bodhisattva instructed Jie Di to call him. Jie Di landed on the cloud and went directly to the cliffside, saying to the Great Sage, “The Bodhisattva has arrived.”

The Great Sage, hearing this, jumped onto the cloud and cried out to him, “You, teacher of seven Buddhas, compassionate lord! What a cruel trick you’ve played on me!”

The Bodhisattva said, “You, you bold and ignorant monkey! I saved you, let you roam free, and then on the sea I gave you advice to serve Master Tang with all your heart. Why do you scold me instead of thanking me for saving your life?”

The Great Sage said, “You’ve done me a terrible injustice! After saving me, why didn’t you just let me go? Instead, you tricked me by sending a magician to lead me astray. This crown of iron is a curse upon my head, and that mantra makes it burn! What kind of a trick is this?”

The Bodhisattva laughed, “You, monkey! You disobey orders and fail to understand the way of practice. If I didn’t constrain you, you’d be making more trouble, deceiving heaven, causing chaos again. You wouldn’t even know better! You need this magic crown to learn restraint!  That’s how you can enter my path of yoga!” 

The Great Sage said, “I'll take this crown! How can you leave that dragon, who committed a grave sin, here to become a demon, and eat Master’s horse?  It is so unfair and unkind!”

The Bodhisattva said, “That dragon was personally chosen by me, and I pleaded with the Jade Emperor to have him sent here. He is to serve the pilgrims. Can a mortal horse, from the East land, withstand the hardships of these thousands of mountains and rivers? It can only be a dragon horse that can reach the sacred Mount Sumeru.  

The Great Sage said, “He’s so afraid of me, why doesn’t he come out?” 

The Bodhisattva told Jie Di, “Go to the edge of the cliff and call out, ‘Ao Run Dragon King, Yulong Sanzi, you come forth, the South Sea Bodhisattva is here.’ He’ll come.”

Jie Di went to the cliffside and called out twice. 

The young dragon leaped from the water, transforming into a human form. He rode on the clouds and bowed to the Bodhisattva, “I thank you, Bodhisattva, for saving my life and waiting so long, but I haven’t heard news of the pilgrim.”

The Bodhisattva pointed at the Great Sage and said, “Isn’t this the eldest disciple of the pilgrim?”

The young dragon said, “Bodhisattva, this is my enemy. I was hungry yesterday and ate his horse. He fought bravely, forcing me back into hiding. He scolded me relentlessly, and I didn't dare to leave. He never mentioned anything about the pilgrim."

“What brings you here?”  

“The Master Tang lost his horse in the Snake Coil Mountain, Eagle’s Sorrow Cliff, and is in great distress.  Sun Wukong, caught between two difficult paths, consulted the local deity who said a dragon, sent by Guanyin, had swallowed it. The Great Sage asked the deity to bring a message to Guanyin, asking her to subdue the dragon and return the horse.”

Guanyin said, “This one is the son of Ao Run from the West Sea. For setting fire to the jeweled hall, his father reported him for rebellion, and he was condemned to death by the Jade Emperor. I personally interceded with the Jade Emperor and brought him down to serve Master Tang. How could he have eaten Master Tang’s horse? I shall go and take care of it.” 

Guanyin descended from her lotus platform, leaving the fairy cave with Jie Di. Riding on auspicious light, they crossed the South China Sea. The poem attests to this:
Buddha spoke the Tripitaka of Honeydew, 
Guanyin spread compassion across the Great Wall.
The profound words of Mahamaya echoed throughout heaven and earth,
The Prajna truth enlightened ghosts and spirits.
So, the Golden Cicada was freed from its shell,
Therefore, Xuanzang was able to cultivate once more. 
It was only the obstruction at Eagle’s Sorrow Cliff, 
That the dragon prince transformed into a horse form.

Soon, Guanyin and Jie Di arrived at Snake Coil Mountain. They hovered in mid-air, their auspicious clouds trailing behind them, and looked down. They saw Sun Wukong berating the cliff edge. Guanyin told Jie Di to summon him. Jie Di descended on the cloud head, bypassing the Tang Sanzang, and arrived at the cliff edge.  He said to Sun Wukong, “The Guanyin is here.”

Sun Wukong, hearing this, leaped onto the cloud and shouted, “Oh, Seventh Buddha’s disciple, compassionate master! What a crafty scheme you have concocted against me!”

Guanyin said, “You arrogant, foolish monkey! I have painstakingly guided you, enabling the seeker of scriptures to arrive. Why don’t you thank me for saving your life, and instead, you yell at me?”

Sun Wukong said, “You have done me a disservice! If you had simply let me go free, to roam as I please, you could have simply told me to protect Master Tang. Why did you make me wear that hat and suffer so much? Why put this iron hoop on my head and make the old monk chant the Tight-Hoop incantation? The pain in my head never ceases! Isn’t this your doing?”

Guanyin laughed, “You monkey! You disobey my orders, refusing the true path. If I didn’t restrain you, you would have surely caused more trouble. This iron hoop is necessary to keep you in check. Only then can you be my disciple!”

Sun Wukong said, “This iron hoop is my curse, is it? Why did you send this wicked dragon, whose sins are countless, here to become a demon and eat Master Tang’s horse? Is this your idea of righteous behavior?”

Guanyin said, “That dragon is my personal plea to the Jade Emperor. I brought him here to serve the seeker of scriptures. How could a mortal horse from the East Land withstand the journey through mountains and rivers? How could it reach the sacred land of Lingshan? Only this dragon horse could make the journey.”

Sun Wukong said, “What about the fact that he’s so afraid of me? Why would he even come out?” 

Guanyin instructed Jie Di, “Go to the cliff edge and call out: ‘Ao Run, the Dragon King, Yulong, the Third Prince, come forth! The Guanyin is here.’ He will come out.”

Jie Di went to the cliff edge and called out twice. The young dragon burst from the water, transforming into a human form. He stepped onto a cloud head and bowed to Guanyin. “I thank the Guanyin for releasing me from my misery. I have waited for a long time, but have not heard any news of the seeker of scriptures.”

Guanyin pointed to Sun Wukong and said, “Isn’t this the Great Disciple of the seeker of scriptures?”


The dragon said, “Guanyin, this is my adversary. I ate his horse yesterday because I was starving. He is strong and drove me back in fear. I hid in the water, afraid to come out, and he never mentioned a word about the seeker of scriptures.”

“What brings you here?”  Jie Di said, “Tang Sanzang lost his horse in Shepan Mountain’s Yingchou Diaojian, leaving Sun Wukong in a difficult position. When we asked the local deity, he said that a dragon sent by the Bodhisattva had swallowed it. The Great Saint asked me to summon the Bodhisattva to subdue that dragon and retrieve the horse.”  The Bodhisattva said, “This one is the son of Ao Run, of the West Sea. He burned the Mingzhu in the temple, for which his father denounced him for insubordination, committing a capital offense in Heaven. I personally pleaded with the Jade Emperor and brought him down, assigning him to serve Tang Sanzang as a steed. How could he have eaten Tang Sanzang’s horse?  Wait, I shall go.” The Bodhisattva descended his lotus platform, leaving the fairy cave directly, riding a beam of auspicious light with Jie Di across the South Sea. There is a poem to attest to this, saying:

The Buddha preached the Tripitaka Sutra,
The Bodhisattva spread kindness throughout the Great Wall.

Mahamaya’s words resonate through heaven and earth,
Prajna’s true words save spirits and ghosts.
Thus, the Golden Cicada shed its shell once more,
Thus, Xuanzang was allowed to embark on his pilgrimage once again.
It was only because of the obstacle of Yingchoujian,
That the dragon son returned, transforming into a horse.

The Bodhisattva and Jie Di arrived at Shepan Mountain in no time.  But in mid-air, they remained on the auspicious clouds, looking down. They saw Sun Wukong shouting by the precipice. The Bodhisattva told Jie Di to summon him. Jie Di landed on the cloud and, without going through Sanzang, reached the precipice, saying to Sun Wukong, “The Bodhisattva has arrived.”

Hearing this, Sun Wukong leaped into the air, calling out, “You, the Master of Seven Buddhas, the compassionate leader! How could you scheme against me?”

The Bodhisattva replied, “You, you audacious, foolish monkey! I’ve tried my best to help you, bringing a pilgrim to save your life. Why don’t you thank me for saving your life, but instead you come here to berate me?” 

Sun Wukong said, “You’ve put me in a terrible situation! You let me go and be carefree, why do you have to keep me at your beck and call? Why did you have me swear an oath to serve Tang Sanzang? Why did you give him a magic headband to wear, causing me endless suffering?  This iron hoop constantly pains me, and I am forced to endure it. Isn't this you tormenting me?”

The Bodhisattva laughed, “You monkey! You disobey orders and reject enlightenment. If I didn’t bind you with this, you would be running amok again, deceiving Heaven and doing as you please.  If you weren't held in check, who knows what havoc you would wreak? Only with this demon head will you finally be willing to enter my path of yoga!”

Sun Wukong said, “Then let this iron head be my demon head! How could you have sent that wicked dragon, guilty of his crimes, to transform into a monster and devour my master’s horse? You let evil flourish! This is most unjust!”

The Bodhisattva said, “That dragon, I personally requested the Jade Emperor to send him here. He is here solely to serve the pilgrim on his journey. Could a mortal horse from the East Land possibly withstand the trials of countless mountains and rivers, and reach the sacred Land of Buddhism? Only with this dragon horse will he be able to make the journey.”

Sun Wukong said, “Since he’s so afraid of me, why doesn’t he come out?”

The Bodhisattva told Jie Di, “Go to the precipice and shout: ‘Ao Run Dragon King, Yulong, the Third Prince, come out! The South Sea Bodhisattva is here.’ He will appear.”

Jie Di went to the precipice and called out twice.  The dragon rose from the waves, transformed into a human form, flew on a cloud, and bowed to the Bodhisattva, saying, “I thank the Bodhisattva for saving my life. I have been waiting here for a long time, but have not heard news of the pilgrim.” 

The Bodhisattva pointed at Sun Wukong and said, “Isn’t this the great disciple of the pilgrim?”

The dragon looked at Sun Wukong and said, “Bodhisattva, this is my adversary. Yesterday, I was famished and devoured his horse. He, being powerful, fought me back, forcing me to retreat in fear. He then cursed me, causing me to hide in my cave.  Not once did he mention the pilgrim.”

If someone had told him at this very moment that he was in love, in love with a passionate love, he would have met the thought with astonishment and perhaps even indignation. And if someone had added that Aglaya's note was a love note, a summons to a love tryst, he would have burned with shame for that person and perhaps even challenged him to a duel. All this was completely sincere, and he had never once doubted or allowed even the slightest "double" thought about the possibility of this girl loving him or even the possibility of his loving her. The possibility of her loving him, "a man like him," he would have considered monstrous. It seemed to him that it was simply a prank on her part, if indeed there was anything there at all; but he was somehow too indifferent to the prank itself and found it quite commonplace; he was preoccupied with something else entirely.  He fully believed the words that had slipped out the previous day from the agitated general, that she laughed at everyone, and at him, at the prince, in particular. He felt no offense whatsoever; in his opinion, this was only natural.  The main thing for him was that tomorrow he would see her again, early in the morning, sit beside her on the green bench, listen to the pistol being loaded, and look at her. That was all he needed. The question of what she intended to say to him and what this important matter, which directly concerned him, was all about, flickered in his mind once or twice. Moreover, he had not the slightest doubt about the actual existence of this "important matter" for which he was summoned, but he hardly thought about it now, to the extent that he didn't even feel the slightest inclination to think about it.

Thinking in this way, Selifan finally plunged into the farthest reaches of abstraction. If Chivkov had been paying attention, he would have learned many details pertaining to himself; but his thoughts were so preoccupied with his subject that only a powerful clap of thunder startled him, causing him to look around. The sky was completely overcast with clouds, and the dusty post road was sprinkled with raindrops. Finally, a thunderclap sounded again, louder and closer, and rain began to pour down suddenly, like from a bucket. At first, striking at an oblique angle, it lashed at one side of the kibitka's body, then the other, then, changing both its direction of attack and becoming completely straight, it drummed directly onto its roof; finally, the spray began to reach his face. This forced him to pull down the leather curtains with two round peepholes, designated for viewing the scenery, and order Selifan to drive faster.

Selifan, interrupted also in the middle of his speech, understood that, indeed, there was no time to lose. He immediately pulled out some piece of grey cloth from under the goats, donned it in his sleeves, grabbed the reins, and shouted to his team of three horses, which were slightly shifting their feet, feeling the pleasant relaxation from the instructive discourse. But Selifan couldn't quite remember how many turns he had passed. Considering and recalling the road somewhat, he guessed that there had been many turns, all of which he had missed. As a Russian person in decisive moments always finds something to do, without delving into distant considerations, he turned right onto the first crossroad and shouted, "Hey, you esteemed gentlemen!" — and galloped off, little thinking where the chosen road would lead.

They had not even reached the top when, above, the painter flung open the door wide and with a deep bow invited K. inside. The girls, however, he repelled, he did not want to let any of them in, no matter how much they pleaded and tried, whether with his permission or against his will. Only the hunchback managed to slip past his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, whirled her around once, and then set her down before the door with the other girls, who, while the painter had left his post, had not dared to cross the threshold. K. did not know how to judge the whole thing, as it seemed as though everything was happening in friendly agreement. The girls at the door stretched their necks one after the other, called out various jokingly meant words to the painter, which K. did not understand, and the painter also laughed, while the hunchback nearly flew in his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed again to K., offered him his hand, and, introducing himself, said: "Artist Titorelli." K. pointed to the door behind which the girls were whispering and said: "You seem to be very popular in the house." "Ah, those faces!" said the painter and searched in vain for the missing button on his nightshirt. He was barefoot and dressed only in a wide, yellowish linen trousers held together with a belt, the long end of which swung freely back and forth. "These faces are a real burden to me," he continued, as he released his nightshirt, whose last button had just broken off, fetched a chair and forced K. to sit down. "I once painted one of them – she's not even here today – and since then they've been following me everywhere. When I'm even here, they only come in if I allow it, but if I'm away, then at least one is always there. They've even had a key made to my door, which they lend each other. It's hard to imagine how annoying it is. For example, I come home with a lady I'm supposed to paint, open the door with my key and find, for example, the hunchback at the table, painting her lips red with a brush, while her little sisters, whom she's supposed to be supervising, are running around and soiling the room in every corner. Or I come home late last night – excuse me, please, considering my state and the mess in the room – so I come home late at night and want to go to bed, and then something bites me on the leg, I look under the bed and pull out something like a… Thing. I don't know why they crowd around me so much, as if I were trying to lure them to me, you must have noticed that. Of course, this also disturbs my work.
