For example, I come home with a lady I'm supposed to paint, open the door with my key and find the hunchbacked one at the table, painting her lips red with a brush, while her little sisters, whom she's supposed to be looking after, run around and dirty the room in every corner. Or I come home late last night - excuse me, please, with regard to my condition and the mess in the room - so I come home late at night and want to go to bed, when something bites me on the leg, I look under the bed and pull out some kind of creature. Why they crowd around me so much, I don't know, you should have noticed that I don't try to entice them. Of course, this also disrupts my work. If this studio weren't provided for me free of charge, I would have moved out long ago." Just then, a little voice called out behind the door, soft and fearful: "Titorelli, can we come in now?" "No," replied the painter. "Not even just me?" it asked again. "No," said the painter, went to the door and bolted it shut.

They hadn't even gotten upstairs when the painter flung the door wide open and, with a deep bow, invited K. in. He turned away the girls, refusing to let any of them enter, no matter how much they begged or tried, whether with his permission or against his will. Only the hunchback managed to slip past his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirt, whirled her around, and then set her down in front of the door with the other girls, who, while the painter had been away from his post, hadn't dared to cross the threshold.

K. didn't know how to make sense of the whole thing; it seemed as if everything were happening in friendly agreement. The girls at the door stretched their necks one after another, calling out various jokingly meant words to the painter, which K. didn't understand. The painter laughed, while the hunchback practically flew in his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed again to K., offered him his hand, and, introducing himself, said: "Art Painter Titorelli." K. pointed at the door behind which the girls were whispering and said: "It seems you are very popular in the house." "Ah, the freaks!" the painter said, and searched in vain to button his nightgown at his neck. He was barefoot and dressed only in a wide, yellowish linen trousers fastened with a belt, whose long end swung freely back and forth. "These freaks are a real burden to me," he continued, as he let go of the nightgown, whose last button had just come undone, fetched a chair, and forced K. to sit down. "I painted one of them – she isn't even here today – and ever since, they've been following me around. If I'm even here, they only come in if I allow it, but if I'm away for even a moment, at least one is always there. They've even gotten a key made to my door, which they lend to each other. You can hardly imagine how annoying it is. For example, I come home with a lady I'm supposed to paint, open the door with my key, and find the hunchback, for instance, at the table, painting her lips red with a brush, while her little sisters, whom she's supposed to be watching, run around and dirty the room in every corner. Or I come home late last night – excuse me, please, considering my state and the disorder in the room – so I come home late last night and want to go to bed, and then something bites me in the leg. I look under the bed and pull out something like that. Why they crowd around me so much, I don't know; you should have noticed that I don't try to lure them to me. Naturally, this also disturbs my work. If this atelier hadn't been given to me for free, I would have moved out long ago." Just then, a little voice called out from behind the door, sweet and timid: "Titorelli, can we come in now?" "No," the painter answered. "Just me, too?" it asked again. "No," said the painter, went to the door and bolted it shut.

“I don’t want oratorical success,” said K., reasoning thus, “that probably wouldn’t be within my grasp anyway. The Examining Magistrate probably speaks much better; it’s part of his profession, after all. What I want is simply a public discussion of a public wrong. Listen: I was arrested about ten days ago, and I laugh at the fact of the arrest itself, but that doesn’t belong here now. I was seized in bed early in the morning; perhaps they – it’s not excluded, as the Examining Magistrate said – had the order to arrest some equally innocent house painter, but they chose me. The adjacent room was occupied by two rough guards. If I were a dangerous robber, they wouldn’t have been able to take better precautions. Besides, these guards were demoralized riffraff, they bombarded me with chatter, wanted to bribe me, wanted to get me to hand over my clothes and laundry under false pretenses, they wanted money, allegedly to bring me breakfast after they shamelessly devoured my own breakfast in front of me. And that wasn’t all. I was taken to a third room in front of the jailer. It was the room of a lady whom I greatly esteem, and I had to watch, for my sake, but without any fault on my part, how this room was, so to speak, defiled by the presence of the guards and the jailer. It wasn’t easy to remain calm, but I managed it. And I asked the jailer, fully calmly – if he were here, he would confirm it – why I had been arrested. What did this jailer, whom I still see before me, sitting on the armchair of the aforementioned lady like a manifestation of the dullest arrogance, answer? My lords, he answered practically nothing, perhaps he really knew nothing; he had arrested me and was content with that. He even went further and brought three low employees from my bank into the room of that lady, who busied themselves with feeling up her photographs, which were her property, and throwing them into disarray. The presence of these employees naturally had another purpose; they were meant, just like my landlady and her maid, to spread the news of my arrest, to damage my public image and, particularly, to shake my position at the bank. Now, none of this, not even in the slightest degree, has succeeded; even my landlady, a very simple person – I want to mention her name here in a respectful manner; her name is Frau Grubach – even Frau Grubach was clever enough to see that such an arrest means nothing more than an attack that unsupervised boys on the street might carry out. I repeat, the whole thing has only caused me inconveniences and temporary annoyance; it could have had much worse consequences, however?”

The incident at the train station struck both Mama and her daughters with near terror. In distress and agitation, Elizaveta Prokofievna practically ran with her daughters all the way home. In her view, so much had happened and been revealed in the incident that, despite the disorder and fright, decisive thoughts were already forming in her head. Yet, everyone understood that something extraordinary had happened, and perhaps, even fortuitously, some kind of extraordinary secret was beginning to emerge. Despite Prince Sh.'s previous assurances and explanations, Evgeny Pavlovich "had now been brought to light," exposed, unveiled, and "formally revealed in his connection with this creature." That's what Elizaveta Prokofievna thought, and even her two elder daughters. The gain from this conclusion was that even more mysteries had accumulated. The girls, though partly annoyed by their mother's excessive fear and such an obvious flight, in the first moment of confusion, didn't dare to bother her with questions. Moreover, for some reason, it seemed to them that their younger sister, Aglaya Ivanovna, might know more about this matter than all three of them combined with their mother. Prince Sh. was also gloomy as night and very pensive. Elizaveta Prokofievna didn't say a word to him throughout the entire journey, and he, it seemed, didn't even notice. Adelaide tried to ask him: "What uncle were they talking about, and what had happened in Petersburg?" But he mumbled something very vague about some inquiries, and that it was all, of course, a nonsense. "There's no doubt about it!" replied Adelaide, and didn't ask about anything else. Aglaya, however, became extraordinarily calm and only remarked on the road that they were already traveling too fast. Once, she turned around and saw the prince catching up with them. Noticing his efforts to catch up, she smiled mockingly and no longer looked back at him.

— Gentlemen, as with everyone, I have committed some unrefined acts in my life, — began the general, — but the strangest thing is that I myself consider this short anecdote, which I'm about to tell, the most vile anecdote of my entire life. Thirty-five years have passed since then, but I've never been able to shake off a certain, so to speak, scratching sensation in my heart. The matter, however, is extraordinarily foolish: I was then just a young lieutenant and serving in the army. You know, a lieutenant: blood is boiling, and the household is meager; I had a valet, Nikifor, at the time, and he was terribly concerned about my household, saving, mending, scraping and cleaning, and even stealing whatever he could snatch to only increase the fortune of the house. He was a most trustworthy and honest man. I, of course, was strict, but just. For some time we were stationed in a town. They gave me a flat in the suburbs with a retired sub-lieutenant and, moreover, a widow. She was a woman of about eighty years old, or at least thereabouts. Her house was old, shabby, wooden, and even poor as she was, she didn't have a servant. But, most importantly, she was distinguished by the fact that she once had a large family and relatives; but some died during her lifetime, others scattered, and others forgot about the old woman, and she had buried her husband forty-five years before.  She lived with a niece for several years before this, a hunchbacked and spiteful woman, they say, like a witch, and even once bit the old woman on the finger, but she too died, so the old woman had been alone for three years. It was boring for me at her place, and it was an empty, useless dwelling. Finally, she stole my rooster. The matter remains unclear to this day, but besides her, there was no one else who could have done it. We had a big quarrel over the rooster, and right at that moment, a situation arose where I was transferred to another apartment at my first request, to the opposite suburb, to the numerous family of a merchant with a large beard, as I remember him now. We moved with Nikifor with joy, leaving the old woman with indignation. Three days pass, I come from lessons, Nikifor reports, "That's pointless, your honor, our bowl was left at the old mistress's, there's nothing to serve soup in." I, of course, am surprised: "How is that, how did our bowl stay with the mistress?" The surprised Nikifor continues to report that the mistress, when we moved out, didn't give him our bowl because since I had broken her own pot, she was holding our bowl as compensation, and that I had supposedly offered her this arrangement myself. Such a baseness on her part, of course, completely drove me out of my mind; my blood boiled, I jumped up, and flew off. I arrive at the old woman's, so to speak, already beside myself; I see her sitting alone in the hallway, in a corner, as if hiding from the sun, propping her cheek with her hand. I immediately, you know, unleashed a whole thunderstorm on her, "Such, you, and so you are!", and, you know, in that Russian way. Only I look, something strange appears: she sits, her face staring at me, her eyes bulging, and not a word in response, and strangely, strangely, she looks as if she's swaying. Finally, I calm down, I look closer, I ask, still not a word in response. I stood in indecision; flies buzzed, the sun was setting, there was silence; in complete confusion, I finally left. Before I even reached home, I was summoned by the major, then I had to go to the company, so I got home only in the evening. Nikifor's first words: "You know, your honor, our mistress died." — "When?" — "About an hour and a half ago, just this evening." That is, at the very moment when I was berating her, she departed. This so shocked me, I tell you, that I barely came to my senses. It even seemed to be thinking, even dreamed at night. Of course, I'm not superstitious, but on the third day I went to the church for her funeral. In a word, the further time goes by, the more I think about it. It's not that, but sometimes you imagine it, and it becomes unpleasant. The main thing is what I finally figured out? Firstly, a woman, so to speak, a human being, what they call in our time, a humane being, lived, lived a long life, and finally, she reached the end. Once she had children, a husband, a family, relatives, all this, so to speak, was boiling around her, all these, so to speak, smiles, and suddenly — complete silence, everything flew out the chimney, she was left alone, like some kind of fly, carrying on its back a curse from time immemorial. And so, finally, God brought her to an end. At sunset, on a quiet summer evening, my old woman flies away — of course, there is a moral here; and at this very moment, instead of a farewell, so to speak, tear, a young, desperate lieutenant, grimacing and swearing, sees her off from the surface of the earth with Russian elements of abusive words for a lost bowl! Without a doubt, I am guilty, and although I have been looking at my act for a long time now, from a distance of years and a change in my nature, as if it were someone else's, I nevertheless continue to regret it. So I repeat, it's strange to me, the more so that if I am guilty, then not entirely: why did she just have to die at that moment? Of course, there is one excuse here: that the act was in some way psychological, but still I couldn't calm down until I took in, fifteen years ago, two permanent sick old women, at my own expense, in the hospice, with the aim of mitigating for them the last days of their earthly life with decent support. I'm thinking of making it eternal, leaving a capital in my will. Well, that's all, then. I repeat, that maybe I have sinned in many things in life, but this case I consider, in conscience, the most vile act of my entire life.

I was, of course, astonished: "How could this be? How did our bowl stay at the old woman's?"  The bewildered Nikifor continued to report that when we were leaving, the old woman refused to give him our bowl because, as I had broken her own pot, she was holding our bowl in return. And, as if I had offered it to her that way. Such lowliness on her part, of course, drove me to the limit; my blood boiled, I jumped up and rushed off.

I arrived at the old woman's, practically beside myself; I see her sitting alone in the hallway, in a corner, as if huddled from the sun, propping her cheek with her hand. Immediately, you know, I unleashed a whole storm upon her, "Such a woman you are!" and, you know, in that Russian way.  But then I noticed something strange: she was sitting there, staring at me, her eyes wide open, and not a word in response. She looked strangely, strangely, as if swaying.

I finally calmed down, looked closer, asked her something, and she still didn't answer. I stood there, undecided. Flies buzzed, the sun was setting, there was silence. In complete confusion, I finally left. Before I even reached home, I was called to the major, and then had to go to my company, so I got home quite late in the evening. The first words Nikifor said were: "You know, sir, our mistress has died." - "When?" - "About an hour and a half ago, this evening." Of course, I am not superstitious, but on the third day I went to church for her funeral. In a word, the further time goes, the more I think about it. It's not that, but sometimes I imagine it, and it becomes uncomfortable. The main thing I concluded was this: first, a woman, a human being, as we call it now, a humane one, lived, lived a long life, and finally came to an end. Once she had children, a husband, a family, relatives - everything around her was bustling, all those, so to speak, smiles, and suddenly - a complete void, everything disappeared, she was left alone, like some kind of fly carrying the curse of ages on itself. Without a doubt, I am guilty, and although I have been looking at my act for a long time now, from a distance of years and a change in my nature, as if it were someone else's, I still regret it. I repeat, I may have sinned in many ways in my life, but this incident, in my conscience, remains the most vile act of my whole life.

“Look at you all huddled together!” Leni called, returning with the cup and stopping in the doorway. They were indeed pressed close, so that with the slightest turn they bumped heads. The merchant, who, besides his small stature, also stooped, had forced K. to hunch down too if he wanted to hear everything. “Just a little while longer!” K. called out to Leni, waving her off impatiently with the hand he still had resting on the merchant’s. “He wanted me to tell him about my trial,” the merchant said to Leni. “Go on, tell him,” she said. She spoke to the merchant affectionately, but also condescendingly, which K. disliked; as he had now realized, the man had some worth, at least he had experiences he knew how to recount well. Leni was probably judging him wrongly. He glared as Leni now took the candle from the merchant, who had held it the whole time, wiped his hand with her apron, and then knelt beside him to scrape off some wax that had dripped from the candle onto his trousers. “They wanted to tell me about the Winkeladvokaten,” K. said, and pushed, without another word, Leni’s hand away. “What do you want?” Leni asked, lightly slapping K. and resuming her work. “Yes, about the Winkeladvokaten,” the merchant said, stroking his forehead as if in thought. K. wanted to help him and said: “They wanted immediate results and so they went to the Winkeladvokaten.” “Quite right,” said the merchant, but didn’t continue. “He probably doesn’t want to talk about it in front of Leni,” thought K., suppressed his impatience to hear the rest immediately, and no longer pressed further.

One day, the four valiant generals hosted a feast in their cave, inviting the six kings to drink. They slaughtered oxen and horses, sacrificed to heaven and earth, and had strange creatures dance and sing. Everyone ate until they were completely drunk.  As they sent the six kings away, the generals rewarded the chieftains and, leaning under the shade of the iron-plated bridge, fell asleep in an instant. The four valiant generals and their troops surrounded them, daring not to speak loudly. Suddenly, two men appeared in the Monkey King's sleep, carrying a decree bearing the words "Sun Wukong" written upon it. They approached without hesitation, bound him with rope, and snatched away his soul. They staggered along, dragging him toward a city. 

The Monkey King gradually sobered up and, looking up, saw a plaque on the city gate with three large characters: "Realm of the Underworld." The Monkey King suddenly understood, "The Realm of the Underworld is where the King of Hell resides. What brings me here?" The two men said, "Your earthly lifespan is coming to an end. We have a decree to lead you here."  

The Monkey King retorted, "Old Sun transcends the three realms and is not within the five elements. He is no longer under his jurisdiction. How dare you come for me?" The two grim reapers tugged and pulled, determined to drag him inside. The Monkey King, enraged, pulled out a precious object from his ear, flicking it, it grew thick and long. With a slight raise of his hand, he smashed the two grim reapers into a bloody paste. He broke free from his bonds, tossed the rope aside, and, wielding his staff, charged into the city.

This frightened the bull-headed ghost to hide and the horse-faced ghost to run in all directions. The ghost soldiers scrambled up to the Hall of Mortal Souls and shouted, "Your Majesty! Disaster! Disaster! A hairy, thundering demon has arrived!"

I've never seen dreams before. They say that for the ancients it was the most ordinary, normal thing – to see dreams. Well, yes: after all, their whole life was just such a terrible carousel: green – orange – Buddha – juice. But we know that dreams are a serious mental illness. Yes, now it's exactly like this: I feel something foreign in my brain – like the finest eyelash in my eye: you feel yourself entirely, but you can't forget about that eye with the eyelash – not for a second...

They knelt and reported, "Your Majesty, we followed your imperial decree to descend to the mortal realm to subdue the demon-immortal Sun Wukong. The Jade Emperor said, "How much skill could a single demon monkey possess? Is it necessary to send more troops?" The Third Prince then stepped forward and pleaded, "We beseech Your Majesty to pardon our deaths! That demon monkey wields an iron staff and first defeated the giant spirit god, then wounded my arm. Outside the cave, he erected a flag with the inscription 'Great Sage Equaling Heaven,' claiming this as his official title. He proclaims that if we grant him this title, he will lay down his arms and surrender. Otherwise, he will attack even Lingxiao Hall."

Upon hearing this, the Jade Emperor was astounded. "How dare that monkey be so arrogant! Immediately, order all troops to eliminate him." 

As he spoke, Tai Bai Jin Xing emerged from the ranks and reported, "That monkey is reckless with words but lacks wisdom. To add troops and fight him will only lead to prolonged conflict and further strain our forces. It would be wiser for Your Majesty to show great compassion, issue a pardon and an edict of amnesty, and offer him the title of Great Sage Equaling Heaven. But, it will be a mere honorary title with no salary or position, allowing him to live under Heaven and Earth, restraining his wicked heart and preventing further arrogance. This will ensure peace and tranquility throughout the universe."

The Jade Emperor said, "I approve of your suggestion." He immediately ordered a proclamation to be written and entrusted it to Jin Xing to deliver.

For more than a week now, the guest gentleman had been living in the city, spending his time at parties and dinners, as they say, very pleasantly. At last he decided to take his visits out of the city and visit the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, to whom he had given his word. Perhaps another, more significant reason, a matter more serious, closer to his heart, had prompted him to do so… But the reader will learn about all this gradually and in due time, if only he has the patience to read the offered novella, which is very long and will widen and expand as it approaches its conclusion, culminating in a grand finale.

Selifan the coachman had been ordered to harness the horses in the familiar carriage early the next morning; Petrusha had been told to stay at home, look after the room and the trunk. It would not be superfluous for the reader to become acquainted with these two serfs of our hero. Although, of course, they are not particularly prominent figures, and what is called secondary, or even tertiary, characters, although the main plot and springs of the poem are not centered on them and only touch upon them lightly, the author is extremely thorough in everything and, despite being a Russian himself, wants to be as meticulous as a German. This, however, will not take much time or space, because not much needs to be added to what the reader already knows, namely that Petrusha wore a somewhat wide brown frock coat from his master's shoulder and, as was customary for people of his station, had a large nose and lips. He was more taciturn than talkative by nature; he even had a noble inclination towards enlightenment, that is, reading books, the contents of which he did not particularly care about: whether it was a love story, a primer, or a prayer book, he read everything with equal attention; if chemistry had been offered to him, he would not have refused it either. He liked not the subject matter of what he read, but rather the act of reading itself, or, better yet, the process of reading, how from letters something eternally emerges, a word that sometimes means God knows what. This reading took place mainly in a lying position in the front room, on the bed and on the mattress, which had become thin and flat from this habit. 

Besides his love of reading, he had two other habits that constituted two other characteristic features: he slept without undressing, as he was, in the same frock coat, and he always carried with him a certain special air, his own peculiar scent, reminiscent of a somewhat stuffy room, so that it was enough for him to place his bed anywhere, even in a room that had never been inhabited before, and to move his coat and belongings there, and it already seemed as if people had been living in that room for ten years.

Chichikov, being a rather sensitive and even in some cases fussy man, after drawing the air into his fresh nose in the morning, only grimaced and shook his head, saying: "You, my friend, what do you know, you're sweating. You should go to the bathhouse." Petrusha didn't answer anything to this and tried to immediately occupy himself with some business; or he would approach with his whip to the master's hanging frock coat, or simply tidy something up. What he was thinking about at that time, when he was silent, - perhaps he was saying to himself: "And you, however, are also quite something, haven't you had enough of repeating the same thing forty times?" - God knows, it's hard to know what a serf thinks at a time like this, when his master gives him instructions. And so, this is what can be said about Petrusha at first glance. Selifan the coachman was a completely different person… But the author is very ashamed to take up the readers' time with people of a lower class for so long, knowing by experience how reluctantly they become acquainted with low-born people. Such is the Russian man: a strong desire to be superior to anyone who is even one rank lower, and a casual acquaintance with a count or prince is better for him than any close friendships. The author even fears for his hero, who is only a collegiate assessor. Provincial advisors, perhaps, will make acquaintances with him, but those who have already reached the ranks of generals, those, God knows, may even cast one of those condescending glances that a proud man throws at everything that crawls at his feet, or, worse yet, may pass by with the deadly indifference that is destructive to the author. The news was relayed from monkey to monkey, layer by layer, until it reached the depths of the cave. "Great King, an old man with a scroll bearing a celestial seal has arrived, claiming to be an emissary from Heaven, bearing a decree for you.”  The Monkey King, overjoyed, declared, "These past few days, I’ve been thinking of visiting Heaven. Now, just as I was contemplating it, an angel arrives to summon me!" He exclaimed, "Bring him in quickly!" The Monkey King hurriedly adjusted his robes and stepped out to greet him.

Venus entered the main chamber and stood facing south, saying, "I am the Western White Jade Star, Venus. I am sent by the Jade Emperor to grant you a decree, summoning you to Heaven to receive your immortal record."  Sun Wukong laughed, “I am honored by the Star's presence." He instructed, "You little ones! Prepare a feast to entertain our guest." Venus replied, "The decree is in my possession and I cannot linger. Please accompany me now, and after your promotion, we can discuss things leisurely." Wukong said, "Thank you for your kindness! Please, let me see you off!" He was awarded a position of honor among the heavenly ranks, but what rank he would receive, we shall reveal in the next installment.

The two rows of pine and bamboo, yearless and nameless, stood serene; the forest of cypress and fir, with color and presence, followed in proud splendor.  They saw that the bell tower and stupa were tall, and the atmosphere of tranquility was established. The resident monks practiced their dhyana, birdsong interspersed with rustling trees, a quietude free from dust, emptiness, and in that emptiness, the true nature of reality was revealed. The poem goes: "Hidden in the temple, in the midst of a mountain sanctuary, the landscape surpasses that of a festival. Such a pure land, rare in the world,  with many monks living in this famous mountain."

The elder dismounted, the monk set down his load, and were about to enter, when a group of monks emerged from the gate. You see, how their appearance was: wearing left-side jeweled hats, robes of spotless white. Copper rings hung from their ears, silken belts encircled their waists. Their steps were slow and steady, wooden fish held in their hands. Their mouths constantly uttered the words,  the ultimate refuge of all beings. 

When the Tripitaka saw them, he stood by the gate and inquired politely. The monk quickly bowed and laughed, saying, "Forgive my oversight. May I ask where you are from? Please, enter, and I will offer you tea." The Tripitaka said: "My disciple and I are emissaries from the eastern land, come to the Leiyin Temple to pay homage to Buddha and seek scriptures. It is late in the day, and we wish to rest in this temple for the night." The monk replied: "Please, come in and sit. Please, come in and sit." The Tripitaka then called to his disciple to lead the horse inside. 

The monk, upon seeing the disciple’s appearance, felt a tremor of fear and asked, "What sort of creature is that pulling the horse?" The Tripitaka whispered: "Hush! Hush! He is easily agitated. If you call him a creature, he will become angry. He is my disciple."

Yet it turned out that the master and his disciple rode their horses and arrived at the mountain gate, where they saw that it was indeed a temple. The many halls and pavilions, the overlapping corridors and houses, all were shrouded in tens of thousands of colorful clouds before the three mountains’ gates; in front of the Five Blessings Hall, a thousand red mists swirled gracefully. On either side stood rows of pines and bamboos, evergreen and timeless in their quiet beauty; while on the other side, a grove of cypress and pine trees, with their varied colors and shapes, exuded an air of proud majesty. The bell and drum tower soared high, the pagoda stood majestic and tall. The quiet monks meditated in peace, the sounds of birds singing in the trees were tranquil. Such solitude, such purity, true serenity. Such emptiness, such clarity, a fruit of true emptiness.

The poem goes: “The hidden emerald nest on the upper terrace of the famous temple, surpasses the most beautiful scenery of the heavens. Truly, such pure land is rare in the human world, while famous mountains are occupied by many monks.”

The elder dismounted, and the disciple rested his burden, just as they were about to enter, a group of monks came out from the gate. You see, they were dressed most uniquely: wearing left-sided comb hats and robes of immaculate white. Copper bells hung from their ears, silk sashes tied around their waists. They walked steadily with steps measured, holding wooden fish in their hands. They constantly chanted, “Gently recite the Prajna Paramita, and utterly take refuge.”

When the Three Baskets saw them, he stood by the door and asked politely, the monk hurriedly bowed, smiling sheepishly, and said, “Greetings to you, travelers. Where are you from? Please come in and I shall present you with tea.” The Three Baskets replied, “I am a disciple from the eastern lands, sent to pray to the Buddha and seek scriptures at Lei Yin Temple. We have arrived here as the day is growing late, and we wish to borrow a night’s rest in your esteemed temple.”

The monk said, “Please, please come in and sit down.” 

The Three Baskets called out to his disciple to lead the horse in. The monk, upon seeing the disciple’s appearance, became somewhat frightened, and asked, “What kind of creature is the one leading the horse?” The Three Baskets whispered, “Hush! Hush! He is easily provoked if you refer to him as something. He is my disciple.”

It is very hard to explain in order how it came to pass that all the Epanchins suddenly and unanimously became possessed by the same thought: that something momentous had happened to Aglaya, and that her fate was at stake.  But as soon as this thought flashed, as if by a sudden revelation, it became clear to all that they had long known and foreseen everything, that everything had been clear even from the time of the "poor knight," even earlier, but that they had not then wanted to believe such a thing. This, the sisters maintained; of course, Lizaveta Prokofievna had foreseen and understood everything before anyone else, and her heart had been "aching" for a long time, but — for how long, indeed? — now the thought of the prince suddenly seemed distasteful to her, precisely because it confused her. 

A question arose which had to be resolved immediately; but not only could it not be resolved, but even the very question that poor Lizaveta Prokofievna was unable to form clearly in her own mind, no matter how hard she tried. It was a difficult matter: "Is the prince good or bad? Is this all good or bad? If it is bad (which is certainly the case), then what exactly is bad about it? And if, perhaps, it is good (which is also possible), then what, again, is good about it?" 

Ivan Fedorovitch, the head of the family, was, of course, first of all surprised, but then he suddenly made a confession that, "God knows, he had also felt something of the sort all along, now and then, as if it were just appearing to him!" He immediately fell silent under the stern gaze of his wife, but he fell silent in the morning, and in the evening, alone with his wife and forced to speak again, he suddenly and as if with particular enthusiasm expressed several unexpected thoughts: "Well, in essence, what..." (Pause). "Of course, all this is very strange if it is true, and he does not dispute that, but..." (Another pause). "But on the other hand, if we look at things straight on, the prince is, God knows, a wonderful young man, and... and... and—well, finally, the name, our family name, all this will give the appearance, so to speak, of support to the family name, which is in a state of humiliation in the eyes of the world, that is, if we look at it from this point of view, that is, because... of course, the world; the world is the world; but still, the prince is not without means, even if only some." He has... and... and... and..." (A long pause and a decisive stumble). Having heard her husband, Lizaveta Prokofievna went beyond all bounds.

K. waited from day to day throughout the next week for a new communication, he couldn't believe that his renunciation of interrogations had been taken literally. And as the expected communication did not arrive by Saturday evening, he assumed that he had been tacitly summoned back to the same house for the same length of time.  Therefore, he went there again on Sunday, this time going straight up the stairs and down the corridors; some people who remembered him greeted him at their doors, but he no longer had to ask anyone and soon came to the right door.  At his knock, it was immediately opened, and without looking further at the familiar woman who remained by the door, he was about to step into the next room. "There's no session today," said the woman. "Why shouldn't there be a session?" he asked, not wanting to believe it. But the woman convinced him by opening the door to the next room. It was really empty and looked even more pathetic in its emptiness than last Sunday. On the table, which stood unchanged on the platform, lay some books. "Can I look at the books?" asked K., not out of particular curiosity, but simply so as not to have been completely useless in coming here. "No," said the woman and closed the door again, "that's not allowed. The books belong to the investigating judge."

The thought of the trial never left him. He had often thought about whether it wouldn't be good to draft a defense and submit it to the court. He wanted to include a short account of his life in it and, for every significant event, explain the reasons for his actions, whether his actions were, in his current judgment, to be condemned or approved, and what reasons he could put forward for this or that. The advantages of such a defense over simply relying on the defense attorney, who was not exactly flawless anyway, were undeniable. K. didn't even know what the attorney was doing; certainly not much, he hadn't summoned him for a month now, and at none of their previous meetings had K. gotten the impression that the man could achieve anything for him. Above all, he had hardly asked him any questions at all. And here there was so much to ask. Asking was the main thing. K. had the feeling that he himself could ask all the necessary questions. Instead of asking, the attorney either talked himself or sat opposite him silently, leaning forward slightly over the desk, probably because of his poor hearing, tugging at a goatee within his beard and staring down at the carpet, perhaps right at the spot where K. had lain with Leni. Every now and then, he gave K. some empty admonitions, the kind you give to children. Just as useless and boring were the speeches that K. intended not to pay a single penny for in the final bill. After the attorney had sufficiently humiliated him, he usually started to cheer him up again. He said he had already won many similar cases, wholly or partially. Cases that, although perhaps not as difficult in reality as this one, outwardly seemed even more hopeless. He had a list of these cases here in the drawer – here he tapped on some drawer of the table – but he couldn't show them to K., as they were confidential. Nevertheless, his great experience gained through all these cases would naturally be of use to K. He had naturally started working on it immediately, and the first submission was almost finished. It was very important because the first impression the defense made often determined the entire course of the proceedings. Unfortunately, he had to point out to K. that it sometimes happened that the first submissions were not even read at the court. They were simply filed and a note was added that the initial examination and observation of the accused were more important than anything written. If the petitioner became insistent, they added, as a rule, that all the documents, including this first submission, would be reviewed in context once all the material was collected. Unfortunately, however, this was usually not the case; the first submission was usually misplaced or completely lost, and even if it remained until the end, as the attorney had only heard from hearsay, it was rarely read. All this was regrettable, but not entirely unfounded. K. should not overlook that the proceedings were not public; they could become public if the court deemed it necessary, but the law did not require publicity. As a result, the court documents, especially the indictment, were inaccessible to the accused and his defense; therefore, one generally did not know, or at least not precisely, what the first submission should be directed against. It could therefore only accidentally contain something relevant to the case. Really accurate and evidence-based submissions could only be drafted later, when the individual charges and their justification became clearer during the questioning of the accused or could be guessed at. Under these circumstances, the defense was naturally in a very unfavorable and difficult position. But that was also intended. The defense was not actually permitted by the law, but only tolerated, and there was even dispute about whether even tolerance could be read from the relevant legal provision. In principle, there were no court-recognized attorneys, all those who appeared before this court as attorneys were in fact only corner attorneys. This naturally had a very demeaning effect on the entire profession, and if K. ever went into the court offices, he could, just to see it for himself, look at the attorney's room. He would probably be horrified by the sight. The small, low room assigned to them alone showed the contempt the court had for these people. Light only came into the room through a small window high up, so that if one wanted to look out, one had to ask a colleague to lift them up, and by the way, one got a face full of smoke from a chimney just outside, that was almost directly in front of it. The floor of the room – to give just one more example of these conditions – had a hole in it for over a year now. Not so big that a person could fall through, but big enough to sink in with one foot. The attorney's room was located on the second attic floor; if one sank in, one's leg hung down into the first attic floor, and right into the hallway where the parties waited. It was no exaggeration to say that such conditions were considered shameful in attorney circles. Complaints to the administration had no effect whatsoever, but the attorneys were strictly forbidden to make any changes to the room at their own expense. But even this treatment of attorneys had its justification. The aim was to suppress the defense as much as possible; everything should be left to the accused himself. Not a bad standpoint in principle, but nothing would be more misguided than to conclude that attorneys were unnecessary for the accused at this court. On the contrary, nowhere else were they as necessary as here. The proceedings were generally not only public, but also hidden from the accused. Of course, only to the extent that was possible, but it was possible to a very large extent. The accused did not have access to the court documents either, and it was very difficult to deduce anything from the interrogations based on these documents, especially for the accused, who was prejudiced and had all sorts of worries that distracted him. This is where the defense came in. During the interrogations, defense attorneys were generally not allowed to be present; therefore, they had to inquire about the interrogation from the accused after the interrogation, and often at the door of the interrogation room, and extract what was useful for the defense from these often already very vague accounts. But this was not the most important thing, because one could not learn much from this, although, of course, as everywhere else, a skilled man learned more than others. The most important thing remained the personal relationships of the attorney; in them lay the main value of the defense. Now, K. had probably already seen from his own experiences that the very bottom of the court organization was not quite perfect, with forgetful and corruptible officials, which somehow gave loopholes in the strict closing of the court. Here, most of the attorneys slipped in, bribes were given and people were eavesdropped on, and there were even cases of theft of documents, at least in earlier times. It was not to be denied that this sometimes produced surprisingly favorable results for the accused in the short term, and these little attorneys would swagger around with it and attract new clients, but for the further course of the trial, it either meant nothing or something bad. Only honest personal relationships, and particularly with higher officials, which naturally meant officials of the lower ranks, had real value. Only through this could the course of the proceedings be influenced, if only imperceptibly at first, but later more and more clearly. This could only be done by a few attorneys, and K.'s choice was very fortunate here. Only perhaps one or two other attorneys could boast of such connections as Dr. Huld. However, these attorneys did not concern themselves with the society in the attorney's room and had nothing to do with it. On the other hand, their connection with the court officials was all the closer. It was not even always necessary for Dr. Huld to go to court, he could just happen to appear in the waiting rooms of the examining magistrates, and depending on his mood, achieve a mostly only seeming success, or not even that. No, K. had seen it himself, the officials, and some quite high ones, would stand there, staring out into the street as if in despair, while the attorney studied the documents at his table to be able to give them good advice. Incidentally, one could see just at such times how seriously these gentlemen took their profession and how easily they fell into despair over obstacles they could not overcome by nature. Their position was not an easy one either; one should not wrong them and not consider their position as easy. The hierarchy and progress of the court was infinite and even for an insider it was unpredictable. However, the proceedings before the courts were generally secret even for the lower officials; they could therefore hardly ever fully follow the progress of the cases they handled. The case appeared in their field of vision without their often knowing where it came from, and it proceeded further without their ever knowing where it was going. Therefore, the lesson that could be drawn from studying the individual stages of a trial, the final decision and its reasons, escaped these officials. They were only allowed to deal with the part of the process that was demarcated for them by the law and knew less about the outcome of their own work than the defense, which usually remained in contact with the accused almost until the end of the trial. Even in this direction, therefore, they could learn something valuable from the defense. It was no wonder that K. should marvel at the officials' irritability, which sometimes manifested itself in a - everyone had this experience - insulting manner towards the parties. All officials were irritable, even if they seemed calm. Naturally, the smaller attorneys suffered most from this. One tells the following story, which seems very plausible. An old official, a good, quiet man, had studied a difficult court case, which had been particularly complicated by the submissions of the attorney, uninterruptedly for a day and a night – these officials are indeed diligent, like no one else. Against dawn, after twenty-four hours, probably not very fruitful work, he went to the entrance door, set himself in ambush there and threw every attorney who wanted to enter down the stairs. The attorneys gathered at the bottom of the stairs and discussed what they should do; on the one hand, they had no real claim to be admitted, they could hardly take any legal action against the official and, as already mentioned, they also had to be careful not to antagonize the officials. On the other hand, every day not spent at court was a day lost for them, so they were very keen to get in. Finally, they agreed to tire the old man out. An attorney was sent up again and again, who climbed the stairs and then met with as much passive resistance as possible.

There was even a hole in the floor of this room – not large enough for a person to fall through, but large enough for one leg to sink in entirely. The lawyers' room was on the second attic floor; if one fell in, their leg would dangle into the first attic floor, right into the hallway where the parties were waiting. It was not an exaggeration to say that these conditions were considered shameful in legal circles. Complaints to the administration had absolutely no effect. However, the lawyers were strictly forbidden from making any changes to the room at their own expense. 

But this treatment of lawyers also had its justification. The court wanted to discourage the defense as much as possible; everything should be left to the defendant himself. This was not a bad standpoint in principle, but it would be a grave mistake to conclude that lawyers were unnecessary in this court. On the contrary, they were more necessary here than anywhere else. The proceedings were not only secret from the public but also from the defendant. Of course, this was only to the extent possible, but it was possible to a very great extent. The defendant also had no access to the court documents, and it was very difficult to glean anything from the interrogations based on the underlying documents, especially for the defendant who was already biased and had all sorts of worries clouding his mind.  

Here the defense stepped in. During interrogations, defenders were generally not allowed to be present; they had to inquire about the interrogation after it was over, preferably still at the door of the interrogation room, and extract whatever was relevant for the defense from these often already very vague reports.

But this was not the most important thing, because one couldn't learn much in this way, although, as everywhere else, a skilled man could learn more. The most important thing remained the lawyer's personal connections, in them lay the main value of the defense. As K. had certainly noticed from his own experiences, the very lowest level of organization in the court system existed here.  

There were forgetful and corruptible employees, which, as it were, created gaps in the strict closure of the court.  It was into these gaps that most lawyers rushed; bribery and eavesdropping took place, and there were even cases of theft of files, at least in earlier times. It was undeniable that, for the moment, some even surprisingly favorable results for the defendant could be achieved in this way.

With this, these small lawyers would proudly parade around and attract new clients. But for the further course of the trial, it meant either nothing or something bad. Only honest personal relationships, with higher officials, which naturally meant only officials of the lower ranks, had real value. Only this could influence the course of the trial, albeit initially subtly, but later increasingly.

Few lawyers could do this, and K.'s choice was very fortunate. Only one or two lawyers could possibly match Dr. Huld in these connections. 

These, however, did not concern themselves with the lawyers in the lawyers' room and had nothing to do with them. But their connection to the court officials was very close. It wasn't even always necessary for Dr. Huld to go to the court; in the waiting rooms of the examining magistrates, he would appear casually and, depending on their mood, achieve a mostly apparent success or not even that.

No, K. had seen it himself: officials, even some very high-ranking ones, would stand forlornly staring out the window while the lawyer studied the files at his desk to be able to give them good advice.

It could also be seen in these situations just how seriously these gentlemen took their profession and how they were driven to despair by obstacles they couldn't overcome by nature. One shouldn't do them an injustice, their position shouldn't be underestimated. The ranking and advancement within the court was endless and even for those who were well-versed in its workings, it was impossible to foresee.

The proceedings before the courts were also generally secret from the lower officials; therefore, they could hardly ever fully follow the progress of the cases they handled. The case appeared in their field of vision without their often knowing its origin, and it continued without their knowing where it went.  The lessons one could draw from studying the individual stages of a trial, the final decision, and the reasons behind it, escaped these officials. They could only deal with the part of the process defined by law for them and knew less about the results of their own work than the defense, which usually remained in contact with the defendant until the end of the trial.

It was no wonder, then, that K. might wonder, if he took all this into account, at the irritability of the officials, which sometimes manifested itself in a way that was offensive towards the parties involved – everyone had this experience. All officials were irritable, even if they seemed calm. Of course, the small lawyers suffered from this especially. 
A story was circulating, which seemed very plausible, illustrating this. An old official, a good, quiet man, had spent a day and night studying a difficult case, which had been particularly complicated by the submissions of the lawyer. 

He had, in fact, been incredibly diligent – these officials were more hardworking than anyone else. Against morning, after twenty-four hours of, probably not very fruitful, work, he went to the entrance door, hid there, and threw every lawyer who tried to enter down the stairs. The lawyers gathered at the bottom of the stairs and discussed what to do.

One day, the Queen Mother of the West held a banquet, opening the Treasure Pavilion. In the Yaochi, she was hosting the "Peach Feast," and summoned the red-robed fairy, the white-robed fairy, the green-robed fairy, the blue-robed fairy, the purple-robed fairy, the yellow-robed fairy, and the green-robed fairy. Each fairy wore a flower basket, and they went to the Peach Garden to pick peaches for the banquet.

As the seven fairies reached the gate of the Peach Garden, they saw the land deities and the celestial officials of the Qitianfu guarding the entrance. The fairies approached and said, "We are here on the Queen Mother's orders to fetch peaches for the banquet." The land deity said, "Wait, fairies. This year is different from previous years. The Jade Emperor has dispatched the Great Sage, Equal of Heaven, to oversee the garden. You must report to the Great Sage before the garden can be entered." The fairies asked, "Where is the Great Sage?" The land deity replied, "The Great Sage is inside the garden. He is resting and sleeping on a pavilion." The fairies said, "In that case, find him, and don't delay."

The land deity and the officials entered the garden together. When they reached the flower pavilion, they didn't see the Great Sage; they only saw his clothes. They searched everywhere but couldn't find him. It turned out that the Great Sage had taken a rest after playing for a while and eating a few peaches. He had transformed into a two-inch tall person and was sleeping under the thick leaves of a large tree. The seven fairies said, "We are here on an order, but we can't find the Great Sage. How can we return empty-handed?" A celestial official said, "Since you are here on an order, don't hesitate. Our Great Sage is used to wandering and probably went to meet friends. You can go pick the peaches, and we will inform him for you." The fairies followed his advice and entered the grove to pick peaches. They first picked two baskets from the front trees, then three baskets from the middle trees. When they reached the back trees, they found that the flowers and fruits were scarce, with only a few hairy, green peaches. Apparently, the Monkey King had eaten them all.

The seven fairies looked around and saw that on a branch to the south, there was only one peach that was half red and half white. The green-robed fairy pulled down the branch with her hand, and the red-robed fairy picked the peach. However, she threw the branch up carelessly. It turned out that the Great Sage was disguised as that branch, and he was awakened by the noise. The Great Sage immediately returned to his original form. He pulled out his golden cudgel from his ear, brandished it, and said in a booming voice, "Who are you, monster, to dare steal my peaches!"

The seven fairies were terrified and immediately knelt down, saying, "Great Sage, please forgive us. We are not monsters, but the seven fairies summoned by the Queen Mother. We came to pick the peaches to hold the grand banquet in the Treasure Pavilion. We saw the land deities and the officials here, but couldn't find the Great Sage. Afraid of delaying the Queen Mother's orders, we picked the peaches without waiting. We beg your forgiveness."

Hearing their explanation, the Great Sage calmed down and said with a smile, "Get up, fairies. Who is invited to the banquet hosted by the Queen Mother?" The fairies replied, "The usual guests are invited." The Great Sage said, "Well then, invite me, old Sun. Why not?"

The fairies said, "We haven't heard of that." The Great Sage said, "I am the Great Sage, Equal of Heaven. Why can't I, old Sun, be invited to this feast?" The fairies replied, "This is the rule for the banquet. We don't know how to proceed now."

The Great Sage said, "I understand. No wonder you're confused. Go and confirm the situation for me. See if it's possible to invite old Sun."

Soon, there were hardly any people left in the entire house: Burdovsky had gone to Ippolit, Keller and Lebedev had gone somewhere else. Only Vera Lebedeva remained for some time in the rooms, quickly changing them from festive to ordinary. Leaving, she peeked into the prince's room. He was sitting at the table, leaning on it with both elbows and covering his head with his hands. She quietly approached him and touched his shoulder; the prince, in bewilderment, looked at her and for almost a minute seemed to be remembering something; but having remembered and understood everything, he suddenly became extremely agitated. Everything, however, was resolved with an extraordinary and passionate request to Vera to knock on his door tomorrow morning, at seven o'clock, with the first carriage. Vera promised; the prince began to implore her, with fervor, not to tell anyone about this; she promised this too, and finally, when she was already about to open the door to leave, the prince stopped her for the third time, took her hands, kissed them, then kissed her on the forehead and, with some “unusual” expression, said to her: “Until tomorrow!” This is at least how Vera later recounted it. She left in great fear for him.

The next morning, she felt a little better when, at eight o'clock, as agreed, she knocked on his door and informed him that the carriage to Petersburg would leave in a quarter of an hour; it seemed to her that he opened the door to her quite refreshed, and even with a smile. In his opinion, he could have returned that very day. It turned out, therefore, that he had found it necessary to tell only her, at this particular moment, that he was leaving for the city.

Approaching the intersection of Gorokhovaya and Sadovaya, he himself was surprised by his extraordinary agitation; he hadn't expected his heart to beat with such pain. One house, probably due to its particular physiognomy, had already begun to attract his attention from afar, and the prince remembered thinking to himself: "This is, surely, the very house." With extraordinary curiosity, he approached to verify his guess; he felt that he would be particularly unhappy if he was right. The house was large, gloomy, three stories high, without any architecture, its color a dirty green. Some, very few, of these houses of this type, built at the end of the last century, had survived precisely in these streets of Petersburg (where everything changes so quickly) almost unchanged. They were built solidly, with thick walls and extremely rare windows; the windows on the lower floor sometimes had grates. Mostly, a money-changer's shop occupied the ground floor. The money-changer, sitting in the shop, rented rooms upstairs. Both outside and inside, there was something inhospitable and arid, everything seemed to be hiding and concealed, and why it seemed so, it was difficult to explain. Architectural combinations of lines, of course, have their own secret. Almost exclusively merchants lived in these houses. Approaching the gates and glancing at the inscription, the prince read: "House of the hereditary honorary citizen Rogin."

Yesterday, meeting you, I came home and conceived one painting. Painters depict Christ according to the Gospels; I would paint him differently: I would show him alone—the disciples sometimes left him alone. I would leave only a small child with him. The child played beside him; perhaps he was telling him something in his childish language, Christ listened, but now fell into thought; his hand involuntarily, forgetfully remained on the child's light head. He looks into the distance, to the horizon; a thought, vast as the whole world, rests in his gaze; his face is sad. The child fell silent, leaned on his knees and, propping his cheek with his hand, lifted his head and gazed at him with thoughtfulness, as children sometimes do. The sun is setting... This is my painting! You are innocent, and in your innocence lies your perfection. Oh, remember only this! What business is it of yours with my passion for you? You are mine now, I will be with you for life... I shall die soon.

The guests returned along the same unpleasant road to the house. Nozdryov led them to his study, though it bore no resemblance to any ordinary study, containing no books or papers; only swords and two guns—one worth three hundred, the other eight hundred rubles hung on the walls. The son-in-law, after inspecting the room, merely shook his head. Next, Nozdryov presented Turkish daggers, one of which was mistakenly engraved: "Master Saveliy Sibiryakov." Then came the music box, which Nozdryov promptly wound up for them. It played agreeably, but in the middle of the piece something seemed to happen, for the mazurka ended with the song "Malbrue went on campaign," and "Malbrue went on campaign" unexpectedly concluded with some long-familiar waltz. Nozdryov had long since stopped winding, but one of the pipes in the music box was particularly lively, refusing to be quiet, and it whistled insistently for a long time afterward. Next, he brought out pipes—wooden, clay, foam, smoked and unsmoked, covered in leather and uncovered, a pipe with a amber mouthpiece recently won, a tobacco pouch embroidered by some countess at a postal station who had fallen head over heels in love with him, whose handles, according to him, were the most subditively superflous—a word that probably meant the highest point of perfection in his vocabulary. After nibbling on some dried fish, they sat down to the table at about five o'clock.  It was evident that a good meal was not the main thing in Nozdryov's life; the dishes were not particularly noteworthy: some were burnt, some were not cooked at all. It seemed that the cook was guided more by inspiration than anything else, simply placing whatever was at hand: if pepper was near, he sprinkled pepper, if cabbage was available, he added cabbage, he tossed in milk, ham, peas—in short, a haphazard medley, as long as it was hot, and the taste, well, that wasn't really the point. 

Nozdryov, however, went to town on the wine: even before the soup was served, he poured his guests each a large glass of port and another glass of a "different" sort, because in provincial and county towns, there was no such thing as plain sherry. Nozdryov ordered a bottle of Madeira, the best of which, he claimed, not even the field marshal himself had tasted. The Madeira was, indeed, almost fiery, because the merchants, knowing the taste of landed gentry who favored good Madeira, generously spiced it with rum, and sometimes even added a bit of vodka to it, confident that Russian stomachs could withstand it all. Then Nozdryov ordered another special bottle, which he said was both Burgundy and Champagne. He poured with great enthusiasm into both glasses, to the son-in-law and Chikchov; Chikchov noticed, however, that Nozdryov himself poured very little for himself. This prompted him to be cautious, and as soon as Nozdryov started to chat or pour wine for his son-in-law, he immediately tipped his glass into the plate. 

After a short while, they brought to the table some rowanberry wine, which, according to Nozdryov, had a perfect cream taste, but in which, to everyone’s surprise, the aroma of eau-de-vie was strongly present. Then they drank some kind of balm, the name of which was so difficult to remember that even the host himself called it something else the next time. The meal was long over, and the wines had been thoroughly tasted, but the guests still sat at the table. Chikchov couldn't bring himself to talk to Nozdryov about the main subject in front of his son-in-law. After all, the son-in-law was a stranger, and the matter required a private and friendly conversation. However, the son-in-law was hardly likely to be dangerous, as he seemed to have had more than enough to drink and, sitting on his chair, was constantly dozing off.  Noticing this himself, he finally tried to excuse himself and go home, but with such a lethargic and listless voice, as if, in a Russian expression, he was putting the bridle on a horse with tongs.

Then came the pipes—wooden, clay, foamy, smoked and un-smoked, covered in leather and uncovered, a fez with a jet mouthpiece, recently won, a cigarette case embroidered by some countess somewhere at a post station who had fallen head over heels in love with him, whose, according to him, handles were the most “subdily superfluous”—a word that probably signified the highest point of perfection for him. Having snacked on balyk, they sat down to the table around five o'clock. The dinner, as it seemed, was not the most important thing in Nozdryov’s life; the dishes did not play a significant role: some things were burned, some things were not cooked at all. It was clear that the cook was guided more by some inspiration and put down whatever came to hand: if there was pepper near him, he sprinkled pepper, if there was cabbage, he shoved cabbage in, he added milk, ham, peas—in short, just stir it up, as long as it was hot, and the taste would work out somehow. But Nozdryov poured on the wine: before the soup was even served, he had already poured each guest a large glass of port and another type of fortified wine, because in provincial and district towns they don't have just plain sherry. Therefore, Nozdryov ordered a bottle of Madeira, which he claimed was better than even the field marshal drank. The Madeira, indeed, even burned in the mouth, because merchants, knowing the taste of landowners who loved good Madeira, watered it mercilessly with rum, and sometimes even poured in some vodka, hoping that Russian stomachs would withstand it all. Then Nozdryov ordered another special bottle, which, according to him, was both Burgundy and Champagne at the same time. He poured very diligently into both glasses, both to the right and left, both to the son-in-law and to Chichikov; Chichikov, however, noticed, somehow in passing, that he didn’t pour much for himself. This made him cautious, and as soon as Nozdryov started talking or pouring for his son-in-law, he immediately tipped his glass into the plate. After a short time, raspberry liqueur was brought to the table, which, according to Nozdryov, had a perfect taste of cream, but in which, to everyone's astonishment, the taste of moonshine was felt in all its strength. Then they drank some kind of balm, which had a name so difficult to remember that even the owner called it by a different name another time. Dinner was long over, and the wines had been sampled, but the guests were still sitting at the table. Chichikov did not want to start talking to Nozdryov in front of his son-in-law about the main subject. After all, the son-in-law was an outsider, and the topic required a private and friendly conversation. However, the son-in-law was unlikely to be a dangerous person, because he seemed to have drunk enough and, sitting in his chair, was constantly nodding off. Noticing this himself, he finally tried to excuse himself and go home, but with such a sluggish and weak voice, as if, in the Russian way, he was slowly tightening the yoke on a horse.

— It's been five days since I've been to see her, — he continued, pausing for a moment. — I'm afraid she'll throw me out. "I'm still my own mistress," she says, "if I want to, I'll send you away completely, and I'll go abroad myself" (that's what she told me about going abroad, — he observed as if in parentheses, and looked at the prince's eyes particularly); sometimes, to be sure, she just teases me, she finds everything about me amusing for some reason. And sometimes she really does frown and scowl, not a word will she utter; that's what I'm afraid of. I thought: I'll start coming not with empty hands, — but that only made her laugh, and then she even got angry. I gave her maid Katya one of my shawls, which, though she had lived in luxury before, maybe she'd never even seen anything like it. But you can't even mention the matter of getting married. What groom is there, when he's even afraid to just visit? So here I sit, and when I can't stand it anymore, I sneak past her house in the street or hide around the corner. Once I almost stood in the light near her gates, — it seemed to me that she had seen something. And she, no doubt, peeped out the window: "What would you have done to me," she said, "if you had caught me cheating?" I couldn't hold back and said: "You know yourself."

But the man did not comply with the request, but kept his hands calmly in his pockets and laughed loudly. "See," he said to the girl, "I was right after all. The gentleman is not comfortable here, not in general." The girl smiled too, but lightly tapped the man's arm with her fingertips, as if he had taken a liberty with K. "But what do you think," the man said, still laughing, "I really do want to lead the gentleman out." "Then that's good," said the girl, tilting her delicate head for a moment. "Don't give too much importance to laughter," the girl said to K., who, having become sad again, stared ahead and seemed to need no explanation, "this gentleman—may I introduce him?" (The gentleman gave permission with a hand gesture) "this gentleman, then, is the Information Provider. He gives all the parties waiting here the information they need, and since our judicial system is not very well-known among the populace, many inquiries are made. He knows the answer to every question, you can try him out if you ever feel like it. But that is not his only advantage, his second advantage is his elegant clothing. We, that is, the civil servants, once thought that since the Information Provider is always the first to deal with parties, for the sake of a dignified first impression, he should also be dressed elegantly. We others, as you can see for yourself, are unfortunately poorly and old-fashionedly dressed; it doesn't make much sense to spend anything on clothes, since we are practically constantly in the offices, and we even sleep here. But, as I said, we thought beautiful clothes were necessary for the Information Provider. Since our administration, which is somewhat peculiar in this regard, could not provide them, we made a collection—parties also contributed—and we bought him this beautiful suit and others. Everything would have been ready to make a good impression, but his laughter spoils it again and frightens people." "That's how it is," said the gentleman sarcastically, "but I don't understand, Miss, why you tell the gentleman all our intimacies or rather, impose them on him, since he doesn't want to know them. Just look at him, apparently preoccupied with his own affairs, sitting there." K. did not even feel like contradicting, the girl's intention may have been a good one, she might have wanted to distract him or give him a chance to gather himself, but the means were misplaced. "I had to explain his laughter to him," the girl said. "It was insulting." "I believe he would forgive even more insulting things if I finally lead him out." K. said nothing, he didn't even look up, he tolerated that the two were discussing him as if he were a thing, it was even more agreeable to him. But suddenly he felt the Information Provider's hand on one arm and the girl's hand on the other. "Come on, you weakling," said the Information Provider. "I thank you both very much," said K., pleasantly surprised, he slowly rose and led the strange hands to the places where he needed support most. "It looks like," the girl whispered in K.'s ear as they moved towards the corridor, "as if I were particularly interested in presenting the Information Provider in a good light, but you may believe it, I really want to tell the truth. He has no hard heart. He is not obliged to lead sick parties out, and yet he does, as you see. Perhaps none of us are heartless, we may all have wanted to help, but as judicial officials we easily get the impression that we are heartless and want to help no one. I suffer from it myself." "Would you like to sit here for a bit?" asked the Information Provider, they were already in the corridor and right in front of the man K. had spoken to earlier. K. was almost ashamed in front of him, he had stood so upright in front of him before, now he had to be supported by two, his hat was balanced by the Information Provider on his spread fingers, his hair was disheveled, his hair hung in his sweat-soaked forehead. But the man seemed to notice none of this, he stood humbly in front of the Information Provider, who looked past him, only seeking to apologize for his presence. "I know," he said, "that the handling of my requests cannot be done today. But I came anyway, I thought I could wait here, it's Sunday, I have time and I'm not disturbing anyone here." "You don't need to apologize so much," said the Information Provider, "Your diligence is quite commendable, you are taking up space unnecessarily here, but I don't want to prevent you from following the progress of your case closely, as long as it doesn't inconvenience me. When one has seen people who shamelessly neglect their duty, one learns to be patient with people like you. Sit down." "How he knows how to talk to parties," the girl whispered. K. nodded, but immediately stood up again when the Information Provider asked him: "Would you like to sit down here?" "No," said K., "I don't want to rest." He had said that with the utmost certainty, in reality, it would have done him a lot of good to sit down. He felt like he was seasick. He felt like he was on a ship in rough seas. It felt like water was crashing against the wooden walls, like a roar was coming from the depths of the corridor, like from breaking water, like the corridor was tilting sideways, and like the waiting parties were sinking and rising on either side. All the more incomprehensible was the calmness of the girl and the man who were leading him. He was at their mercy, if they let him go, he would fall like a plank. From their small eyes, sharp glances darted back and forth, their even steps K. felt, without joining them, for he was almost carried from step to step. Finally, he realized that they were speaking to him, but he didn't understand them, he only heard the noise that filled everything and through which a constant, high-pitched tone, like a siren, seemed to sound. "Louder," he whispered with his head bowed, ashamed, because he knew they had spoken loudly enough, although incomprehensible to him. Then finally, as if the wall in front of him had been ripped open, a fresh breeze blew towards him, and he heard someone say beside him: "First he wants to go, then you can tell him a hundred times that this is the exit, and he doesn't move." K. realized that he was standing in front of the exit door, which the girl had opened. He felt as if all his strength had suddenly returned, to get a taste of freedom, he stepped onto a step and said goodbye from there to his companions, who bent down to him. "Thank you very much," he repeated, pressed their hands repeatedly, and only let go when he saw that they, accustomed to the office air, were struggling with the relatively fresh air that was coming from the stairs. They could barely answer, and the girl would have probably stumbled, if K. hadn't quickly closed the door. K. stood still for a moment, smoothed his hair with the help of a pocket mirror, picked up his hat, which was lying on the next step—the Information Provider had probably thrown it there—and then ran down the stairs, so fresh and in such long leaps that he was almost scared by this turnaround. Such surprises had never been caused to him by his otherwise very solid health. Did his body want to revolutionize and prepare him for a new process, since he endured the old one so effortlessly? He did not entirely reject the thought of going to a doctor soon, but at least he could decide that for himself—he wanted to spend all future Sunday mornings better than this one.

The prince stood utterly crushed; they said afterward that he had “turned deathly pale”; indeed, his legs seemed to be giving way. Finally, through the terrible din of voices, he made out that they were deciding to act together with him and asked him for his address in the city. He had no address; they advised him to stay at a hotel. The prince thought for a moment and gave the address of his old hotel, the very same one where he had had his fit five weeks earlier. Then he set off again for Rogozhin’s.
